chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter I
paragraphs: "Well, Prince, so Genoa and Lucca are now just family estates of the Bonapartes. But I'm warning you — if you don't tell me this means war, if you keep trying to defend the atrocities committed by that Antichrist — and I truly believe he is the Antichrist — then I'm done with you. You're no longer my friend, no longer my 'faithful slave,' as you like to call yourself! But how are you? I can see I've frightened you — sit down and tell me everything." [speaking in French]

It was July 1805, and the speaker was the well-known Anna Pavlovna Scherer, lady-in-waiting and favorite of the Empress Maria Fedorovna. These were the words with which she greeted Prince Vasili Kuragin, a man of high rank and influence, who was the first to arrive at her reception. Anna Pavlovna had been coughing for several days. She was suffering from what she called la grippe — "the flu" being a fashionable new word in St. Petersburg at the time, used only by the elite.
Every one of her invitations, without exception written in French and delivered that morning by a footman in scarlet livery, read as follows:

"If you have nothing better to do, Count (or Prince), and if the prospect of spending an evening with a poor invalid doesn't seem too terrible, I would be delighted to see you tonight between seven and ten. — Annette Scherer."

"Good heavens, what a fierce attack!" replied the prince, not the least bit thrown by this greeting. He had just walked in wearing an embroidered court uniform with knee breeches and buckled shoes, decorations gleaming on his chest and a calm expression on his broad, flat face. He spoke in that polished French in which our grandparents not only conversed but actually thought, with the gentle, patronizing tone that comes naturally to a man of importance who has spent a lifetime in high society and at court. He approached Anna Pavlovna, kissed her hand — offering her a view of his bald, perfumed, gleaming head — and settled comfortably into the sofa.

"First of all, dear friend, tell me how you're feeling. Put your friend's mind at ease," he said, his tone unchanged — beneath the politeness and show of concern, one could detect indifference and even irony.
"How can anyone be well when they're suffering morally? How can anyone be calm in times like these, if they have any feeling at all?" said Anna Pavlovna. "You'll stay the whole evening, I hope?"
"There's the party at the English ambassador's. Today is Wednesday. I really must make an appearance," said the prince. "My daughter is coming to pick me up."
"I thought today's party had been canceled. I must say, all these celebrations and fireworks are getting tiresome."

"If they had known you wanted it canceled, the entertainment would have been called off," said the prince — who, like a wound-up clock, said things out of habit that he didn't even expect anyone to believe.
"Oh, stop teasing! So, what's been decided about the Novosiltsev dispatch? You know everything."
"What is there to say?" the prince replied in a cold, bored tone. "What's been decided? They've decided that Bonaparte has burned his bridges, and I believe we're about to burn ours."

Prince Vasili always spoke in a languid way, like an actor going through the motions of a stale role. Anna Pavlovna, on the other hand, despite being forty, brimmed with energy and passion. Being an enthusiast had become her social calling, and sometimes, even when she didn't feel like it, she would work herself into a state of excitement just to meet the expectations of people who knew her. The faint smile that always played around her lips — though it didn't quite suit her aging features — expressed, like a spoiled child's, a constant awareness of her charming flaw, which she neither wished to correct, nor could, nor saw any reason to.
In the middle of a conversation about politics, Anna Pavlovna burst out:

"Oh, don't talk to me about Austria! Maybe I don't understand these things, but Austria has never wanted war and doesn't want it now. She's betraying us! Russia alone must save Europe. Our gracious sovereign understands his sacred calling and will stay true to it. That is the one thing I believe in! Our wonderful, noble emperor must fulfill the greatest role on earth, and he is so virtuous and good that God will not abandon him. He will fulfill his destiny and crush the monster of revolution, which has grown more terrible than ever in the person of this murderer and villain! We alone must avenge the blood of the righteous... Who else can we count on? England, with her merchant's soul, cannot and will not understand Emperor Alexander's nobility of spirit. She has refused to give up Malta. She keeps looking for some hidden agenda behind everything we do. What answer did Novosiltsev receive? None. The English haven't understood — and can't understand — our Emperor's selflessness, his desire for nothing but the good of humanity. And what have they promised? Nothing! And the little they have promised, they won't deliver! Prussia keeps saying Bonaparte is invincible, that all of Europe is powerless against him... And I don't believe a word from Hardenberg or Haugwitz. This famous Prussian neutrality is just a trap. I believe only in God and in the great destiny of our beloved sovereign. He will save Europe!"
She stopped suddenly, smiling at her own outburst.

"I think," said the prince with a smile, "that if they had sent you instead of our dear Wintzingerode, you would have won the King of Prussia's agreement by sheer force. You're so eloquent. Will you give me a cup of tea?"

"In a moment. By the way," she added, calming down, "I'm expecting two very interesting men tonight: the Vicomte de Mortemart, who is connected to the Montmorencys through the Rohans — one of the finest French families. He's one of the true émigrés, the good kind. And also the Abbé Morio. Do you know that profound thinker? He's been received by the Emperor. Had you heard?"

"I'll be delighted to meet them," said the prince. "But tell me," he added with studied casualness, as if the thought had only just occurred to him — though in fact this question was the real reason for his visit — "is it true that the Dowager Empress wants Baron Funke appointed as first secretary in Vienna? The baron, by all accounts, is a rather poor specimen."
Prince Vasili wanted to secure this post for his own son, but others were working through the Dowager Empress Maria Fedorovna to get it for the baron.
Anna Pavlovna nearly closed her eyes, as if to say that neither she nor anyone else had the right to question what the Empress desired.
"Baron Funke was recommended to the Dowager Empress by her sister," was all she said, in a dry, somber tone.

At the mention of the Empress, Anna Pavlovna's face instantly took on an expression of deep, sincere devotion and respect, mixed with sadness — as it did every time she spoke of her illustrious patroness. She added that Her Majesty had been pleased to show Baron Funke a great deal of esteem, and once again her face clouded with sorrow.

The prince was silent and appeared indifferent. But with the womanly and courtier-like quickness that was second nature to her, Anna Pavlovna managed both to rebuke him — for daring to speak that way about a man the Empress had endorsed — and to console him at the same time, so she said:
"Now, about your family. Did you know that since your daughter made her debut in society, everyone has been raving about her? They say she's stunningly beautiful."
The prince bowed to show his appreciation.

"I often think," she continued after a brief pause, moving closer to the prince and smiling warmly, as if to signal that political talk was over and it was time for more personal conversation — "I often think about how unfairly life's joys are distributed. Why has fate given you two such wonderful children? I'm not counting Anatole, your youngest — I don't care for him," she added in a tone that allowed no argument, raising her eyebrows. "Two such charming children. And you appreciate them less than anyone, which means you don't deserve them."
She flashed her rapturous smile.
"I can't help it," said the prince. "Lavater would have said I lack the bump of fatherly affection."

"Don't joke — I want to have a serious talk with you. You know, I'm not happy with your younger son. Between us" — and her face took on its melancholy look — "he was discussed at Her Majesty's court, and people pitied you..."
The prince said nothing, but she looked at him pointedly, waiting for a response. He frowned.

"What do you want me to do?" he said finally. "You know I did everything a father could for their education, and both of them turned out to be fools. Hippolyte is at least a quiet fool, but Anatole is a loud one. That's the only difference between them." He said this with a smile more natural and lively than usual, and the wrinkles around his mouth revealed something unexpectedly coarse and unpleasant.
"And why do men like you even have children? If you weren't a father, I'd have nothing to reproach you for," said Anna Pavlovna, gazing upward thoughtfully.
"I am your faithful slave, and only to you can I confess that my children are the curse of my life. It's my cross to bear. That's how I make sense of it. There's nothing to be done!"
He said no more, but conveyed his resignation to cruel fate with a gesture. Anna Pavlovna thought for a moment.

"Have you ever considered marrying off your wayward son Anatole?" she asked. "They say old maids have a mania for matchmaking, and although I haven't developed that weakness yet, I do know a young woman who is very unhappy living with her father. She's a relative of yours — Princess Marya Bolkonskaya."
Prince Vasili didn't reply, but with the quick memory and sharp instincts of a man of the world, he tilted his head to show he was considering the idea.

"You know," he said at last, clearly unable to pull himself away from the gloomy track of his thoughts, "Anatole costs me forty thousand rubles a year? And," he added after a pause, "what will it be in five years if he keeps this up?" Then he said: "That's what we fathers have to endure... Is this princess of yours wealthy?"

"Her father is very rich and very stingy. He lives in the country. He's the well-known Prince Bolkonsky who was forced to retire from the army under the late Emperor and was nicknamed 'the King of Prussia.' He's very clever but eccentric, and a bore. The poor girl is miserable. She has a brother — I think you know him — he recently married Lise Meinen. He's one of Kutuzov's aides-de-camp and will be here tonight."

"Listen, dear Annette," said the prince, suddenly taking Anna Pavlovna's hand and for some reason pressing it downward. "Arrange this for me, and I will be your most devoted slave — slafe with an 'f,' as one of my village elders spells it in his reports. She's rich, she's from a good family — that's all I need."

And with the easy, familiar grace that was so characteristic of him, he lifted the lady-in-waiting's hand to his lips, kissed it, then swung it playfully back and forth as he lounged in his armchair, gazing off in another direction.

"Wait," said Anna Pavlovna, thinking it over. "I'll speak to Lise — young Bolkonsky's wife — this very evening, and perhaps we can arrange it. I'll begin my career as a matchmaker on your family's behalf."

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter II
paragraphs: Anna Pavlovna's drawing room was gradually filling up. The cream of Petersburg society had gathered — people of widely different ages and temperaments, but all belonging to the same social circle. Prince Vasili's daughter, the beautiful Helene, had come to collect her father for the ambassador's party; she wore a ball gown and her lady-in-waiting badge. The young Princess Bolkonskaya, known as the most captivating woman in Petersburg, was also there. She had married the previous winter, and being pregnant, she avoided large social events and attended only small receptions like this one. Prince Vasili's son Hippolyte had arrived with Mortemart, whom he introduced. The Abbe Morio and many others had come as well.
* The most captivating woman in Petersburg.

To each new arrival, Anna Pavlovna said, "You haven't met my aunt yet," or "You don't know my aunt?" and with great solemnity led each guest over to a small elderly woman wearing large ribbon bows on her cap, who had sailed in from another room as soon as guests began to arrive. Turning her gaze slowly from the visitor to her aunt, Anna Pavlovna announced each person's name and then moved on.

Every visitor went through the ritual of greeting this old aunt whom none of them knew, none of them wanted to know, and none of them cared about. Anna Pavlovna watched these introductions with mournful, solemn interest and silent approval. The aunt said the same thing to each of them — asking about their health and her own, and about Her Majesty's health, which, thank God, was better today. Each visitor, too polite to show impatience, left the old woman with a sense of relief at having completed an irritating obligation and did not return to her for the rest of the evening.

The young Princess Bolkonskaya had brought some needlework in a gold-embroidered velvet bag. Her pretty little upper lip, on which a faint dark down was just visible, was slightly too short for her teeth, but this only made it lift more sweetly — and it was especially charming when she occasionally drew it down to meet her lower lip. As is always the case with truly attractive women, her imperfection — the short upper lip and half-open mouth — seemed to be her own unique form of beauty. Everyone brightened at the sight of this pretty young woman, so soon to become a mother, so full of life and health, and carrying her burden so lightly. Old men and dull, dispirited young ones who spent time in her company felt as though they too were becoming, like her, full of life and energy. Everyone who spoke to her, catching her bright smile and the constant gleam of her white teeth, felt they were in an especially good mood that day.

The little princess circled the table with quick, short, swaying steps, her workbag on her arm, and cheerfully smoothing out her dress, she sat down on a sofa near the silver samovar as if everything she did was a delight both to herself and to everyone around her. "I've brought my needlework," she said in French, showing off her bag and addressing the whole room. "And Annette, I hope you haven't played a trick on me," she added, turning to her hostess. "You wrote that it would be a small gathering, and look how badly I'm dressed." She spread her arms to display her short-waisted, lace-trimmed gray dress, cinched with a broad ribbon just below the bust.
"Don't worry, Lise, you will always be prettier than anyone else," Anna Pavlovna replied.

"You know," said the princess in the same voice, still in French, turning to a general, "my husband is abandoning me. He's going off to get himself killed. Tell me, what is this wretched war even for?" she added, addressing Prince Vasili, and without waiting for an answer she turned to speak to his daughter, the beautiful Helene.
"What a delightful woman that little princess is!" Prince Vasili said to Anna Pavlovna.

One of the next guests to arrive was a heavyset young man with closely cropped hair, spectacles, the light-colored breeches fashionable at the time, a very high collar, and a brown dress coat. This stout young man was the illegitimate son of Count Bezukhov, a famous grandee from Catherine the Great's era who was now on his deathbed in Moscow. The young man had not yet entered military or civil service, having only recently returned from being educated abroad, and this was his first appearance in society. Anna Pavlovna greeted him with the minimal nod she reserved for the lowest-ranking guests in her drawing room. But despite this chilly welcome, a look of anxiety and alarm — as if at the sight of something too large and out of place — crossed her face when she saw Pierre enter. He was certainly bigger than the other men in the room, but her unease could only have been about the clever yet shy, observant and unaffected expression that set him apart from everyone else there.
"How good of you, Monsieur Pierre, to come visit a poor invalid," said Anna Pavlovna, exchanging a worried glance with her aunt as she led him over.

Pierre mumbled something unintelligible and kept looking around the room as if searching for something. On his way to the aunt, he smiled warmly at the little princess, greeting her like an old friend.

Anna Pavlovna's concern proved justified — Pierre walked away from the aunt before she had finished her speech about Her Majesty's health. Anna Pavlovna seized him in alarm: "Do you know the Abbe Morio? He's a most fascinating man."
"Yes, I've heard about his scheme for perpetual peace. It's very interesting but hardly practical."

"You think so?" said Anna Pavlovna, just trying to say something so she could escape to attend to her hostess duties. But Pierre now committed the reverse offense. First he had left a lady before she finished talking to him; now he kept talking to one who wanted to get away. Head bent, feet planted wide apart, he launched into his reasons for thinking the abbe's plan was unrealistic.
"We'll discuss it later," said Anna Pavlovna with a smile.

Having freed herself from this young man who had no idea how to behave in society, she resumed her duties as hostess, keeping watch over everything, ready to step in wherever conversation flagged. Like the foreman of a spinning mill who, after setting all the machines going, walks around checking for a stopped spindle here or a squeaking one there, and hurries to adjust or restart the machinery — so Anna Pavlovna moved through her drawing room, approaching a silent group here, a too-loud one there, and with a word or slight rearrangement kept the conversational engine running smoothly. But through it all, her anxiety about Pierre was obvious. She kept a nervous eye on him as he drifted toward the group around Mortemart to listen in, and again when he moved on to another group centered on the abbe.

Pierre had been educated abroad, and this reception was the first he had attended in Russia. He knew that all the intellectual stars of Petersburg had gathered here, and like a child in a toy shop, he didn't know where to look first, afraid of missing some brilliant conversation. Seeing the self-assured, polished expressions on every face, he kept expecting to hear something deeply profound. At last he made his way to Morio. Here the conversation seemed interesting, and he stood waiting for a chance to share his own views, as young people are so eager to do.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter III
paragraphs: Anna Pavlovna's reception was in full swing. The conversational spindles hummed steadily on all sides. Apart from the aunt, beside whom sat only one elderly lady who looked rather out of place in this glittering company with her thin, careworn face, the whole gathering had arranged itself into three groups. One, mostly male, had formed around the abbe. Another, consisting of younger people, was clustered around the beautiful Princess Helene — Prince Vasili's daughter — and the little Princess Bolkonskaya, very pretty and rosy, though a touch too plump for her age. The third group was gathered around Mortemart and Anna Pavlovna.

The vicomte was a pleasant-looking young man with soft features and polished manners who clearly considered himself a celebrity, but out of politeness modestly placed himself at the circle's disposal. Anna Pavlovna was obviously presenting him as a special treat for her guests. Just as a skilled chef serves up a piece of meat as a rare delicacy that no one who had seen it in the kitchen would have wanted to eat, Anna Pavlovna served up first the vicomte and then the abbe as particularly choice morsels. The group around Mortemart immediately began discussing the execution of the Duc d'Enghien. The vicomte explained that the Duc d'Enghien had died because of his own noble nature, and that there were specific reasons for Bonaparte's hatred of him.
"Oh yes! Tell us all about it, Vicomte," said Anna Pavlovna with a satisfied feeling that the phrase had a certain Louis XV elegance to it.
The vicomte bowed and smiled graciously, signaling his willingness. Anna Pavlovna arranged a group around him and invited everyone to listen to his story.

"The vicomte knew the duke personally," Anna Pavlovna whispered to one guest. "The vicomte is a wonderful storyteller," she said to another. "You can tell he belongs to the very best society," she told a third. And so the vicomte was presented to the company in the most flattering light possible, like a beautifully garnished roast on a silver platter.
The vicomte was about to begin his story and gave a subtle smile.
"Come over here, Helene dear," said Anna Pavlovna to the beautiful young princess, who was sitting some distance away at the center of another group.

The princess smiled. She rose with the same unchanging smile she had worn since entering the room — the smile of a woman who knows she is perfectly beautiful. With a slight rustle of her white dress trimmed with moss and ivy, a gleam of white shoulders, glossy hair, and sparkling diamonds, she passed between the men who stepped aside for her, looking at none of them yet smiling at all, as if graciously allowing each one the privilege of admiring her lovely figure and shapely shoulders, back, and bosom — which, as was the fashion, were very much on display. She seemed to bring the glamour of a ballroom with her. Helene was so beautiful that she showed not a trace of flirtation — on the contrary, she even seemed embarrassed by her overwhelming and irresistible beauty. She appeared to want to diminish its effect, but couldn't.

"How lovely!" said everyone who saw her; and the vicomte raised his shoulders and dropped his eyes, as if startled by something extraordinary, when she took her seat across from him and turned her unchanging smile on him as well.
"Madame, I doubt my abilities before such an audience," he said with a smile, inclining his head.

The princess rested her bare, round arm on a small table and didn't bother replying. She waited with a smile. Throughout the story she sat upright, glancing now at her beautiful round arm — its shape slightly altered where it pressed against the table — and now at her even more beautiful bosom, where she adjusted a diamond necklace. From time to time she smoothed the folds of her dress, and whenever the story produced an effect, she would glance at Anna Pavlovna, immediately copy the expression on the lady-in-waiting's face, and then settle back into her radiant smile.
The little princess had also left the tea table and followed Helene over.
"Wait a moment, let me get my needlework... Now then, what are you thinking about?" she said, turning to Prince Hippolyte. "Bring me my workbag."
There was a general stir as the princess, smiling and chattering merrily to everyone at once, sat down and cheerfully arranged herself in her seat.
"There, now I'm all set," she said, and asking the vicomte to begin, she took up her work.
Prince Hippolyte, having fetched the workbag, pulled up a chair next to hers and sat down.

The charming Hippolyte was remarkable for his extraordinary resemblance to his beautiful sister, but even more so because — despite this resemblance — he was strikingly ugly. His features were like hers, but while everything in her face was illuminated by a joyful, self-assured, youthful, and constantly animated smile, and by the classical beauty of her figure, his face was dulled by a look of imbecility and a fixed expression of sulky self-importance, and his body was thin and weak. His eyes, nose, and mouth all seemed squeezed into a vacant, weary grimace, and his arms and legs were always falling into unnatural positions.
"This isn't going to be a ghost story, is it?" he said, sitting down beside the princess and hastily adjusting his lorgnette, as if he couldn't begin speaking without this instrument.
"Why, no, my dear fellow," said the surprised narrator with a shrug.
"Because I hate ghost stories," said Prince Hippolyte, in a tone suggesting he only grasped the meaning of his own words after they left his mouth.

He spoke with such self-assurance that his listeners couldn't tell whether what he said was very clever or very stupid. He wore a dark green coat, breeches in a shade he called cuisse de nymphe effrayée — "frightened nymph's thigh" — along with shoes and silk stockings.

The vicomte told his story very neatly. It was an anecdote, then making the rounds, about the Duc d'Enghien having gone secretly to Paris to visit the actress Mademoiselle George; at her house he had encountered Bonaparte, who also enjoyed the famous actress's favors, and in the duke's presence, Napoleon had one of his notorious fainting fits, leaving him at the duke's mercy. The duke had spared his life, and this act of generosity Bonaparte later repaid with a death sentence.
The story was very pretty and engaging, especially the moment when the two rivals suddenly recognized each other; the ladies looked quite stirred.
"Charming!" said Anna Pavlovna, casting an inquiring look at the little princess.
"Charming!" whispered the little princess, poking her needle into her work as if to show that the story was so fascinating she couldn't possibly continue sewing.

The vicomte appreciated this silent praise and, smiling gratefully, prepared to go on — but just then Anna Pavlovna, who had been keeping an anxious eye on the young man who alarmed her so much, noticed that Pierre was talking too loudly and too heatedly with the abbe. She hurried to the rescue. Pierre had managed to start a conversation with the abbe about the balance of power, and the abbe, clearly intrigued by the young man's earnest naivety, was laying out his favorite theory. Both were talking and listening too eagerly and too naturally — which was exactly what Anna Pavlovna disapproved of.

"The means are... the balance of power in Europe and the rights of the people," the abbe was saying. "All it takes is for one powerful nation like Russia — however barbaric people may call her — to place herself selflessly at the head of an alliance dedicated to maintaining Europe's balance of power, and it would save the world!"
"But how do you achieve that balance?" Pierre was beginning to say.

At that moment Anna Pavlovna came up and, giving Pierre a stern look, asked the Italian how he was finding the Russian climate. The Italian's face instantly changed, taking on an offensively sugary expression that was clearly his habit when talking to women.

"I am so enchanted by the brilliance of the wit and culture in this society, especially its female members, in whose company I have had the honor of finding myself, that I haven't yet had time to think about the climate," he said.
Without letting either the abbe or Pierre escape, Anna Pavlovna brought them into the larger circle where she could keep a better eye on them.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter IV
paragraphs: Just then another visitor entered the drawing room: Prince Andrei Bolkonsky, the little princess's husband. He was a very handsome young man of medium height with sharp, well-defined features. Everything about him — from his weary, bored expression to his quiet, measured step — formed a striking contrast with his lively little wife. It was obvious that he not only knew everyone in the room but found them all so tiresome that it exhausted him to look at or listen to them. And of all the faces that bored him, none seemed to bore him as much as that of his pretty wife. He turned away from her with a grimace that spoiled his handsome face, kissed Anna Pavlovna's hand, and surveyed the room through narrowed eyes.
"You're going off to the war, Prince?" said Anna Pavlovna.
"General Kutuzov," said Bolkonsky, speaking French and stressing the last syllable of the general's name in the French manner, "has been kind enough to take me on as an aide-de-camp..."
"And Lise, your wife?"
"She'll go to the country."
"Aren't you ashamed to deprive us of your charming wife?"

"Andrei," said his wife, addressing her husband in the same flirtatious tone she used with other men, "the vicomte has been telling us the most wonderful story about Mademoiselle George and Bonaparte!"

Prince Andrei screwed up his eyes and turned away. Pierre, who had been watching Prince Andrei from the moment he entered with happy, affectionate eyes, now came over and took his arm. Before looking to see who it was, Prince Andrei frowned again, his face expressing annoyance at whoever was touching him — but when he saw Pierre's beaming face, he broke into an unexpectedly warm and genuine smile.
"Well, well! So you've made it into high society too?" he said to Pierre.
"I knew you'd be here," Pierre replied. "I'll come have supper with you. May I?" he added quietly, so as not to interrupt the vicomte's ongoing story.

"No, impossible!" said Prince Andrei, laughing and squeezing Pierre's hand to show that the question didn't even need asking. He was about to say more, but at that moment Prince Vasili and his daughter stood up to leave, and the two young men rose to let them pass.

"You must excuse me, dear Vicomte," said Prince Vasili to the Frenchman, holding him down by the sleeve in a friendly way to keep him from rising. "This wretched party at the ambassador's is dragging me away from your company. I'm so sorry to leave your delightful gathering," he added, turning to Anna Pavlovna.

His daughter, Princess Helene, passed between the chairs, lightly holding up the folds of her dress, the smile shining even more radiantly on her beautiful face. Pierre watched her with an expression of rapture, almost awe, as she went by.
"Very beautiful," said Prince Andrei.
"Very," agreed Pierre.

As he passed, Prince Vasili caught Pierre's hand and said to Anna Pavlovna: "Educate this bear for me! He's been staying at my house for a whole month and this is the first time I've seen him in society. Nothing does a young man more good than the company of clever women."

Anna Pavlovna smiled and promised to take Pierre under her wing. She knew his father was connected to Prince Vasili. The elderly lady who had been sitting with the old aunt got up hurriedly and caught Prince Vasili in the entrance hall. All the pretend interest she had been putting on had vanished from her kind, tear-worn face, which now showed only worry and fear.
"What about my son Boris, Prince?" she said, hurrying after him into the hall. "I can't stay in Petersburg any longer. Tell me, what news can I bring back to my poor boy?"

Although Prince Vasili listened reluctantly and somewhat rudely to the elderly lady, even showing signs of impatience, she gave him an ingratiating, pleading smile and grabbed his hand so he couldn't walk away.
"What would it cost you to put in a word to the Emperor? He'd be transferred to the Guards immediately," she said.

"Believe me, Princess, I'm ready to do everything I can," Prince Vasili replied, "but it's difficult for me to ask the Emperor. I'd suggest you try Rumyantsev through Prince Golitsyn. That would be the best approach."

The elderly lady was Princess Drubetskaya, from one of Russia's best families, but she was poor, and having been out of society for a long time, she had lost her old connections. She had come to Petersburg now solely to arrange a transfer to the Guards for her only son. It was specifically to see Prince Vasili that she had wangled an invitation to Anna Pavlovna's reception and had sat through the vicomte's story. Prince Vasili's words frightened her, and a bitter look darkened her once-handsome face — but only for a moment. Then she smiled again and gripped Prince Vasili's arm even tighter.

"Listen, Prince," she said. "I have never asked you for anything before and I never will again, and I have never reminded you of my father's friendship with you. But now I beg you, for God's sake, to do this for my son — and I will always think of you as my benefactor." She added quickly: "No, don't be angry — just promise me! I've already tried Golitsyn and he refused. Be the kind man you've always been," she pleaded, trying to smile even as tears filled her eyes.
"Papa, we'll be late," said Princess Helene, turning her beautiful head and glancing over her classically sculpted shoulder as she stood waiting by the door.

Influence in society, however, is a form of capital that must be spent carefully if it's to last. Prince Vasili understood this, and having realized long ago that if he helped everyone who asked, he'd soon have no favors left for himself, he had become sparing with his connections. But in Princess Drubetskaya's case, after her second appeal, he felt something close to a twinge of conscience. She had reminded him of something that was perfectly true: he owed his early career to her father. Besides, he could see from her manner that she was one of those women — usually mothers — who, once they've set their minds on something, won't stop until they get what they want, and are prepared to keep asking day after day, hour after hour, and even to make scenes if necessary. This last thought tipped the balance.

"My dear Anna Mikhaylovna," he said with his usual combination of familiarity and weariness, "it's practically impossible to do what you're asking. But to show you my devotion and how much I respect your father's memory, I'll do the impossible — your son will be transferred to the Guards. Here's my hand on it. Satisfied?"
"My dear benefactor! This is exactly what I expected — I knew how kind you are!" He turned to go.

"Wait — one more thing! Once he's transferred to the Guards..." she hesitated. "You're on good terms with Mikhail Illarionovich Kutuzov... Could you recommend Boris to him as an adjutant? Then I could finally rest easy, and then..."
Prince Vasili smiled.

"No, I won't promise that. You have no idea how Kutuzov has been besieged since his appointment as commander in chief. He told me himself that every woman in Moscow has conspired to foist their sons on him as adjutants."
"No, but promise me! I won't let you go! My dear benefactor..."
"Papa," said his beautiful daughter in the same tone as before, "we're going to be late."
"Well then — goodbye! You hear her?"
"So you'll speak to the Emperor tomorrow?"
"Certainly. But about Kutuzov, I can't promise anything."

"Do promise — promise, Vasili!" cried Anna Mikhaylovna as he left, wearing the smile of a coquettish girl — a smile that had probably come naturally to her once but now sat oddly on her careworn face.

She had clearly forgotten her age and was deploying every old feminine trick out of sheer habit. But the instant the prince was gone, her face snapped back to its former cold, artificial expression. She returned to the group where the vicomte was still talking and once again pretended to listen, waiting for the moment when it would be time to leave. Her mission was accomplished.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter V
paragraphs: "And what do you think of this latest farce — the coronation in Milan?" asked Anna Pavlovna. "And the comedy of the people of Genoa and Lucca coming to petition Monsieur Bonaparte, and Monsieur Bonaparte sitting on a throne and granting the wishes of nations? Priceless! It's enough to make your head spin! It's as if the whole world has gone mad."
Prince Andrei looked straight at Anna Pavlovna with a sardonic smile.

"'God gave it to me — let anyone who touches it beware!'" he said, quoting the phrase. "They say he was magnificent when he said that." He repeated the words in Italian: "'Dio mi l'ha dato. Guai a chi la tocchi!'"
* God has given it to me, let him who touches it beware!
"I hope this proves to be the last straw," Anna Pavlovna continued. "The monarchs of Europe will not be able to tolerate this man who threatens everything."

"The monarchs? I won't speak for Russia," said the vicomte, polite but despairing. "The monarchs, madame... What did they do for Louis XVII, for the Queen, or for Madame Elizabeth? Nothing!" He grew more animated. "And believe me, they are reaping the consequences of their betrayal of the Bourbon cause. The monarchs! They're actually sending ambassadors to congratulate the usurper."
He sighed disdainfully and shifted in his seat.

Prince Hippolyte, who had been staring at the vicomte through his lorgnette for some time, suddenly turned to face the little princess, asked for a needle, and began tracing the Conde coat of arms on the table. He explained it to her with the same gravity as if she had asked him to do it.
"Bar gules, engrailed gules and azure — House of Conde," he said. [speaking in French]
The princess listened with a smile.

"If Bonaparte stays on the throne of France for one more year," the vicomte continued, with the air of a man who knows his subject better than anyone and doesn't bother listening to others, following only his own train of thought, "things will have gone too far. Through intrigue, violence, exile, and executions, French society — I mean good French society — will be destroyed forever, and then..."
He shrugged and spread his hands. Pierre wanted to jump in — the conversation fascinated him — but Anna Pavlovna, who had been watching him, cut in first:

"Emperor Alexander," she said, with the sadness that always accompanied any mention of the imperial family, "has declared that he will let the French people choose their own form of government. And I believe that once they are free of the usurper, the entire nation will throw itself into the arms of its rightful king," she concluded, trying to be gracious to the royalist emigre.
"That seems doubtful," said Prince Andrei. "The Vicomte is quite right that things have already gone too far. I think it would be very hard to go back to the old order."
"From what I've heard," said Pierre, blushing as he broke into the conversation, "almost all the French aristocracy has already gone over to Bonaparte's side."
"That's what the Bonapartists say," the vicomte replied without looking at Pierre. "At the moment it's hard to know what French public opinion really is."
"Bonaparte himself has said so," remarked Prince Andrei with a sarcastic smile.
It was clear that he disliked the vicomte and was directing his barbs at him, though without looking his way.

"'I showed them the path to glory, but they would not follow it,'" Prince Andrei continued after a brief pause, quoting Napoleon's words. "'I opened my antechambers and they crowded in.' I don't know how justified he was in saying that."

"Not in the least," the vicomte replied. "After the duke's murder, even his most devoted admirers stopped seeing him as a hero. If some people," he added, turning to Anna Pavlovna, "ever did consider him a hero, then after the duke's murder there was one more martyr in heaven and one fewer hero on earth."

Before Anna Pavlovna and the others could smile their appreciation at this bon mot, Pierre barged into the conversation again, and though Anna Pavlovna was sure he'd say something inappropriate, she couldn't stop him.
"The execution of the Duc d'Enghien," Pierre declared, "was a political necessity, and it seems to me that Napoleon showed greatness of soul by not being afraid to take full responsibility for it."
"God! Dear God!" Anna Pavlovna whispered in horror.
"What's that, Monsieur Pierre? You think assassination shows greatness of soul?" said the little princess, smiling and pulling her needlework closer.
"Oh! Oh!" several voices exclaimed.
"Brilliant!" said Prince Hippolyte in English, slapping his knee.
The vicomte merely shrugged. Pierre looked solemnly at his audience over his spectacles and went on.

"I say this," he continued with a kind of desperation, "because the Bourbons fled from the Revolution and left the people in chaos, and Napoleon was the only one who understood the Revolution and brought it under control. So for the greater good, he couldn't hold back on account of a single life."
"Won't you come sit at the other table?" Anna Pavlovna suggested.
But Pierre pressed on, ignoring her completely.

"No," he cried, growing more and more passionate, "Napoleon is great because he rose above the Revolution, crushed its worst excesses, kept everything good about it — equality before the law, freedom of speech and the press — and that is the only reason he gained power."
"Yes, and if, having gained power, he had given it back to the rightful king instead of using it to commit murder, then I would call him a great man," the vicomte remarked.

"He couldn't do that. The people gave him power specifically so he would free them from the Bourbons, and because they recognized his greatness. The Revolution was a magnificent thing!" Pierre continued, his desperate, provocative declaration revealing both his extreme youth and his burning need to say everything on his mind.
"What? Revolution and regicide — a magnificent thing? Well, after that... But won't you please come to this other table?" Anna Pavlovna repeated.
"Rousseau's Social Contract," said the vicomte with a tolerant smile.
"I'm not talking about regicide. I'm talking about ideas."
"Yes — ideas of robbery, murder, and regicide," an ironic voice interjected.

"Those were extremes, certainly, but that's not the important part. What matters are the rights of man, freedom from prejudice, and equality of citizens — and all of these Napoleon has preserved in full."

"Liberty and equality," the vicomte said with contempt, as if finally deciding to show this young man how foolish his words were. "Grand phrases that have long been discredited. Who doesn't love liberty and equality? Even our Savior preached liberty and equality. Have people become happier since the Revolution? On the contrary. We wanted liberty, but Bonaparte destroyed it."

Prince Andrei watched the exchange with an amused smile, looking from Pierre to the vicomte and back to their hostess. At the first moment of Pierre's outburst, Anna Pavlovna — despite all her social experience — had been horrified. But when she saw that his sacrilegious words hadn't actually enraged the vicomte, and convinced herself that it was impossible to silence Pierre, she rallied and joined the vicomte in a vigorous counterattack.
"But my dear Monsieur Pierre," she said, "how do you explain the fact that a great man executed a duke — or even any ordinary man — who was innocent and untried?"
"I'd like to know," said the vicomte, "how monsieur explains the 18th Brumaire. Wasn't that a fraud? It was a swindle, and not at all the behavior of a great man!"
"And the prisoners he killed in Africa? That was terrible!" said the little princess, shuddering.
"He's a despicable man, whatever you say," declared Prince Hippolyte.

Pierre, not knowing whom to answer, looked around at all of them and smiled. His smile was unlike anyone else's. When he smiled, his serious, even rather somber expression was instantly replaced by something completely different — a childlike, kind, even somewhat foolish look that seemed to beg forgiveness.
The vicomte, who was meeting Pierre for the first time, saw clearly that this young radical was not nearly as frightening as his words suggested. Everyone fell silent.

"How can you expect him to answer all of you at once?" said Prince Andrei. "Besides, when judging a statesman, you have to distinguish between his actions as a private individual, as a general, and as an emperor. At least, that's how I see it."
"Yes, yes, exactly!" Pierre chimed in, delighted by this support.

"One must admit," Prince Andrei continued, "that Napoleon the man was great on the bridge at Arcola, and in the hospital at Jaffa where he took the hands of plague victims. But... there are other actions that are hard to justify."
Prince Andrei, who had clearly wanted to smooth over the awkwardness of Pierre's remarks, stood up and signaled to his wife that it was time to leave.
Suddenly Prince Hippolyte sprang to his feet, waving for everyone's attention and asking them all to sit back down:

"I heard a wonderful story about Moscow today and I must share it with you. Forgive me, Vicomte — I have to tell it in Russian or the joke won't work..." And Prince Hippolyte began telling his story in the kind of Russian a Frenchman would speak after about a year in Russia. Everyone waited, so emphatically and eagerly did he demand their attention.

"There is in Moscow a lady, a certain dame, and she is very stingy. She always has to have two footmen standing behind her carriage, and very large ones. That was her preference. And she had a lady's maid who was also tall. She said..."
Here Prince Hippolyte paused, clearly struggling to collect his thoughts.
"She said... Oh yes! She said, 'Girl,' to the maid, 'put on a livery, get up behind the carriage, and come with me while I make my rounds.'"

At this point Prince Hippolyte began sputtering and burst out laughing well before his audience, which didn't help his storytelling. A few people, including the elderly lady and Anna Pavlovna, managed a smile.

"Off she went. Then suddenly there was a huge gust of wind. The girl lost her hat and her long hair tumbled down..." He could no longer contain himself and went on, between gasps of laughter: "And then the whole world could see..."

And that was the end of the anecdote. Though no one could understand why he had told it, or why it needed to be told in Russian, Anna Pavlovna and the others appreciated Prince Hippolyte's social instinct in so agreeably defusing Pierre's unpleasant and ill-mannered outburst. After the anecdote, the conversation dissolved into trivial small talk about recent and upcoming balls, the theater, and who would be meeting whom, and when, and where.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter VI
paragraphs: Having thanked Anna Pavlovna for a charming evening, the guests began to leave.

Pierre was clumsy. Heavyset, about average height, broad-shouldered, with enormous red hands — he didn't know how to enter a drawing room, as the saying goes, and even less how to leave one, meaning how to say something particularly gracious on the way out. On top of that, he was absent-minded. When he got up to go, he grabbed the general's three-cornered hat instead of his own and stood fidgeting with the plume until the general asked for it back. All this clumsiness and social ineptitude was redeemed, however, by his kind, simple, and modest expression. Anna Pavlovna turned to him and, with a Christian gentleness that conveyed forgiveness for his outburst, nodded and said: "I hope to see you again, but I also hope you'll change your views, my dear Monsieur Pierre."

He didn't reply — only bowed — but once again everyone noticed his smile, which said nothing except perhaps: "Opinions are opinions, but you can see what a perfectly decent fellow I am." And everyone, including Anna Pavlovna, felt this.

Prince Andrei had gone out into the entrance hall and, turning his back to the footman helping him on with his cloak, was listening indifferently to his wife chatting with Prince Hippolyte, who had also come out into the hall. Prince Hippolyte stood close to the pretty, pregnant princess, staring at her through his eyeglass.
"Go inside, Annette, or you'll catch cold," said the little princess, saying goodbye to Anna Pavlovna. "It's all settled," she added in a low voice.
Anna Pavlovna had already managed to speak to Lise about the match she was scheming between Anatole and the little princess's sister-in-law.
"I'm counting on you, my dear," said Anna Pavlovna, also quietly. "Write to her and let me know what her father thinks about it. Goodbye!" — and she went back inside.
Prince Hippolyte approached the little princess and, leaning his face close to hers, began whispering something.

Two footmen — the princess's and his — stood holding a shawl and a cloak, waiting for the conversation to end. They listened to the French sentences, which meant nothing to them, with an air of comprehension but careful not to seem like they were actually trying to understand. The princess, as always, talked with a smile and listened with a laugh.
"I'm so glad I didn't go to the ambassador's," said Prince Hippolyte, "— so tedious. It's been a lovely evening, hasn't it? Lovely!"
"They say the ball will be excellent," replied the princess, puckering her downy little lip. "All the beautiful women in society will be there."

"Not all of them — because you won't be there. Not all," said Prince Hippolyte with a beaming smile; and snatching the shawl from the footman — practically pushing the man aside — he began wrapping it around the princess. Whether from clumsiness or on purpose (no one could tell), after adjusting the shawl he kept his arm around her for a long time, as though embracing her.
Still smiling, she gracefully stepped away, turning to glance at her husband. Prince Andrei's eyes were closed — he looked so weary and sleepy.
"Ready?" he asked his wife, looking past her.

Prince Hippolyte hastily threw on his cloak, which in the latest fashion reached all the way to his heels, and stumbling over it, ran out to the porch after the princess, whom a footman was helping into the carriage.
"Princess, goodbye!" he called out, tripping over his words as much as his feet. [speaking in French]
The princess was gathering her skirts to take her seat in the dark carriage; her husband was adjusting his saber; Prince Hippolyte, pretending to help, was getting in everyone's way.
"If you don't mind, sir," said Prince Andrei in Russian, in a cold, unfriendly tone, to Prince Hippolyte, who was blocking his path.
"I'm expecting you, Pierre," said the same voice, but now gentle and warm.
The coachman started off and the carriage wheels clattered away. Prince Hippolyte stood on the porch laughing in bursts while he waited for the vicomte, whom he had promised to take home.

"Well, my dear fellow," said the vicomte, settling in beside Hippolyte in the carriage, "your little princess is very charming — very charming indeed, quite French." He kissed his fingertips. Hippolyte burst out laughing. [speaking in French]
"You know, you're quite the rogue despite those innocent looks of yours," the vicomte continued. "I feel sorry for the poor husband — that little officer who puts on the airs of a king."
Hippolyte sputtered with laughter and said between chuckles: "And you were saying Russian ladies can't match French ones? You just have to know how to handle them."

Pierre, arriving at the house first, went straight into Prince Andrei's study as if he lived there. Out of habit he immediately flopped onto the sofa, grabbed the first book that came to hand from the shelf — it was Caesar's Commentaries — and propping himself on one elbow, began reading it somewhere in the middle.
"What have you done to Mademoiselle Scherer? She'll be ill after tonight," said Prince Andrei, walking into the study and rubbing his small white hands.
Pierre rolled his whole body over, making the sofa creak. He turned his eager face toward Prince Andrei, smiled, and waved a hand dismissively.
"That abbe is very interesting, but he's got it all wrong... In my view, perpetual peace is possible, but — I'm not sure how to put it — not through some balance of political power..."
It was clear that Prince Andrei had no interest in this kind of abstract conversation.

"You can't go around saying everything you think, my friend. Well then, have you finally decided on something? Are you going to be a guardsman or a diplomat?" Prince Andrei asked after a brief silence.
Pierre sat up on the sofa with his legs tucked under him.
"Honestly, I still don't know. I don't like either option."
"But you have to choose something! Your father expects it."

Pierre had been sent abroad at the age of ten with an abbe as his tutor, and had stayed away until he was twenty. When he returned to Moscow, his father dismissed the abbe and told the young man: "Now go to Petersburg, look around, and choose a profession. I'll agree to whatever you decide. Here's a letter to Prince Vasili, and here's money. Write and tell me everything, and I'll support you in any way I can." Pierre had been trying to choose a career for three months now, and still hadn't decided on anything. This was the decision Prince Andrei was asking about. Pierre rubbed his forehead.
"But he must be a Freemason," Pierre said suddenly, referring to the abbe he had met that evening.
"That's all nonsense," Prince Andrei interrupted him. "Let's talk about real things. Have you been to see the Horse Guards?"

"No, I haven't. But here's what I've been thinking and wanted to tell you. There's a war on against Napoleon. If it were a war for freedom, I'd understand it — I'd be the first to enlist. But to help England and Austria fight the greatest man in the world — that isn't right."

Prince Andrei just shrugged at Pierre's naive words. He adopted the expression of someone who finds it pointless to respond to such nonsense — though in reality it would have been hard to give any better answer than what he said next.
"If no one fought unless they were personally convinced of the cause, there would be no wars," he said.
"And that would be wonderful," said Pierre.
Prince Andrei smiled ironically.
"Maybe it would be wonderful, but it will never happen..."
"Well, then why are you going to war?" Pierre asked.
"Why? I don't know. I have to. And besides..." He paused. "I'm going because the life I'm living here doesn't suit me!"

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter VII
paragraphs: The rustle of a woman's dress came from the next room. Prince Andrei seemed to shake himself awake, and his face took on the same expression it had worn at Anna Pavlovna's party. Pierre pulled his feet off the sofa. The princess walked in. She had changed into a house dress as fresh and elegant as the one before. Prince Andrei stood and politely pulled out a chair for her.

"How is it," she began, in French as always, settling briskly and fussily into the armchair, "how is it that Annette never married? How silly you men are, not to have married her! Forgive me for saying so, but you have no understanding of women whatsoever. What an argumentative person you are, Monsieur Pierre!"

"And I'm still arguing with your husband. I can't understand why he wants to go to war," Pierre replied, speaking to the princess without any of the awkwardness young men typically show around young women.
The princess flinched. Pierre's words had clearly struck a nerve.

"That's exactly what I keep telling him!" she exclaimed. "I don't understand it — I simply cannot understand why men can't live without wars. How is it that we women don't want any part of it, don't need it? You be the judge between us. I'm always saying to him: Here you are, Uncle's aide-de-camp, a brilliant position. Everyone knows you, everyone admires you. Just the other day at the Apraksins', I heard a lady ask, 'Is that the famous Prince Andrei?' I really did!" She laughed. "He's so well received everywhere. He could easily become aide-de-camp to the Emperor himself. You know the Emperor spoke to him so graciously. Annette and I were just discussing how to arrange it. What do you think?"
Pierre glanced at his friend and, seeing that he didn't like this conversation, said nothing.
"When do you leave?" he asked instead.

"Oh, don't talk about him leaving — don't! I can't bear to hear it," said the princess in the same petulant, playful tone she had used with Hippolyte in the drawing room, a tone that was so clearly out of place in this intimate family setting where Pierre was practically a member. "When I think that all these wonderful connections will be severed... And then you know, Andrei..." She gave her husband a meaningful look. "I'm frightened — I'm frightened!" she whispered, a shiver running through her.
Her husband looked at her as if surprised to find someone besides Pierre in the room, and addressed her in a tone of icy politeness.
"What is it you're afraid of, Lise? I don't understand," he said.
"There — you see what selfish creatures men are! All of them, every one! Just for some whim of his own, God knows why, he's abandoning me and locking me away in the country alone."
"With my father and sister, don't forget," Prince Andrei said gently.
"Alone all the same — without my friends... And he expects me not to be frightened."

Her voice had turned querulous, and her lip was pulled up in a way that gave her not a cheerful but an animal, squirrel-like expression. She paused, apparently feeling it was improper to mention her pregnancy in front of Pierre, even though that was really the heart of the matter.
"I still don't understand what you're afraid of," Prince Andrei said slowly, not taking his eyes off his wife.
The princess blushed and threw up her hands in a gesture of despair.
"No, Andrei, I have to say — you've changed. You've changed so much..."
"Your doctor says you should go to bed earlier," said Prince Andrei. "You should go."
The princess said nothing, but suddenly her short, downy lip began to tremble. Prince Andrei stood up, shrugged, and paced the room.
Pierre looked over his spectacles with innocent surprise, first at one, then at the other, and shifted as if about to stand up himself, but then changed his mind.

"Why should I care that Monsieur Pierre is here?" the little princess burst out, her pretty face suddenly twisting into a tearful grimace. "I've been wanting to ask you for a long time, Andrei — why have you changed toward me? What have I done to you? You're going off to war, and you have no pity for me. Why?"
"Lise!" was all Prince Andrei said. But that single word contained a plea, a warning, and above all a conviction that she would regret her own words. She went on regardless:
"You treat me like a sick person, or a child. I can see it! Did you act this way six months ago?"
"Lise, please stop," Prince Andrei said, more firmly now.
Pierre, growing more and more distressed as he listened, stood up and approached the princess. He seemed unable to bear the sight of tears and was on the verge of crying himself.
"Calm down, Princess! It only seems that way because... I assure you, I've experienced... I mean... because... No, forgive me! I'm in the way here... No, please don't be upset... Goodbye!"
Prince Andrei caught him by the hand.
"No, wait, Pierre! The princess is too kind to want to deprive me of the pleasure of your company this evening."
"No — he only ever thinks of himself," the princess muttered, unable to hold back her angry tears.
"Lise!" said Prince Andrei sharply, his voice reaching the pitch that signals exhausted patience.

Suddenly the angry, squirrel-like expression on the princess's pretty face gave way to a look of endearing, pitiful fear. Her beautiful eyes darted a sideways glance at her husband's face, and her own took on the timid, apologetic look of a dog wagging its drooping tail — quickly but without conviction.
"Oh God, oh God!" she murmured, and gathering up her dress with one hand, she went to her husband and kissed him on the forehead.
"Good night, Lise," he said, standing and kissing her hand with the courtesy he might show a stranger.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter VIII
paragraphs: The friends sat in silence. Neither wanted to be the first to speak. Pierre kept glancing at Prince Andrei; Prince Andrei rubbed his forehead with his small hand.
"Let's go have supper," he said with a sigh, heading for the door.

They entered the elegant, newly decorated, and luxurious dining room. Everything — from the napkins to the silver, china, and glassware — bore that stamp of newness found in the homes of the recently married. Halfway through supper, Prince Andrei leaned his elbows on the table and, with a look of agitation Pierre had never seen on his face before, began to speak like a man who has been holding something in for a long time and has finally decided to let it out.

"Never, never get married, my friend! That's my advice: don't marry until you can honestly say you've done everything you're capable of, and until you've stopped being in love with the woman you've chosen and can see her as she truly is — otherwise you'll make a terrible, irreversible mistake. Marry when you're old and useless — or everything good and noble in you will be squandered on trivialities. Yes! Yes! Yes! Don't look at me like that. If you marry while you still expect something of yourself, you'll discover at every turn that it's all over for you, everything is closed off — except the drawing room, where you'll stand in line alongside court lackeys and idiots! But what's the use of talking about it..." He waved his hand dismissively.
Pierre took off his spectacles, which made his face look different — his good-natured expression even more apparent — and stared at his friend in astonishment.

"My wife," Prince Andrei continued, "is an excellent woman — one of those rare women with whom a man's honor is safe. But, God, what I wouldn't give to be unmarried right now! You are the first and only person I'm telling this to, because I'm fond of you."

As he said this, Prince Andrei looked nothing like the Bolkonsky who had lounged in Anna Pavlovna's armchairs, muttering polished French phrases through half-closed eyes. Every muscle of his thin face was quivering with intensity; his eyes, which usually seemed drained of all vitality, now blazed with a fierce light. It was clear that the more lifeless he appeared in ordinary life, the more passionate he became in these moments of near-feverish agitation.

"You don't understand why I'm saying this," he continued, "but it's the whole story of life. You were talking about Bonaparte and his career" — though Pierre had not mentioned Bonaparte — "but when Bonaparte was working toward his goal, he went step by step. He was free. He had nothing to think about except his objective, and he reached it. But tie yourself to a woman, and like a prisoner in chains, you lose all freedom! And whatever hope and strength you have left only weighs you down and fills you with regret. Drawing rooms, gossip, balls, vanity, and pettiness — that's the enchanted circle I can't escape from. I'm going off to war now — the greatest war there ever was — and I know nothing, I'm good for nothing. I'm very charming and have a sharp wit," Prince Andrei continued, "and at Anna Pavlovna's they hang on my every word. And that stupid crowd my wife can't live without, and those women... If you only knew what society women really are — what women in general really are! My father is right. They're selfish, vain, stupid, shallow in everything — that's what women are when you see them as they truly are! No, don't get married, my friend. Don't marry!" he concluded.
"It seems strange to me," said Pierre, "that you — you of all people — should consider yourself incapable and your life wasted. You have everything ahead of you, everything. And you..."
He didn't finish, but his tone made clear how deeply he admired his friend and how much he expected of him.

"How can he say such things?" Pierre thought to himself. He saw his friend as a model of perfection, because Prince Andrei possessed in the highest degree precisely those qualities Pierre himself lacked — what might best be described as strength of will. Pierre was constantly amazed by Prince Andrei's calm way of dealing with everyone, his extraordinary memory, his vast reading — he had read everything, knew everything, and had an opinion on everything — but above all by his capacity for work and discipline. And if Pierre sometimes noticed that Andrei lacked a talent for philosophical reflection, to which Pierre himself was particularly drawn, he saw even this not as a flaw but as a sign of strength.
Even in the best, friendliest, and simplest relationships, praise and encouragement are essential — just as grease is needed to keep wheels turning smoothly.
"My part is played out," said Prince Andrei. "What's the point of talking about me? Let's talk about you," he added after a pause, smiling at his own reassuring thoughts.
That smile was immediately mirrored on Pierre's face.

"But what is there to say about me?" said Pierre, his face relaxing into an easy, cheerful smile. "What am I? An illegitimate son!" He suddenly blushed deeply, and it was obvious that saying this had cost him a great effort. "Without a name and without money... And it really..." But he didn't say what "it really" was. "For now, I'm free and doing fine. I just have absolutely no idea what I should do with myself. I wanted to ask your advice seriously."
Prince Andrei looked at him kindly, yet his gaze — warm and affectionate as it was — conveyed a sense of his own superiority.

"I'm fond of you, especially because you're the one genuinely alive person in our whole circle. Yes, you're doing fine! Choose whatever you like — it's all the same. You'll be fine anywhere. But listen: stop spending time with the Kuragins and living that kind of life. It doesn't suit you at all — all that debauchery and dissipation."
"What can I say, my friend?" Pierre answered with a shrug. "Women, my dear fellow — women!"
"I don't understand it," Prince Andrei replied. "Respectable women — that's another matter. But the Kuragin sort of women, the 'wine and women' crowd — I don't understand that!"

Pierre was living at Prince Vasili Kuragin's house and sharing the dissolute lifestyle of his son Anatole — the same Anatole they were planning to reform by marrying him off to Prince Andrei's sister.

"You know what?" said Pierre, as if suddenly struck by a happy thought. "Seriously, I've been thinking about this for a while... Living this way, I can't think clearly about anything. My head aches and I spend all my money. He invited me out tonight, but I'm not going."
"You give me your word of honor?"
"On my honor!"

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter IX
paragraphs: It was past one in the morning when Pierre left his friend. It was a cloudless northern summer night. Pierre hailed an open cab, intending to go straight home. But the closer he got to the house, the more impossible it seemed to fall asleep on a night like this. It was light enough to see far down the empty street — it felt more like morning or evening than the middle of the night. On the way, Pierre remembered that Anatole Kuragin was expecting the usual crowd for cards that evening, after which there was typically a drinking session followed by the kind of excursion Pierre was particularly fond of.
"I should really go to Kuragin's," he thought.

But then he immediately remembered his promise to Prince Andrei not to go. And then, as happens with people of weak character, his desire to enjoy the familiar pleasures of debauchery was so overwhelming that he decided to go anyway. The thought immediately came to him that his promise to Prince Andrei didn't really count, since before he had made it he had already promised Prince Anatole he would come. "Besides," he thought, "all these 'words of honor' are just conventions with no real meaning — especially when you consider that by tomorrow you could be dead, or something so extraordinary could happen that honor and dishonor would amount to the same thing!" Pierre often indulged in this kind of reasoning, undoing all his decisions and resolutions. He went to Kuragin's.

When he reached the large house near the Horse Guards barracks where Anatole lived, Pierre walked through the lit porch, climbed the stairs, and went in through the open door. There was no one in the entrance hall; empty bottles, cloaks, and boots were scattered around. The place smelled of alcohol, and from somewhere in the distance came the sound of voices and shouting.

Cards and supper were over, but the guests hadn't left yet. Pierre tossed off his cloak and entered the first room, which was littered with the remains of supper. A footman, thinking no one was watching, was sneaking sips from the leftover glasses. From the third room came laughter, the shouts of familiar voices, the growling of a bear, and a general commotion. Eight or nine young men were crowding around an open window. Three others were roughhousing with a young bear, one of them pulling it by its chain and trying to sic it on the rest.
"A hundred on Stevens!" shouted one.
"No holding on!" yelled another.
"I'm betting on Dolokhov!" cried a third. "Kuragin, separate their hands."
"Leave the bear alone — there's a real bet going on."
"In one go, or he loses!" shouted a fourth.

"Yakov, bring a bottle!" shouted the host — a tall, handsome fellow standing in the middle of the group without his coat, his fine linen shirt unbuttoned at the front. "Hold on, everyone... Here's Petya! Good man!" he cried, addressing Pierre.

Another voice, belonging to a man of average height with striking light-blue eyes — a voice that stood out among the drunken din for its sober clarity — called from the window: "Over here! Settle the bets!" This was Dolokhov, an officer of the Semenov regiment, a notorious gambler and duelist who was living with Anatole. Pierre looked around cheerfully, smiling.
"I don't get it. What's going on?"
"Hang on, he's not drunk enough yet! Bring a bottle," said Anatole, grabbing a glass from the table and going over to Pierre.
"First — you have to drink!"

Pierre drank one glass after another, watching the tipsy guests from under his brows as they crowded around the window again, and listening to their chatter. Anatole kept refilling Pierre's glass while explaining that Dolokhov had made a bet with Stevens, an English naval officer, that he could drink an entire bottle of rum while sitting on the outer window ledge of the third floor with his legs dangling over the edge.
"Go on, drink it all," said Anatole, handing Pierre the last glass, "or I won't let you leave!"
"No, I won't," said Pierre, pushing Anatole aside, and he walked over to the window.
Dolokhov was gripping the Englishman's hand and clearly, distinctly repeating the terms of the bet, directing himself particularly at Anatole and Pierre.

Dolokhov was of medium height, with curly hair and light-blue eyes. He was about twenty-five. Like all infantry officers, he wore no mustache, so his mouth — the most striking feature of his face — was fully visible. Its lines were remarkably fine. The middle of the upper lip formed a sharp wedge that closed firmly against the lower one, and something like two separate smiles constantly played at the corners. This, together with the fearless, insolent intelligence in his eyes, made his face impossible to ignore. Dolokhov was a man of modest means and no connections. Yet although Anatole spent tens of thousands of rubles, Dolokhov lived with him and had established himself in such a position that everyone who knew them — including Anatole — respected Dolokhov more. He could play any card game and almost always won. No matter how much he drank, he never lost his wits. Both Kuragin and Dolokhov were among the most notorious rakes and troublemakers in all of Petersburg.

The bottle of rum was brought. Two footmen, clearly flustered and intimidated by all the shouting and orders from the young gentlemen, were trying to pry out the window frame that prevented anyone from sitting on the outer sill.
Anatole swaggered up to the window with the urge to smash something. He shoved the footmen aside and yanked at the frame, but couldn't budge it. He punched out a pane of glass.
"You try it, Hercules," he said, turning to Pierre.
Pierre grabbed the crossbeam, pulled hard, and ripped the heavy oak frame out with a crash.
"Take the whole thing out, or they'll think I'm holding on," said Dolokhov.
"Is the Englishman bluffing? Eh? Everything good?" said Anatole.

"Perfect," said Pierre, watching Dolokhov approach the window with the bottle of rum in his hand. Through the opening, the light of the sky was visible — dawn blending into the lingering glow of sunset.
Dolokhov, bottle still in hand, leaped onto the windowsill. "Listen!" he called out, standing there and addressing the room. Everyone fell silent.

"I bet fifty imperials" — he spoke French so the Englishman could understand, though his French wasn't very good — "I bet fifty imperials... or would you prefer to make it a hundred?" he added, turning to the Englishman. [speaking in French]
"No, fifty," the Englishman replied.

"Fine. Fifty imperials... that I will drink an entire bottle of rum without taking it from my lips, sitting outside the window on this ledge" — he bent down and pointed to the sloping ledge outside — "without holding on to anything. Agreed?"
"Agreed," said the Englishman.
Anatole turned to the Englishman and, grabbing him by a coat button and looking down at him (the Englishman was short), began repeating the terms of the wager in English.
"Wait!" Dolokhov shouted, banging the bottle on the windowsill for attention. "Hold on, Kuragin. Listen! If anyone else does the same thing, I'll pay them a hundred imperials. Understood?"

The Englishman nodded but gave no sign whether he intended to take up the challenge himself. Anatole wouldn't let go of him, and though the Englishman kept nodding to show he understood, Anatole went on translating Dolokhov's words into English. A thin young man, a hussar of the Life Guards who had been losing all evening, climbed up on the windowsill, leaned out, and looked down.
"Oh! Oh! Oh!" he muttered, staring down at the stone pavement far below.
"Shut up!" Dolokhov barked, shoving him away from the window. The young man stumbled back into the room, tripping over his spurs.

Setting the bottle on the windowsill within easy reach, Dolokhov climbed carefully and slowly through the window and lowered his legs over the outside. Bracing himself against both sides of the window frame, he settled into position on the ledge, released his hands, shifted slightly right, then left, and picked up the bottle. Anatole brought two candles and placed them on the sill, though it was already quite light outside. Dolokhov's back in its white shirt and his curly head were lit from both sides. Everyone pressed toward the window — the Englishman in front. Pierre stood smiling but silent. One man, older than the rest, suddenly pushed forward with a frightened, angry expression and tried to grab Dolokhov's shirt.
"Stop this — this is insanity! He'll be killed!" said this more sensible man.
Anatole held him back.
"Don't touch him! You'll startle him and then he really will be killed. You hear me? What then?"
Dolokhov turned around and, gripping the sides with both hands again, resettled himself.
"If anyone interferes again," he said, forcing the words out one by one through his thin, pressed lips, "I'll throw them down there myself. Now then!"

With that, he turned back around, let go with both hands, took the bottle, raised it to his lips, tilted his head back, and lifted his free hand for balance. One of the footmen who had bent down to pick up broken glass froze in that position, his eyes locked on the window and on Dolokhov's back. Anatole stood rigid, eyes wide. The Englishman watched from the side, lips pursed. The man who had tried to stop it all ran to the corner of the room and threw himself face-down on a sofa against the wall. Pierre covered his face — a faint smile lingering there out of habit, though his features now showed only horror and fear. Everyone was still. Pierre took his hands from his eyes. Dolokhov still sat in the same position, but his head was thrown further back now, his curly hair brushing his shirt collar, and the hand holding the bottle was rising higher and higher, trembling with the strain. The bottle was visibly emptying, tilting ever higher, his head leaning further back. "Why is it taking so long?" Pierre wondered. It felt like more than half an hour had passed. Suddenly Dolokhov's spine arched backward and his arm trembled violently — enough to make his whole body start sliding on the sloping ledge. As he slipped, his head and arm wavered even more from the effort. One hand moved as if to grab the windowsill but stopped short of touching it. Pierre covered his eyes again and told himself he would never open them. Then suddenly — movement all around him. He looked up: Dolokhov was standing on the windowsill, his face pale but radiant.
"It's empty."
He tossed the bottle to the Englishman, who caught it neatly. Dolokhov jumped down into the room. He reeked of rum.
"Bravo!... What a man!... Now that's a bet!... You devil!" voices called out from all sides.
The Englishman pulled out his wallet and began counting out the money. Dolokhov stood there frowning, saying nothing. Pierre leaped onto the windowsill.
"Gentlemen! Who wants to bet with me? I'll do the same thing!" he shouted suddenly. "I don't even need a bet — just bring me a bottle! I'll do it... Bring me a bottle!"
"Let him do it, let him," said Dolokhov with a smile.
"Are you out of your mind?... Absolutely not!... You get dizzy just going up stairs!" several voices protested.
"I'll drink it! Give me a bottle of rum!" Pierre roared, slamming the table with a determined, drunken fist and moving to climb out the window.
They grabbed him by both arms, but he was so strong that anyone who touched him went flying.
"No, you'll never handle him that way," said Anatole. "Wait, I'll talk him down... Listen! I'll take your bet tomorrow, but right now we're all heading out."
"Let's go then!" Pierre shouted. "Let's go! And we're bringing the bear with us."
And he caught the bear, scooped it up in his arms, lifted it off the ground, and began dancing around the room with it.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter X
paragraphs: Prince Vasili kept the promise he had made to Princess Drubetskaya, who had spoken to him about her only son Boris on the evening of Anna Pavlovna's reception. The matter was brought to the Emperor's attention, an exception was made, and Boris was transferred to the Semenov Guards with the rank of cornet. He did not, however, receive any appointment to Kutuzov's staff, despite all of Anna Mikhaylovna's efforts and pleading. Shortly after Anna Pavlovna's party, Anna Mikhaylovna returned to Moscow and went straight to her wealthy relatives, the Rostovs, with whom she always stayed when in town. It was here that her beloved Boris — who had only recently entered a regular army regiment and was now being transferred to the Guards as a cornet — had been raised and had lived for years. The Guards had already left Petersburg on the tenth of August, and Boris, who had stayed behind in Moscow to get his equipment, was to catch up with them on the march to Radzivilov.

It was the feast of St. Natalia, and therefore the name day of two of the Rostovs — the mother and the youngest daughter — both named Nataly. Since morning, carriages drawn by six horses had been arriving and departing nonstop, bringing visitors to Countess Rostova's large house on Povarskaya Street, well known to everyone in Moscow. The countess and her beautiful eldest daughter sat in the drawing room receiving the steady stream of congratulatory callers.

The countess was a woman of about forty-five with a thin face of an Eastern type, clearly worn out from childbearing — she had given birth twelve times. A languidness in her movements and speech, born of exhaustion, gave her a dignified air that commanded respect. Princess Anna Mikhaylovna Drubetskaya, as a member of the household, was also seated in the drawing room, helping to greet and entertain the guests.
