The young people were in one of the inner rooms, seeing no need to participate in receiving visitors. The count himself met each guest and saw them off, inviting everyone to stay for dinner.

"I'm so very, very grateful to you, my dear" — he called everyone "my dear" without exception or variation, whether they outranked him or not — "thank you on my own behalf and for our two lovely name-day girls. But you must come to dinner, or I'll be offended, my dear! On behalf of the whole family, I insist — please come, my dear!" He repeated this to everyone, with the same expression on his full, cheerful, clean-shaven face, the same firm handshake, and the same quick, repeated bows. As soon as he had seen one visitor off, he returned to whoever was still in the drawing room, pulled up a chair, and with his legs spread jauntily and his hands on his knees — looking like a man who knows how to enjoy life — he would rock back and forth contentedly, making observations about the weather or asking after people's health, sometimes in Russian and sometimes in dreadful but thoroughly confident French. Then, like a man who is tired but won't shirk his duty, he would get up to see the next set of guests off, smoothing his thin gray hair over his bald spot, and once again invite them to dinner. Sometimes, on his way back from the entrance hall, he would cut through the conservatory and pantry into the grand marble dining room, where tables were being set for eighty guests. Watching the footmen carry in silverware and china, move tables into position, and unfold damask tablecloths, he would call over Dmitri Vasilyevich — a man of good family who managed all his affairs — and, eyeing the enormous table with satisfaction, would say: "Well, Dmitri, make sure everything is just right. Good! The main thing is the service — that's what matters." And with a contented sigh he would head back to the drawing room.

"Marya Lvovna Karagina and her daughter!" the countess's gigantic footman announced in his bass voice as he entered the drawing room. The countess thought for a moment and took a pinch of snuff from a gold box decorated with her husband's portrait.
"These visitors are wearing me out. But fine — I'll see her, and then no more. She's so affected. Show her in," she told the footman in a weary voice, as if saying: "Very well — finish me off."
A tall, heavy-set woman with a proud bearing, accompanied by her round-faced, smiling daughter, entered the drawing room in a rustle of dresses.

"Dear Countess, it's been ages!... She's been laid up, poor thing... the Razumovsky ball... and Countess Apraksina... I was so delighted..." Animated women's voices came tumbling over each other, blending with the rustle of dresses and the scraping of chairs. Then began one of those conversations that lasts only until, at the first pause, the guests stand up in a swish of fabric and say, "I'm so delighted... Mama's health... Countess Apraksina..." and then, rustling once more, file out to the entrance hall, put on their cloaks and capes, and drive away. The topic of the day was the illness of Count Bezukhov — the famous, wealthy heartthrob of Catherine the Great's era — and his illegitimate son Pierre, the one who had made such a scene at Anna Pavlovna's party.
"I feel so sorry for the poor count," said the visitor. "His health is so bad, and now this trouble with his son on top of everything — it's enough to kill him!"
"What trouble?" asked the countess, as if she didn't know what the visitor was referring to, though she had already heard the story of Count Bezukhov's woes a good fifteen times.

"That's modern education for you!" exclaimed the visitor. "Apparently this young man was left to do as he pleased while abroad, and now in Petersburg I hear he's been doing such terrible things that the police expelled him from the city."
"You don't say!" replied the countess.

"He fell in with bad company," Anna Mikhaylovna put in. "Prince Vasili's son, this Pierre, and a certain Dolokhov have reportedly been up to God knows what! And they've all had to pay for it. Dolokhov has been stripped of his rank and reduced to a common soldier, and Bezukhov's son has been sent back to Moscow. Anatole Kuragin's father managed to hush up his son's part in it somehow, but even he was ordered out of Petersburg."
"But what exactly did they do?" asked the countess.

"They're absolute hooligans, especially Dolokhov," the visitor replied. "He's the son of Marya Ivanovna Dolokhova — such a decent woman — but imagine this: those three got hold of a bear somewhere, stuck it in a carriage, and drove off to visit some actresses! When the police tried to intervene, do you know what the young men did? They tied a policeman and the bear back to back and tossed them into the Moika Canal. And there was the bear swimming around with the policeman on its back!"
"What a picture that policeman must have made, my dear!" the count shouted, shaking with laughter.
"Oh, how terrible! How can you laugh at such a thing, Count?"
But even the ladies couldn't help laughing.

"They barely managed to rescue the poor man," the visitor continued. "And to think this is Kirill Vladimirovich Bezukhov's son, amusing himself like this! And everyone said he was so well-educated and clever. So much for his foreign education! I hope no one in Moscow will receive him, despite all his money. They wanted to introduce him to me, but I flatly refused — I have my daughters to think about."

"Why do you say this young man is so rich?" asked the countess, turning away from the girls, who immediately put on expressions of studied indifference. "His children are all illegitimate. I believe Pierre is illegitimate too."
The visitor made a gesture with her hand.
"He must have twenty of them at least."
Princess Anna Mikhaylovna joined the conversation, clearly wanting to demonstrate her connections and knowledge of high-society matters.
"Here's the thing," she said meaningfully, also dropping to a half-whisper. "Everyone knows Count Kirill's reputation... He's lost count of his own children. But this Pierre was always his favorite."
"How handsome the old man still was just a year ago!" remarked the countess. "I've never seen a more handsome man."

"He's aged terribly," said Anna Mikhaylovna. "Well, as I was saying — through his wife, Prince Vasili is the next heir. But the count is very fond of Pierre, oversaw his education, and even petitioned the Emperor on his behalf. So when the count dies — and he's so ill that it could happen any day; Dr. Lorrain has come from Petersburg — nobody knows who will inherit his enormous fortune: Pierre or Prince Vasili. Forty thousand serfs and millions of rubles! I know all about it — Prince Vasili told me himself. Besides, Kirill Vladimirovich is my mother's second cousin. He's also my Boris's godfather," she added, as if attaching no importance whatsoever to this fact.
"Prince Vasili arrived in Moscow yesterday. I hear he's come on some official inspection," the visitor remarked.
"Yes, but between us," said the princess, "that's just a pretext. The real reason is that he's come to see Count Kirill Vladimirovich, having heard how ill he is."

"But you know, my dear, that was really a hilarious prank," said the count. Noticing that the older visitor wasn't listening, he turned to the young ladies. "I can just picture the face that policeman made!"

And as he waved his arms, mimicking the policeman, his portly body shook with a rich, deep laugh — the laugh of a man who always eats well and, in particular, drinks well. "So please — do come for dinner!" he said.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter XI
paragraphs: A silence fell. The countess looked at her guests with a friendly smile that did nothing to hide the fact that she wouldn't mind if they got up and left. The visitor's daughter was already smoothing down her dress with a questioning glance at her mother when, suddenly, from the next room came the sound of children's footsteps running toward the door, a chair crashing over, and then a girl of about thirteen — hiding something in the folds of her short muslin dress — burst in and stopped dead in the middle of the room. She clearly hadn't meant her dash to carry her this far. Behind her in the doorway appeared a university student with a crimson collar, a Guards officer, a girl of fifteen, and a plump, rosy-cheeked boy in a short jacket.
The count leaped up and, swaying from side to side, threw his arms wide and wrapped them around the girl who had run in.
"There she is!" he exclaimed with a laugh. "My darling girl, whose name day it is! My sweetheart!"
"My dear, there's a time and place for everything," said the countess with mock severity. "You spoil her, Ilya," she added, turning to her husband.
"Happy name day, my dear! What a charming child," said the visitor, addressing the mother.

This dark-eyed, wide-mouthed girl — not pretty, but brimming with life — with her bare childish shoulders heaving and shaking her bodice after the run, black curls tossed back, thin bare arms, little legs in lace-trimmed drawers, and feet in flat slippers — was at that enchanting age when a girl is no longer a child but not yet a young woman. Wriggling free from her father, she ran to bury her flushed face in the lace of her mother's shawl, paying no attention whatsoever to the scolding, and started laughing. Between gasps of laughter, she tried in broken phrases to explain about a doll she had pulled from the folds of her dress.

"Look!... My doll... Mimi... Look..." was all Natasha could get out — everything struck her as hilarious. She leaned against her mother and burst into such a loud, ringing laugh that even the prim visitor couldn't help joining in.
"Now then — take yourself and your monster away," said the mother, pushing her daughter back with pretend sternness, and turning to the visitor added: "She's my youngest."
Natasha lifted her face from her mother's shawl for a moment, glanced up at her through tears of laughter, and buried it again.
The visitor, obliged to witness this family scene, felt she should participate somehow.
"Tell me, dear," she said to Natasha, "is this Mimi a relative of yours? Your daughter, perhaps?"
Natasha didn't like the visitor's condescending tone about childish things. She didn't answer, just looked at her with a serious expression.

Meanwhile the younger generation — Boris (the officer, Anna Mikhaylovna's son), Nikolai (the university student, the count's eldest son), Sonya (the count's fifteen-year-old niece), and little Petya (his youngest boy) — had all settled in the drawing room and were clearly struggling to contain the excitement and amusement written all over their faces. It was obvious that back in the rooms they had just burst out of, the conversation had been far more entertaining than the drawing room talk of society gossip, weather, and Countess Apraksina. Every now and then they caught each other's eyes, barely able to suppress their laughter.

The two young men — the student and the officer, childhood friends — were the same age and both good-looking, though quite different. Boris was tall and fair, with a calm, handsome face and regular, refined features. Nikolai was shorter, with curly hair and an open, expressive face. Dark hair was already appearing on his upper lip, and his whole expression radiated energy and enthusiasm. Nikolai blushed as he entered the drawing room. He clearly tried to think of something to say but failed. Boris, on the other hand, was immediately at ease. He calmly and humorously recounted how he had known the doll Mimi when she was still quite a young lady, before her nose was broken — how she had aged in the five years he had known her, and how her skull had cracked right across. As he said this, he glanced at Natasha. She turned away from him and looked at her younger brother, who was squinting and shaking with suppressed laughter. Unable to hold it in any longer, she leaped up and ran out of the room as fast as her nimble little feet could carry her. Boris didn't laugh.
"You were about to go out, weren't you, Mama? Shall I have the carriage brought around?" he asked his mother with a smile.
"Yes, yes — go tell them to get it ready," she answered, returning his smile.
Boris quietly left the room and went to look for Natasha. The plump little boy ran after them angrily, as if annoyed that their plans had been disrupted.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter XII
paragraphs: The only young people left in the drawing room — apart from the young lady visitor and the countess's eldest daughter, who was four years older than her sister and already carried herself like an adult — were Nikolai and Sonya, the niece. Sonya was a slender little brunette with tender eyes veiled by long lashes, thick black braids wound twice around her head, and a warm olive tone to her skin, especially visible in her slender but graceful and toned arms and neck. In the smoothness of her movements, the softness and flexibility of her small limbs, and a certain shyness and reserve, she resembled a pretty half-grown kitten that promises to become a beautiful cat. She clearly felt it was proper to show interest in the adult conversation by smiling, but despite her best efforts, her eyes kept drifting — beneath their thick, long lashes — to her cousin who was about to leave for the army, with such intense girlish adoration that her smile couldn't fool anyone for a second. It was obvious that the kitten had settled down only to leap up again with renewed energy and play with her cousin the moment they could escape the drawing room, as Natasha and Boris had already done.

"Well, yes, my dear," said the count, addressing the visitor and gesturing toward Nikolai. "His friend Boris has become an officer, and out of friendship, my boy here is leaving university — and his old father — to join the army. And he had a position waiting for him in the Archives Department! Now that's friendship for you, wouldn't you say?"
"But they say war has been declared," the visitor replied.
"People have been saying that for ages," said the count, "and they'll go on saying it, and that'll be the end of it. Now that's friendship for you, my dear," he repeated. "He's joining the hussars."
The visitor, unsure what to say, shook her head.
"It's got nothing to do with friendship," Nikolai burst out, his face flushing as he turned away as if stung by an insult. "It's not about friendship at all. I simply feel the army is my calling."
He glanced at his cousin and the young lady visitor; both were watching him with approving smiles.

"Schubert, the colonel of the Pavlograd Hussars, is dining with us today. He's been on leave here and he's taking Nikolai back with him. There's nothing to be done!" said the count, shrugging his shoulders and speaking lightly about something that clearly upset him.

"I've already told you, Papa," said his son, "that if you don't want me to go, I'll stay. But I know I'm useless anywhere except in the army. I'm not a diplomat or a government clerk — I don't know how to hide what I feel." As he spoke, he kept stealing glances — with all the flirtatiousness of a handsome young man — at Sonya and the young lady visitor.
The little kitten, devouring him with her eyes, seemed ready at any moment to spring up and show her playful nature.

"All right, all right!" said the old count. "He always gets so fired up! This Bonaparte has turned all their heads — they all think about how he went from being a nobody to becoming Emperor. Well, well — God willing, it'll turn out fine," he added, not noticing the visitor's sarcastic smile.
The adults turned to discussing Bonaparte. Julie Karagina addressed young Rostov.
"What a shame you weren't at the Arkharovs' on Thursday. It was so dull without you," she said, giving him a sweet smile.

The young man, flattered, moved his chair closer to hers with a charming smile and began a whispered conversation with the beaming Julie — completely oblivious to the fact that his easy smile had stabbed Sonya's heart. She blushed and forced an unnatural smile. In the middle of his conversation, he glanced over at her. She shot him a look of passionate anger, and barely able to hold back her tears or keep the fake smile on her face, she stood up and left the room. All of Nikolai's animation evaporated. He waited for the first break in conversation and then, looking distressed, left the room to find Sonya.
"How transparent these young people are with their feelings!" said Anna Mikhaylovna, watching Nikolai go. "Cousinhood is a dangerous neighborhood," she added. [speaking in French]
* Cousinhood is a dangerous neighborhood.

"Yes," said the countess, once the brightness the young people had brought to the room had faded. She spoke as if answering a question no one had asked but which was always on her mind. "And how much suffering, how much worry you have to endure to be able to enjoy them! And really, the worry is greater than the joy. You're always anxious — always! Especially at this age, which is so dangerous for both girls and boys."
"It all depends on the upbringing," the visitor remarked.

"Yes, you're quite right," the countess continued. "Until now, thank God, I've always been my children's friend and had their complete trust" — she said this in the manner of so many parents who imagine their children have no secrets from them. "I know I'll always be my daughters' first confidante, and that if Nikolai, with his impulsive nature, does get into trouble — boys can't help it — he will never turn out like those Petersburg young men."

"Yes, they are wonderful, wonderful children," chimed in the count, who always resolved any question that puzzled him by declaring everything to be wonderful. "Just imagine — wants to be a hussar! What can you do, my dear?"
"What a charming creature your younger girl is," said the visitor. "A little volcano!"

"Yes, a real volcano," the count agreed. "Takes after me! And that voice of hers — though she's my daughter, I'll say it honestly: she'll be a singer, a second Salomoni! We've hired an Italian to give her lessons."
"Isn't she a bit young for that? I've heard it can damage the voice to train it at that age."
"Not at all!" the count replied. "Our mothers used to get married at twelve or thirteen."

"And she's already in love with Boris — can you imagine?" said the countess with a gentle smile, glancing at Boris, and then went on, clearly preoccupied by a thought that was always on her mind. "You see, if I were strict with her and forbade it... who knows what they might get up to behind my back" — she meant they would be kissing — "but as things are, I know every word she says. She comes running to me of her own accord every evening and tells me everything. Maybe I spoil her, but it really does seem like the best approach. I was much stricter with her older sister."
"Yes, I was brought up quite differently," remarked the beautiful eldest daughter, Countess Vera, with a smile.

But her smile didn't enhance Vera's beauty the way smiles usually do; on the contrary, it gave her an unnatural and therefore unpleasant expression. Vera was good-looking, not at all unintelligent, quick to learn, well brought up, and had a pleasant voice; what she said was both true and appropriate. And yet, strangely, everyone — visitors and countess alike — looked at her as if puzzled by why she had spoken, and they all felt uncomfortable.
"People always try too hard with their eldest children, trying to make something exceptional of them," said the visitor.
"No use denying it, my dear — our countess here was too ambitious with Vera," said the count. "But so what? She's turned out wonderfully all the same," he added with a wink at Vera.
The guests rose and took their leave, promising to come back for dinner.
"The nerve! I thought they'd never leave," the countess said once she had shown them out.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter XIII
paragraphs: When Natasha ran out of the drawing room, she only went as far as the conservatory. There she stopped and stood listening to the conversation still going on in the drawing room, waiting for Boris to come out. She was already growing impatient and was stamping her foot, ready to cry because he wasn't coming, when she heard the young man's measured footsteps approaching — neither fast nor slow. At this, Natasha darted in among the potted plants and hid.

Boris paused in the middle of the room, looked around, brushed a speck of dust from his uniform sleeve, and walked up to a mirror to examine his handsome face. Natasha, perfectly still, watched from her hiding place to see what he would do. He stood before the mirror for a moment, smiled to himself, and walked toward the far door. Natasha nearly called out to him but then thought better of it. "Let him look for me," she decided. Boris had barely gone when Sonya rushed in through the other door — flushed, tearful, and muttering angrily. Natasha's first impulse was to run out to her, but she stayed hidden, watching like an invisible observer to see what was happening in the world. She was experiencing a strange, new kind of pleasure. Sonya, muttering to herself, kept glancing toward the drawing room door. It opened, and Nikolai walked in.
"Sonya, what's the matter? What is it?" he said, rushing over to her.
"It's nothing, nothing — leave me alone!" Sonya sobbed.
"I know what this is about."
"Well, if you know, then all the better — you can go back to her!"
"So-o-onya! Come on! How can you torture yourself — and me — over something so silly?" said Nikolai, taking her hand.
Sonya didn't pull her hand away. She stopped crying. Natasha, motionless and barely breathing, watched from her hiding place with shining eyes. "What's going to happen next?" she wondered.
"Sonya! What does anyone else in the world matter to me? You — you alone are everything!" said Nikolai. "And I'll prove it to you."
"I don't like you talking that way."
"Then I won't — just forgive me, Sonya!" He drew her close and kissed her.
"Oh, how lovely!" thought Natasha. And when Sonya and Nikolai had left the conservatory, she slipped out and called for Boris.

"Boris, come here," she said with a sly, knowing look. "I have something to tell you. Over here — come here!" And she led him into the conservatory, to the spot among the plant tubs where she had been hiding.
Boris followed her, smiling.
"What is it?" he asked.
She grew flustered, looked around, and spotting the doll she had dropped on one of the tubs, picked it up.
"Kiss the doll," she said.
Boris looked at her eager face attentively and kindly but didn't respond.
"You don't want to? Fine — come here then," she said, moving deeper among the plants and tossing the doll aside. "Closer — closer!" she whispered.
She caught hold of the young officer's sleeve, and an expression of solemnity and fear appeared on her flushed face.
"And me? Would you like to kiss me?" she whispered, barely audibly, glancing up at him from under her brows — smiling and almost crying with excitement.
Boris blushed.
"You're so funny!" he said, bending toward her and blushing even deeper — but he waited and did nothing.
Suddenly she jumped onto a plant tub so she was taller than him, wrapped both her thin bare arms around his neck, and tossing back her hair, kissed him right on the lips.
Then she slipped down on the other side of the tubs and stood there with her head hanging.
"Natasha," he said, "you know I love you, but..."
"You're in love with me?" Natasha interrupted.
"Yes, I am — but please, let's not do things like that... In four years... then I'll ask for your hand."
Natasha thought about it.
"Thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen," she counted on her slender little fingers. "All right! Then it's settled?"
A smile of joy and satisfaction lit up her eager face.
"Settled!" Boris replied.
"Forever?" said the little girl. "Until death itself?"
She took his arm and, her face glowing with happiness, walked with him into the next room.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter XIV
paragraphs: After receiving her guests, the countess was so exhausted that she ordered the porter to let no more visitors in — though he was told to make sure to invite everyone who came "to congratulate" to stay for dinner. The countess wanted a private talk with her childhood friend, Princess Anna Mikhaylovna, whom she hadn't properly seen since her return from Petersburg. Anna Mikhaylovna, her face careworn but kind, pulled her chair closer to the countess.
"With you I can be completely honest," said Anna Mikhaylovna. "There aren't many of us old friends left! That's why I treasure your friendship so much."
Anna Mikhaylovna glanced at Vera and paused. The countess squeezed her friend's hand.
"Vera," she said to her eldest daughter, who was clearly not the favorite, "where is your sense of tact? Can't you see you're not wanted here? Go be with the other girls, or..."
The beautiful Vera smiled dismissively but didn't look the slightest bit hurt.
"If you'd told me sooner, Mama, I would have left," she said, getting up to go to her room.

But passing through the sitting room, she noticed two couples — one pair at each window. She stopped and smiled disdainfully. Sonya was sitting close to Nikolai, who was copying out verses for her — the first he had ever written. Boris and Natasha were at the other window and stopped talking the moment Vera came in. Sonya and Natasha looked up at Vera with guilty, happy faces.
It was sweet and touching to see these girls in love — but the sight clearly did not stir any pleasant feelings in Vera.
"How many times have I asked you not to take my things?" she said. "You have your own room." And she took the inkstand from Nikolai.
"Just a minute, just a minute," he said, dipping his pen.
"You always manage to do things at the wrong moment," Vera went on. "You came bursting into the drawing room like that — everyone was embarrassed for you."
Although what she said was perfectly fair — perhaps precisely for that reason — no one responded, and the four of them simply stared at her. She lingered in the room, inkstand in hand.
"And at your age, what kind of secrets can there be between Natasha and Boris, or between you two? It's all nonsense!"
"Vera, what does it matter to you?" said Natasha gently, coming to everyone's defense.
She seemed more than usually kind and affectionate toward everyone that day.
"Very silly," said Vera. "I'm embarrassed for you. Secrets, indeed!"
"Everyone has their own secrets," Natasha shot back, her voice rising. "We don't meddle with you and Berg."
"I should hope not," said Vera, "because there could never be anything improper in my behavior. But I will tell Mama how you've been carrying on with Boris."
"Natalya Ilyinichna has been perfectly proper toward me," Boris remarked. "I have no complaints."

"Stop it, Boris! You're such a diplomat — it's really exhausting," said Natasha, her voice wounded and trembling slightly. She used the word "diplomat" — very fashionable among the children at the time — in its own special meaning. "Why does she have to bother me?" she added, turning to Vera. "You'll never understand, because you've never loved anyone. You have no heart! You're a Madame de Genlis and nothing more" — this nickname, bestowed on Vera by Nikolai, was considered a devastating insult — "and your greatest pleasure is making people miserable! Go flirt with Berg all you want," she finished sharply.
"At least I don't chase after young men in front of guests..."
"Well, now you've done what you came to do," Nikolai cut in. "You've said unpleasant things to everyone and upset them. Let's go to the nursery."
All four of them, like a flock of startled birds, jumped up and left the room.
"The unpleasant things were said to me," Vera remarked. "I didn't say anything unpleasant to anyone."
"Madame de Genlis! Madame de Genlis!" laughing voices shouted through the door.

The beautiful Vera, who had such an irritating and unpleasant effect on everyone, merely smiled, apparently unmoved by what had been said to her, and went to the mirror to fix her hair and scarf. Looking at her own handsome face, she seemed to grow even colder and calmer.
In the drawing room, the conversation between the mothers continued.

"Oh my dear," said the countess, "my life is no bed of roses either. Don't I know that at the rate we're spending, our money won't last? It's all because of the club and his easygoing nature. Even in the country we get no rest — theatricals, hunting, and God knows what else! But enough about me — tell me how you managed everything. I'm always amazed at you, Annette: how at your age you can rush around alone in a cab to Moscow, to Petersburg, to see all those ministers and important people, and deal with them all so cleverly! It's remarkable. How did you get it arranged? I could never manage that."

"Oh, my love," Anna Mikhaylovna answered, "may God spare you from ever knowing what it's like to be left a widow without means, with a son you love more than anything in the world! You learn a lot. That lawsuit taught me everything. When I need to see one of those important people, I write a note — 'Princess So-and-so requests an audience with So-and-so' — and then I take a cab and go myself, two, three, four times until I get what I want. I don't care what anyone thinks of me."

"And who did you go to about Boris?" asked the countess. "Your son is already an officer in the Guards, while my Nikolai is going as a mere cadet. There's nobody to put in a word for him. Who did you approach?"

"Prince Vasili. He was so kind. He agreed to everything at once and presented the matter to the Emperor," Princess Anna Mikhaylovna said enthusiastically, completely forgetting all the humiliation she had endured to achieve her goal.

"Has Prince Vasili aged much?" asked the countess. "I haven't seen him since we acted together in the Rumyantsovs' theatricals. I expect he's forgotten me. He used to pay me such attention in those days," the countess said with a smile.

"He's exactly the same as ever," Anna Mikhaylovna replied, "overflowing with charm. His position hasn't gone to his head at all. He said to me: 'I'm sorry I can do so little for you, dear Princess. I am at your service.' Yes, he's a fine man and a very kind relative. But, Nataly, you know how much I love my son — I would do anything for his happiness! And my finances are in such a terrible state that my situation is truly desperate," Anna Mikhaylovna continued, dropping her voice sadly. "My wretched lawsuit eats up everything I have and goes nowhere. Would you believe it — I literally don't have a penny and I don't know how to outfit Boris." She took out her handkerchief and began to cry. "I need five hundred rubles, and all I have is a single twenty-five-ruble note. I'm in an impossible position... My only hope now is Count Kirill Vladimirovich Bezukhov. If he won't help his own godson — you know he is Boris's godfather — and give him some allowance, then everything I've done will have been for nothing... I won't be able to equip him."
The countess's eyes filled with tears, and she sat thinking in silence.

"I often wonder — though perhaps it's sinful to think this way," said the princess, "there sits Count Kirill Vladimirovich Bezukhov, so rich, all alone... that enormous fortune... and what is his life worth to him? It's a burden. Meanwhile Boris's life is just beginning..."
"Surely he'll leave Boris something," said the countess.

"God only knows, my dear! These rich grandees are so selfish. Still — I'll take Boris and go see him right now, and I'll speak my mind plainly. Let people think what they will — it makes no difference to me when my son's future is at stake." The princess stood up. "It's two o'clock now and you dine at four. There's just enough time."
And like the practical Petersburg woman she was, who knew how to make every minute count, Anna Mikhaylovna sent for her son and went out to the entrance hall with him.
"Goodbye, my dear," she said to the countess, who saw her to the door, and added in a whisper so Boris wouldn't hear: "Wish me luck."

"Going to see Count Kirill Vladimirovich, are you, my dear?" said the count, emerging from the dining room into the hall. "If he's feeling better, do ask Pierre to come to dinner. He's been to our house before — even danced with the children. Be sure to invite him! We'll see how Taras outdoes himself today. He says Count Orlov never gave a dinner like the one we're putting on!"

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter XV
paragraphs: "My dear Boris," said Princess Anna Mikhaylovna to her son as Countess Rostova's carriage carried them along the straw-covered street and turned into the wide courtyard of Count Kirill Vladimirovich Bezukhov's mansion. "My dear Boris," the mother said, drawing her hand from beneath her old cloak and placing it gently and tenderly on her son's arm, "be kind and attentive to him. Count Kirill Vladimirovich is your godfather, after all, and your future depends on him. Remember that, my dear, and be sweet to him — the way you know so well how to be."
"If I thought anything would come of it besides humiliation..." her son replied coolly. "But I promised, and I'll do it for your sake."

Although the hall porter saw a carriage standing at the entrance, after looking over the mother and son — who had walked straight through the glass porch between the rows of statues without being announced — and casting a pointed glance at the lady's shabby old cloak, he asked whether they wanted the count or the princesses. When he heard they wanted the count, he informed them that His Excellency was worse today and was not receiving anyone.
"We might as well go back," said the son in French. [speaking in French]
"My darling!" his mother exclaimed imploringly, again touching his arm, as if her touch might soothe or inspire him.
Boris said nothing more but looked at his mother questioningly without removing his cloak.

"My good man," said Anna Mikhaylovna to the porter in a gentle tone, "I know Count Kirill Vladimirovich is very ill... that's why I've come. I'm a relative. I won't disturb him. I just need to see Prince Vasili Sergeyevich — he's staying here, isn't he? Please announce me."
The porter reluctantly pulled a bell that rang upstairs and turned away.
"Princess Drubetskaya to see Prince Vasili Sergeyevich!" he called out to a footman in knee breeches, buckled shoes, and a tailcoat who came running down the stairs and peered over from the landing.
The mother smoothed the folds of her dyed silk dress in front of a large Venetian mirror on the wall, then briskly climbed the carpeted stairs in her worn-down shoes.
"Remember, my dear," she said to her son, squeezing his arm once more, "you promised me!"
The son, eyes lowered, followed her quietly.
They entered a large hall from which a door led to the rooms assigned to Prince Vasili.

Just as the mother and son reached the middle of the hall and were about to ask directions of an elderly footman who had jumped up at their approach, a bronze door handle turned and Prince Vasili emerged — wearing a velvet house coat with a single decoration on his chest, as was his custom at home — seeing off a handsome, dark-haired man. This was the celebrated Petersburg physician, Dr. Lorrain.
"So it's certain?" said the prince.
"Prince, to err is human, but..." the doctor replied, swallowing his r's and pronouncing the Latin with a French accent. [speaking in Latin]
* To err is human.
"Very well, very well..."

Noticing Anna Mikhaylovna and her son, Prince Vasili dismissed the doctor with a bow and approached them silently, with an inquiring look. Boris noticed that a sudden expression of deep sorrow crossed his mother's face, and he smiled faintly.
"Oh, Prince! What sad circumstances bring us together again! And how is our dear patient?" she said, as though completely unaware of the cold, hostile look directed at her.

Prince Vasili stared at her and at Boris with puzzled suspicion. Boris bowed politely. Prince Vasili, without acknowledging the bow, turned to Anna Mikhaylovna and answered her question with a slight movement of his head and lips, indicating very little hope for the patient.
"Is it possible?" Anna Mikhaylovna exclaimed. "Oh, how terrible! It's frightening to even think about... This is my son," she added, gesturing toward Boris. "He wanted to thank you in person."
Boris bowed politely again.
"Believe me, Prince, a mother's heart will never forget what you have done for us."

"I'm glad I could be of service, my dear Anna Mikhaylovna," said Prince Vasili, adjusting his lace cuff. His tone and manner here in Moscow — toward Anna Mikhaylovna, whom he had done a favor — carried an air of far greater importance than it had in Petersburg at Anna Scherer's reception.
"Try to serve well and prove yourself worthy," he added, addressing Boris with a touch of sternness. "I'm glad to hear it... You're here on leave?" he went on in his usual indifferent tone.

"I'm waiting for orders to join my new regiment, Your Excellency," Boris replied, showing neither irritation at the prince's brusque manner nor eagerness to chat, but speaking so calmly and respectfully that Prince Vasili gave him a searching look.
"Are you living with your mother?"
"I'm staying with Countess Rostova," Boris replied, adding again, "Your Excellency."
"That is, with Ilya Rostov, who married Natalya Shinshina," said Anna Mikhaylovna.

"I know, I know," Prince Vasili answered in his monotone. "I never could understand how Natalya brought herself to marry that rough bear! A perfectly absurd and stupid man — and a gambler, too, from what I hear."

"But a very good-hearted man, Prince," Anna Mikhaylovna said with a sad little smile, as though she too agreed the count deserved criticism but was asking him not to be too harsh on the poor old fellow. "What do the doctors say?" she asked after a pause, her careworn face again expressing deep concern.
"They hold out little hope," replied the prince.

"And I would so like to thank Uncle once and for all for his kindness to Boris and me. He is Boris's godfather, after all," she added, in a tone suggesting this fact should mean a great deal to Prince Vasili.
Prince Vasili grew thoughtful and frowned. Anna Mikhaylovna could see he was afraid she might prove a rival for Count Bezukhov's fortune, and she quickly moved to reassure him.

"If it weren't for my sincere affection and devotion to Uncle," she said — pronouncing the word "Uncle" with particular ease and confidence — "I know his character: noble, upright... but he has no one with him except the young princesses. They're still so young..." She lowered her head and continued in a whisper: "Has he received the last rites, Prince? These final moments are beyond price! Things can't get any worse, and he absolutely must be prepared, if he's this ill. We women, Prince," she added with a tender smile, "always know how to handle these situations. I simply must see him, however painful it may be for me. I'm used to suffering."
The prince evidently understood her, and also understood — as he had at Anna Pavlovna's — that it would be very difficult to get rid of Anna Mikhaylovna.
"Wouldn't such a visit be too much for him, dear Anna Mikhaylovna?" he said. "Let's wait until evening. The doctors are expecting a crisis."
"But one can't delay at a moment like this, Prince! Think of the welfare of his soul. Oh, it's terrible — the duties of a Christian..."

A door from one of the inner rooms opened and one of the princesses — the count's niece — came out, her face cold and stern. The striking disproportion between her long body and short legs was immediately noticeable. Prince Vasili turned to her.
"How is he?"
"The same. But what do you expect, with all this commotion..." said the princess, looking at Anna Mikhaylovna as though she were a stranger.

"Oh, my dear, I barely recognized you!" said Anna Mikhaylovna with a bright smile, bustling lightly up to the count's niece. "I've come to help you nurse my uncle. I can imagine what you've been through," she added, rolling her eyes sympathetically upward.

The princess made no reply and didn't even smile, but left the room. Anna Mikhaylovna took off her gloves and, having established her position, settled into an armchair and invited Prince Vasili to sit beside her.

"Boris," she said to her son with a smile, "I'll go in to see the count — my uncle. You go visit Pierre in the meantime, and don't forget to give him the Rostovs' dinner invitation. I don't suppose he'll come?" she added, turning to the prince.

"On the contrary," the prince replied, clearly having grown dispirited, "I'd be only too glad if you'd take that young man off my hands... He's right here, and the count hasn't asked for him even once."
He shrugged. A footman led Boris down one flight of stairs and up another to Pierre's rooms.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter XVI
paragraphs: Pierre, as it turned out, had never managed to choose a career in Petersburg. He had been expelled from the city for disorderly conduct and sent back to Moscow. The story the visitors told at the Rostovs' was true — Pierre really had helped tie a policeman to a bear. He had been in Moscow for several days now, staying as usual at his father's house. Though he expected the story of his escapade had already reached Moscow and that the ladies attending his father — who had never been favorably disposed toward him — would use it to turn the count against him, he nevertheless went to his father's wing of the house on the day he arrived. Entering the drawing room where the princesses spent most of their time, he greeted the three ladies: two were sitting at embroidery frames while the third read aloud. The reader was the eldest — the one who had encountered Anna Mikhaylovna. The two younger ones were embroidering; both were rosy and pretty, differing only in that one had a small mole on her lip which made her considerably more attractive. Pierre was received as though he were a plague victim. The eldest princess stopped reading and stared at him in silent alarm; the second wore exactly the same expression; while the youngest — the one with the mole, who had a cheerful, lively disposition — bent over her frame to hide a smile, presumably at the entertaining scene she anticipated. She pulled her thread through the canvas and, barely able to contain her laughter, leaned down as if studying the pattern.
"Hello, cousin," said Pierre. "Don't you recognize me?"
"I recognize you only too well. All too well."
"How is the count? May I see him?" Pierre asked, awkward as always but completely unembarrassed.
"The count is suffering both physically and mentally, and it seems you have done your best to add to his mental suffering."
"May I see the count?" Pierre asked again.

"Hmm... If you want to kill him — kill him outright — then by all means, go see him. Olga, go check whether Uncle's broth is ready — it's nearly time," she added, making it clear to Pierre that they were busy and occupied with caring for his father, while he, Pierre, was only busy causing trouble.
Olga left the room. Pierre stood looking at the sisters, then bowed and said: "Then I'll go to my rooms. Let me know when I can see him."
He walked out, followed by the quiet but clear laughter of the sister with the mole.

The next day Prince Vasili arrived and settled into the count's house. He sent for Pierre and told him: "My dear fellow, if you're going to behave here the way you did in Petersburg, things will end very badly for you. That's all I have to say. The count is extremely ill, and you must not see him at all."
Since then Pierre had been left alone and had spent all his time in his rooms upstairs.

When Boris appeared at his door, Pierre was pacing back and forth across his room, pausing now and then at a corner to thrust menacingly at the wall, as though running through an invisible opponent with a sword, and glaring fiercely over his spectacles before resuming his march, muttering unclear words and gesticulating.

"England is finished," he said, scowling and pointing his finger at an unseen figure. "Mr. Pitt, as a traitor to the nation and the rights of man, is sentenced to..." But before Pierre — who at that moment was imagining himself to be Napoleon, having just completed the perilous crossing of the English Channel and captured London — could pronounce Pitt's sentence, he noticed a handsome, well-built young officer standing in his doorway. Pierre stopped. He had last seen Boris when the boy was fourteen and had completely forgotten him, but in his typical impulsive, open-hearted way, he grabbed Boris's hand with a warm smile.
"Do you remember me?" Boris asked quietly, with a pleasant smile. "I've come with my mother to visit the count, but it seems he isn't well."
"Yes, apparently he's ill. People are always disturbing him," Pierre answered, trying to figure out who this young man was.
Boris could tell that Pierre didn't recognize him but didn't see any need to introduce himself. Without the slightest embarrassment, he looked Pierre straight in the eye.
"Count Rostov invites you to dinner today," he said, after a pause long enough to make Pierre uncomfortable.

"Ah, Count Rostov!" Pierre exclaimed happily. "So you're his son, Ilya? Imagine that — I didn't recognize you at first! Do you remember how we went to Sparrow Hills with Madame Jacquot? That was ages ago..."

"You're mistaken," Boris said deliberately, with a confident, slightly ironic smile. "I'm Boris, son of Princess Anna Mikhaylovna Drubetskaya. Rostov the father is Ilya, and his son is Nikolai. I never knew any Madame Jacquot."
Pierre shook his head and waved his hands as if shooing away a swarm of gnats.

"Oh dear — what am I thinking? I've gotten everything mixed up. There are so many relatives in Moscow! So you're Boris? Right, of course. Well, now we know where we stand. What do you think about the Boulogne expedition? If Napoleon gets across the Channel, the English are in for a rough time. I think the whole thing is perfectly feasible — as long as Villeneuve doesn't ruin everything!"
Boris knew nothing about the Boulogne expedition; he didn't read the newspapers and had never heard the name Villeneuve.

"We here in Moscow are more interested in dinner parties and gossip than in politics," he said in his calm, ironic way. "I don't know anything about it and haven't given it any thought. Moscow mainly occupies itself with rumors," he continued. "Right now everyone is talking about you and your father."

Pierre smiled his good-natured smile, almost as if worried that his companion might say something he would later regret. But Boris spoke clearly, precisely, and coolly, looking Pierre straight in the eye.
"Moscow has nothing better to do than gossip," Boris went on. "Everyone is wondering who the count will leave his fortune to, though he may well outlive us all — which I sincerely hope he does..."
"Yes, it's all very unpleasant," Pierre broke in. "Very unpleasant."
Pierre was still nervous that this officer might inadvertently say something awkward.
"And it must seem to you," said Boris, blushing slightly but maintaining his tone and composure, "it must seem to you that everyone is trying to get something out of the rich man?"
"That's exactly what it seems like," Pierre thought to himself.

"But I want to say, to avoid any misunderstanding, that you would be completely wrong to count me or my mother among such people. We are very poor, but precisely because your father is rich, I don't consider myself his relative. Neither my mother nor I would ever ask for or accept anything from him."

It took Pierre a long time to understand, but when he did, he leaped off the sofa, grabbed Boris by the elbow in his quick, clumsy way, and — blushing far more deeply than Boris — began speaking with a mixture of shame and agitation.
"Wait — this is extraordinary! You don't think I... Who could possibly... I know perfectly well..."
But Boris cut him off again.

"I'm glad I've spoken frankly. Perhaps you didn't like hearing it? Please forgive me," he said, managing to put Pierre at ease rather than the other way around, "but I hope I haven't offended you. I make it a rule to always speak my mind... So, what answer shall I bring back? Will you come to dinner at the Rostovs'?"
And Boris, having apparently discharged a burdensome duty, extracted himself neatly from an awkward situation — and deposited someone else into one — and became perfectly agreeable again.

"No, but listen," said Pierre, calming down. "You really are a remarkable person! What you just said was good — very good. Of course you don't know me. We haven't seen each other since we were children. You might have thought that I... I understand, completely. I couldn't have done it myself — I wouldn't have had the nerve. But it's wonderful. I'm very glad to have met you. And it's funny," he added after a pause, "that you should have suspected me!" He began to laugh. "Well, so what! I hope we'll get to know each other better." He squeezed Boris's hand. "You know, I haven't been in to see the count even once. He hasn't asked for me... I feel sorry for him as a person, but what can you do?"
"So do you think Napoleon will actually get an army across the Channel?" Boris asked with a smile.
Pierre could see Boris wanted to change the subject, and being of the same mind, he launched into an explanation of the advantages and disadvantages of the Boulogne expedition.

A footman came to summon Boris — the princess was leaving. Pierre, wanting to get to know Boris better, promised to come to dinner. Pressing his hand warmly and looking at him affectionately over his spectacles, he watched him go. After Boris left, Pierre continued pacing his room for a long time — no longer running an imaginary sword through imaginary enemies, but smiling as he thought about this pleasant, intelligent, and determined young man.
As so often happens in early youth — especially for someone who leads a solitary life — he felt an inexplicable warmth toward this young man and made up his mind that they would become friends.
Prince Vasili saw the princess off. She was holding a handkerchief to her eyes, her face streaked with tears.

"It's terrible, terrible!" she was saying. "But whatever the cost, I'll do my duty. I'll come back and spend the night. He mustn't be left like this. Every moment is precious. I can't understand why his nieces keep putting it off. Perhaps God will help me find a way to prepare him!... Goodbye, Prince! May God give you strength..."
"Goodbye, my dear," Prince Vasili replied, turning away from her. [speaking in French]
"Oh, he's in a terrible state," the mother said to her son when they were in the carriage. "He barely recognizes anyone."
"I don't understand, Mama — what is his attitude toward Pierre?" the son asked.
"The will shall reveal that, my dear. Our fate depends on it too."
"But why do you expect him to leave us anything?"
"Oh, my dear! He's so rich, and we're so poor!"
"Well, that's hardly sufficient reason, Mama..."
"Oh, God! How terribly ill he is!" the mother exclaimed.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter XVII
paragraphs: After Anna Mikhaylovna drove off with her son to visit Count Kirill Vladimirovich Bezukhov, Countess Rostova sat alone for a long time, pressing her handkerchief to her eyes. At last she rang the bell.
"What's taken you so long, my dear?" she said irritably to the maid who had kept her waiting several minutes. "Don't you wish to serve me? I'll find you another position."
The countess was upset by her friend's grief and humiliating poverty, and her bad mood — as always — expressed itself in calling the maid "my dear" and speaking to her with pointed politeness.
"I'm very sorry, ma'am," the maid answered.
"Ask the count to come to me."
The count came waddling in to see his wife, wearing his usual slightly guilty expression.
"Well, little countess! What a game saute with Madeira we're going to have, my dear! I tasted it. The thousand rubles I paid for Taras were money well spent. He's worth every kopeck!"
He sat down beside his wife, elbows on his knees, running his fingers through his gray hair.
"What can I do for you, little countess?"
"Well, you see, my dear... What's that stain?" she said, pointing to his waistcoat. "It's the saute, I imagine," she added with a smile. "The thing is, Count — I need some money."
Her face turned sad.
"Oh, little countess!..." And the count began fumbling for his wallet.
"Quite a lot, Count. I need five hundred rubles," she said, and taking out a cambric handkerchief, she started wiping the spot on her husband's waistcoat.
"Right away, right away! Hey, who's there?" he called out in the tone of a man who is absolutely certain that the people he summons will rush to obey. "Send Dmitri to me!"
Dmitri — a man of good family who had been raised in the count's household and now managed all his affairs — stepped quietly into the room.

"Here's what I need, my good fellow," the count said to the respectful young man. "Bring me..." He thought for a moment. "Yes — bring me seven hundred rubles. But mind, don't bring the kind of torn, dirty bills you brought last time. Nice clean ones, for the countess."
"Yes, Dmitri — clean notes, please," said the countess with a deep sigh.

"When would you like them, Your Excellency?" asked Dmitri. "Allow me to mention... But don't worry," he added quickly, noticing the count's breathing grow heavy and rapid — always a sign of approaching anger. "Forgive me, I was getting sidetracked... Shall I bring them right away?"
"Yes, yes — exactly! Bring them. Give them to the countess."
"What a treasure that Dmitri is," the count added with a smile once the young man had left. "Nothing is ever 'impossible' with him. That's something I can't stand! Everything is possible."
"Oh, money, Count — money! The grief it causes in this world," the countess said. "But I desperately need this amount."
"You, my little countess, are a well-known spendthrift," said the count, and having kissed his wife's hand, he headed back to his study.

When Anna Mikhaylovna returned from Count Bezukhov's, the money — all in clean notes — was lying ready under a handkerchief on the countess's small table. Anna Mikhaylovna could tell something was on her friend's mind.
"Well, my dear?" asked the countess.
"Oh, he's in a terrible state! You wouldn't recognize him, he's so ill. I was only there a few minutes and barely said a word..."
"Annette, for heaven's sake — don't refuse me," the countess began, a blush appearing on her thin, dignified, elderly face that looked very odd there. She took the money from under the handkerchief.
Anna Mikhaylovna instantly understood her intention and leaned forward, ready to embrace the countess at the right moment.
"This is for Boris — from me — for his outfit."

Anna Mikhaylovna was already in her arms, weeping. The countess wept too. They wept because they were friends, and because they were kindhearted, and because they — childhood friends — had been forced to think about something as base as money, and because their youth was gone... But those tears were sweet to both of them.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter XVIII
paragraphs: Countess Rostova, with her daughters and a large number of guests, was already seated in the drawing room. The count had taken the gentlemen into his study and was showing them his prized collection of Turkish pipes. From time to time he popped out to ask: "Hasn't she arrived yet?" They were waiting for Marya Dmitrievna Akhrosimova, known in society as the "terrible dragon" — a lady distinguished not for wealth or rank but for common sense and blunt honesty. Marya Dmitrievna was known to the imperial family as well as to all of Moscow and Petersburg. Both cities marveled at her, privately laughed at her rudeness, and traded stories about her — while every last person, without exception, respected and feared her.

In the count's smoke-filled study, the men were talking about the war that had been announced in a manifesto, and about the army draft. None of them had actually seen the manifesto, but they all knew it had been published. The count sat on the sofa between two smoking, chatting guests. He neither smoked nor talked, but kept tilting his head from side to side, watching the smokers with obvious pleasure and listening to his two neighbors' conversation, which he encouraged by playing one off against the other.

One of them was a sallow, clean-shaven civilian with a thin, wrinkled face — already aging, though he dressed like the most fashionable young man. He sat with his legs drawn up on the sofa as if completely at home and, with an amber mouthpiece jammed deep in his mouth, was inhaling smoke in quick bursts and squinting. This was Shinshin, an old bachelor, a cousin of the countess's and a man with what Moscow society called "a sharp tongue." He seemed to be looking down on his companion. The other man was a fresh-faced, rosy Guards officer — immaculately washed, brushed, and buttoned — who held his pipe in the middle of his mouth and gently drew in the smoke with his red lips, letting it out in perfect rings. This was Lieutenant Berg, an officer in the Semenov regiment with whom Boris was to travel to join the army — the same Berg about whom Natasha had teased her sister Vera, calling him Vera's "intended." The count sat between the two men and listened attentively. His favorite pastime, apart from boston — a card game he adored — was listening, especially when he managed to set two talkative people against each other.

"Well then, old boy, my most honorable Alphonse Karlovich," said Shinshin with an ironic laugh, mixing the most ordinary Russian with the choicest French phrases — a hallmark of his speech. "You're planning to make your fortune from government service, are you?" [speaking in French]
* You expect to make an income out of the government.
"No, Pyotr Nikolaevich; I merely want to show that the cavalry offers far fewer advantages than the infantry. Just consider my own position, Pyotr Nikolaevich..."

Berg always spoke quietly, politely, and with great precision. His conversation always centered entirely on himself; he could remain perfectly calm and silent when the talk had nothing to do with him, without any discomfort to himself or others. But the moment the conversation turned to him, he would begin speaking at length with obvious satisfaction.

"Consider my position, Pyotr Nikolaevich. If I were in the cavalry, I'd receive no more than two hundred rubles every four months, even with the rank of lieutenant. But as it is, I get two hundred and thirty," he said, looking at Shinshin and the count with a beaming, contented smile, as if it were self-evident that his success must be everyone else's fondest wish too.

"Besides that, Pyotr Nikolaevich, by transferring to the Guards I'll be in a more prominent position," Berg continued, "and vacancies come up much more often in the infantry Guards. And just think what you can do with two hundred and thirty rubles! I even manage to save a little and send some to my father." He blew a smoke ring.

"So that squares the accounts... A German always knows how to squeeze blood from a stone, as the saying goes," Shinshin remarked, shifting his pipe to the other side of his mouth and winking at the count. [speaking in French]
* So that squares matters.

The count burst out laughing. The other guests, hearing that Shinshin was in good form, came closer to listen. Berg, oblivious to both irony and indifference, went on explaining how by transferring to the Guards he had already leapfrogged his former classmates from the Cadet Corps; how in wartime the company commander might get killed and he, as the senior man in the company, could easily succeed to the post; how popular he was with everyone in the regiment; and how pleased his father was with him. Berg clearly enjoyed telling all this and didn't seem to suspect that other people might have their own interests. But everything he said was so primly measured, and the innocence of his youthful self-centeredness was so transparent, that he won over his listeners in spite of themselves.
"Well, my boy, you'll do well wherever you end up — on foot or on horseback — I'll vouch for that," said Shinshin, patting him on the shoulder and swinging his feet off the sofa.
Berg smiled happily. The count, followed by his guests, moved into the drawing room.

It was the moment just before a large dinner when the assembled guests, waiting for the call to hors d'oeuvres, avoid starting any long conversation but feel obliged to move around and chat, to show they are not at all impatient for their food. The hosts keep glancing toward the door and exchanging looks, and the visitors try to guess from these glances who or what is being waited for — some important relative who hasn't arrived, or a dish that isn't ready.
* Hors d'oeuvres.

Pierre had arrived just at dinnertime and was sitting awkwardly in the middle of the drawing room on the first chair he had found, blocking everyone's way. The countess tried to draw him into conversation, but he just gazed around naively through his spectacles, as if looking for someone, and answered all her questions with single syllables. He was in the way, and he was the only person who didn't notice it. Most of the guests, having heard the story about the bear, studied this big, heavyset, quiet man with curiosity, wondering how such a clumsy, modest fellow could have pulled such a stunt on a policeman.
"You've only recently arrived?" the countess asked him.
"Yes, madame," he replied, looking around the room. [speaking in French]
"You haven't met my husband yet?"
"No, madame." He smiled in a way that was completely out of place.
"You've been in Paris recently, I believe? It must be very interesting."
"Very interesting."

The countess exchanged a glance with Anna Mikhaylovna. The latter understood she was being asked to entertain this young man and, sitting down beside him, began talking about his father. But he answered her, as he had the countess, in monosyllables. The other guests chatted among themselves. "The Razumovskys... It was charming... You're too kind... Countess Apraksina..." could be heard on all sides. The countess stood up and walked into the ballroom.
"Marya Dmitrievna?" her voice called out from there.
"The one and only," came the answer in a gruff voice, and Marya Dmitrievna entered the room.

All the unmarried women and even the married ones — except the very oldest — rose to their feet. Marya Dmitrievna paused in the doorway. Tall and stout, she held her fifty-year-old head high, its gray curls piled up, and surveyed the guests as she deliberately pushed up her wide sleeves as if rolling them for work. Marya Dmitrievna always spoke in Russian.

"Health and happiness to the birthday girl and her children," she said in her booming voice that drowned out everything else. "Well, you old rascal," she said to the count, who was kissing her hand, "bored in Moscow, are you? Nowhere to run your hounds? But what can you do at your age? Just look how these chicks are growing up" — she pointed at the girls. "Like it or not, you'll have to start finding them husbands..."

"Well," she said, "how's my little Cossack?" — Marya Dmitrievna always called Natasha a Cossack — and she stroked the child's arm as Natasha came up boldly and cheerfully to kiss her hand. "I know she's a little rascal, but I like her."

She pulled a pair of pear-shaped ruby earrings from her enormous handbag and, giving them to the beaming, rosy Natasha who was glowing with the pleasure of her name day, she turned away immediately and addressed Pierre.

"Hey there, come here, friend!" she said, softening her voice to a high, gentle tone. "Come here, my dear..." And she pushed her sleeves up even higher, in an ominous gesture. Pierre approached her, looking childlike through his spectacles.

"Closer, closer, friend! I used to be the only person who told your father the truth when he was riding high, and with you it's clearly my duty too." She paused. Everyone fell silent, sensing this was only the prologue.
"A fine young man you are! My word! A fine one! His father is on his deathbed, and he's out tying policemen to bears! You should be ashamed of yourself, sir — ashamed! Better you'd gone off to war."
She turned away and gave her hand to the count, who was struggling not to burst out laughing.
"Well, I think it's time for dinner, isn't it?" said Marya Dmitrievna.

The count led the way in with Marya Dmitrievna; the countess followed on the arm of a hussar colonel — an important figure for the family since Nikolai was to join his regiment. Then came Anna Mikhaylovna with Shinshin. Berg escorted Vera. The smiling Julie Karagina went in with Nikolai. After them came more couples, filling the entire dining room, and finally the children, their tutors, and governesses followed one by one. Footmen bustled about, chairs scraped, the band struck up from the gallery, and the guests settled into their places. The orchestra soon gave way to the clatter of knives and forks, the hum of conversation, and the soft footsteps of servants. At one end of the table sat the countess with Marya Dmitrievna on her right and Anna Mikhaylovna on her left, the other ladies further down. At the other end sat the count, with the hussar colonel on his left and Shinshin and the other gentlemen on his right. Midway down the long table, the young people sat on one side — Vera next to Berg, Pierre beside Boris — and on the other, the children with their tutors and governesses. The count kept peering through the crystal decanters and fruit displays at his wife and her tall blue-ribboned cap, busily filling his neighbors' glasses without neglecting his own. The countess, without shirking her hostess duties, threw meaningful glances from behind the pineapples at her husband, whose flushed face and bald head seemed redder than ever against his gray hair. At the ladies' end, a constant stream of chatter flowed; at the men's end, the voices grew louder and louder, especially the hussar colonel's, who ate and drank so copiously, growing ever more flushed, that the count held him up as an example to everyone. Berg was telling Vera with tender smiles that love is not an earthly but a heavenly feeling. Boris was pointing out the various guests to his new friend Pierre, and exchanging glances with Natasha across the table. Pierre said little but studied the unfamiliar faces and ate a great deal. Of the two soups he chose the turtle with savory pastries and then worked through every dish and every wine without skipping a single one. The wines were presented by the butler, who crept up behind each guest's shoulder with the bottle wrapped in a napkin and whispered: "Dry Madeira... Hungarian... Rhine wine." Of the four monogrammed crystal glasses before his place, Pierre would hold out whichever one came to hand and drink with pleasure, gazing with growing warmth at the other guests. Natasha, sitting opposite, watched Boris the way a thirteen-year-old girl watches the boy she loves and has just kissed for the first time. Occasionally that same look fell on Pierre, and that funny, lively little girl's glance made him want to laugh without knowing why.

Nikolai was seated some distance from Sonya, next to Julie Karagina, and was again chatting with her with that same involuntary smile. Sonya wore a polite smile but was clearly tormented by jealousy — now turning pale, now blushing, straining to overhear what Nikolai and Julie were saying to each other. The governess kept glancing around anxiously, as if bracing to defend the children against any slight. The German tutor was trying to memorize every dish, wine, and dessert so he could write a full account of the dinner to his family back in Germany. He was deeply offended when the butler, napkin-wrapped bottle in hand, passed right by him. He frowned, trying to look as though he didn't want any of that wine, but was mortified because no one understood that his interest was not thirst or gluttony — it was purely a conscientious desire for knowledge.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter XIX
paragraphs: At the men's end of the table, the conversation was growing more and more animated. The colonel announced that the declaration of war had already been published in Petersburg and that a copy — which he had seen with his own eyes — had been sent by courier that very day to the commander in chief.
"And why the devil are we going to fight Bonaparte?" Shinshin remarked. "He's already shut Austria up, and I'm afraid we're next."
The colonel was a stout, tall, ruddy-faced German, clearly devoted to the service and patriotically Russian. He took offense at Shinshin's remark.

"It iss for ze reason, my goot sir," he said, speaking with a heavy German accent, "for ze reason zat ze Emperor knows zat. He declares in ze manifesto zat he cannot view viz indifference ze danger zreatening Russia, and zat ze safety and dignity of ze Empire as vell as ze sanctity of its alliances..." He emphasized this last word as if it contained the heart of the matter.
Then, with the flawless bureaucratic memory that was his hallmark, he recited from the opening of the manifesto:

...and the wish, which constitutes the Emperor's sole and absolute aim — to establish peace in Europe on firm foundations — has now led him to dispatch part of the army abroad and to create the conditions for the attainment of that purpose.
"Zat, my dear sir, is vy..." he concluded, drinking a glass of wine with dignity and looking to the count for approval.

"Do you know the proverb: 'Jerome, Jerome, stay at home, turn the spindle on your own'?" said Shinshin, his brows furrowed, a mocking smile on his face. "That suits us perfectly. Suvorov — now there was a man who knew what he was doing. And even he was beaten flat. And where are we supposed to find Suvorovs today? I ask you!" he said, switching constantly between French and Russian. [speaking in French]
*Do you know the proverb?
*(2) That suits us perfectly.
*(3) Flat, utterly.
*(4) I ask you.

"Ve must fight to ze last dr-r-rop of our blood!" the colonel roared, pounding the table. "And ve must die for our Emperor, and zen all vill be vell. And ve must discuss it as little as po-o-ossible" — he lingered on the word — "as po-o-ossible," he repeated, turning to the count again. "Zat is how ve old hussars see it, and zere's an end of it! And you, young man — young hussar — how do you see it?" he added, turning to Nikolai, who had abandoned his dinner companion the moment the war came up and was listening with rapt attention.

"I completely agree with you," Nikolai replied, his face flushing. He turned his plate around and shifted his wineglasses with the kind of determination and desperation you'd show when facing mortal danger. "I am convinced that we Russians must either die or conquer," he declared — and then realized, as did everyone else, that his words had come out too earnest and emphatic for the occasion, making them awkward.
"What you just said was splendid!" said his dinner partner Julie.
Sonya trembled from head to toe, blushing crimson — from her ears down to her neck and shoulders — the whole time Nikolai was speaking.
Pierre listened to the colonel's speech and nodded approvingly.
"Well said," he agreed.
"Now that's a real hussar!" the colonel bellowed, thumping the table again.

"What's all that racket about down there?" Marya Dmitrievna's deep voice suddenly called from the other end of the table. "Why are you banging the table? And why are you getting so worked up? Do you think the French are actually here?"
"I am speaking ze troos," the hussar colonel replied with a smile.
"It's all about the war," the count shouted down the table. "You know my son's going, Marya Dmitrievna? My boy is going."

"I have four sons in the army and I don't fret about it. Everything is in God's hands. You can die in your bed just as easily as God might spare you in battle," Marya Dmitrievna replied, her deep voice carrying effortlessly the full length of the table.
"That's true!"
The conversations split again — women's talk at one end, men's at the other.
"You won't ask," Natasha's little brother was saying. "I know you won't!"
"I will," Natasha replied.
Her face suddenly lit up with reckless, joyful determination. She half rose from her seat, her eyes inviting Pierre, who sat across from her, to watch what was coming, and turned to her mother:
"Mama!" rang out the clear contralto notes of her childish voice, audible from one end of the table to the other.
"What is it?" asked the countess, startled; but seeing from her daughter's expression that it was just mischief, she wagged a stern finger at her with a threatening shake of her head.
The entire table fell silent.
"Mama! What dessert are we having?" And Natasha's voice rang out even more firm and determined.
The countess tried to frown but couldn't. Marya Dmitrievna wagged her plump finger.
"Cossack!" she said threateningly.
Most of the guests, unsure how to react to this outburst, looked to the adults for guidance.
"You'd better watch yourself!" said the countess.
"Mama! What dessert are we having?" Natasha called out again, boldly and merrily, confident her prank would be well received.
Sonya and chubby little Petya collapsed in giggles.
"See? I asked," Natasha whispered to her little brother and to Pierre, glancing at him once more.
"Ice cream — but you won't get any," said Marya Dmitrievna.
Natasha realized there was nothing to fear and decided to press even Marya Dmitrievna.
"Marya Dmitrievna! What kind of ice cream? I don't like plain ice cream."
"Carrot flavor."
"No! What kind, Marya Dmitrievna? What kind?" she nearly shrieked. "I want to know!"

Marya Dmitrievna and the countess burst out laughing, and every guest joined in. They weren't laughing at Marya Dmitrievna's answer — they were laughing at the sheer audacity and charm of this little girl who had dared to take on Marya Dmitrievna.

Natasha only relented when told there would be pineapple ice cream. Before dessert, champagne was poured. The band struck up again, the count and countess kissed, and the guests rose from their seats to "congratulate" the countess, reaching across the table to clink glasses with the count, the children, and each other. Footmen rushed about once more, chairs scraped, and in the same order they had entered — but with considerably redder faces — the guests filed back to the drawing room and the count's study.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter XX
paragraphs: Card tables were set up, groups formed for boston, and the count's guests settled themselves in the two drawing rooms, the sitting room, and the library.

The count, holding his cards in a fan, struggled to stay awake through his usual post-dinner drowsiness and laughed at everything. The young people, at the countess's suggestion, gathered around the clavichord and harp. Julie played first at everyone's request. After she had performed a little piece with variations on the harp, she joined the other girls in begging Natasha and Nikolai — who were known for their musical talent — to sing something. Natasha, who was being treated like a grown-up, was clearly very proud of this but at the same time felt shy.
"What should we sing?" she asked.
"'The Brook,'" Nikolai suggested.
"All right then — quick! Boris, come here," said Natasha. "But where's Sonya?"
She glanced around the room and, not seeing her friend, ran off to find her.

She tried Sonya's room first — no luck. Then the nursery — not there either. Natasha concluded she must be on the trunk in the hallway. The hallway trunk was the designated mourning place for the younger females of the Rostov household. And sure enough, there was Sonya, lying face down on the nurse's old feather mattress on top of the trunk, crumpling her gauzy pink dress beneath her, hiding her face in her slender fingers, and sobbing so hard that her bare little shoulders shook. Natasha's face — which had been radiant with happiness all day — suddenly changed: her eyes went fixed, a shiver ran down her broad neck, and the corners of her mouth pulled downward.

"Sonya! What is it? What's wrong?... Ooh... ooh... ooh...!" Natasha's wide mouth opened, making her look quite ugly, and she began to wail like a baby for no reason other than that Sonya was crying. Sonya tried to lift her head to explain but couldn't, and buried her face deeper in the mattress. Natasha sat down on the blue-striped featherbed, threw her arms around her friend, and wept alongside her. With an effort, Sonya finally sat up, wiped her eyes, and began to explain.

"Nikolai is leaving in a week — his papers have come — he told me himself — but I shouldn't cry," she said, showing Natasha a paper she was holding — the verses Nikolai had written. "I shouldn't be crying, but you can't... nobody can understand... what a wonderful soul he has!"
And she began crying again because he had such a wonderful soul.

"It's easy for you... I'm not jealous... I love you and Boris too," she went on, gathering a little strength. "He's nice... there's nothing standing in your way. But Nikolai is my cousin... you'd need... the Metropolitan himself would have to grant a dispensation... and even then it might not work. And if she tells Mama" — Sonya considered the countess her mother and called her that — "that I'm ruining Nikolai's prospects and that I'm heartless and ungrateful, when really... God is my witness" — she crossed herself — "I love her so much, and all of you, only Vera... And why? What have I done to her? I'm so grateful I'd willingly sacrifice everything, but I have nothing to sacrifice..."
Sonya couldn't go on and hid her face in her hands and the featherbed again. Natasha began to comfort her, but her own face showed she understood the full weight of her friend's trouble.
"Sonya," she suddenly exclaimed, as if she had guessed the real reason for the grief, "Vera said something to you after dinner, didn't she? Didn't she?"

"Yes — these verses that Nikolai wrote himself, and I copied out some others, and she found them on my table and said she'd show them to Mama, and that I'm ungrateful, and that Mama would never let him marry me, and that he'll marry Julie instead. You've seen how he's been with her all day... Natasha, what have I done to deserve this?"
She began sobbing even harder than before. Natasha pulled her up, hugged her, and — smiling through her own tears — started to comfort her.

"Sonya, don't believe her, darling! Don't believe any of it! Remember how we all three talked in the sitting room after supper — you, me, and Nikolai? Remember? We worked out how everything could be arranged, and how wonderful it would all be. I don't remember all the details, but don't you remember how it could all work out? There's Uncle Shinshin's brother — he married his own first cousin. And we're only second cousins! And Boris says it's perfectly possible. I told him all about it, you know. And he's so clever and so kind!" said Natasha. "Don't cry, Sonya, dear heart, darling Sonya!" She kissed her and laughed. "Vera is just being mean — don't mind her! Everything will work out, and she won't say anything to Mama. Nikolai will tell her himself, and he doesn't care a bit about Julie."
Natasha kissed her hair.
Sonya sat up. The little kitten brightened — eyes sparkling — and seemed ready to raise its tail, spring down on soft paws, and start batting at a ball of yarn the way kittens should.
"Do you think so? Really? Truly?" she said, quickly smoothing her dress and hair.
