"Really, truly!" Natasha answered, tucking a stray curl back under her friend's braid.
They both laughed.
"Well then — let's go sing 'The Brook.'"
"Let's go!"
"Do you know — that fat Pierre sitting across from me is so funny!" Natasha said suddenly, stopping in her tracks. "I feel so happy!"
And she broke into a run down the hallway.

Sonya, brushing away some feather down that clung to her and tucking the verses into the bodice of her dress against her thin little chest, ran after Natasha through the corridor to the sitting room, her face flushed, her steps light and joyful. At the guests' request, the young people sang the quartet "The Brook," which everyone loved. Then Nikolai sang a song he had just learned:
At nighttime in the moon's fair glow / How sweet, as fancies wander free, / To feel that in this world there's one / Who still is thinking but of thee!
That while her fingers touch the harp / Wafting sweet music o'er the lea, / It is for thee thus swells her heart, / Sighing its message out to thee...
A day or two, then bliss unspoiled, / But oh! till then I cannot live!...
He hadn't finished the last verse before the young people started getting ready to dance in the great hall, and from the musicians' gallery came the sounds of shuffling feet and tuning instruments.

Pierre was sitting in the drawing room where Shinshin had drawn him into a political discussion — as one does with a man recently returned from abroad — in which several others joined, and which bored Pierre thoroughly. When the music began, Natasha came in and walked straight up to him, laughing and blushing:
"Mama told me to ask you to dance."
"I'm afraid I'll mess up the figures," Pierre said. "But if you'll be my teacher..." And lowering his big arm, he offered it to the slender little girl.

While the couples arranged themselves and the musicians tuned up, Pierre sat down with his little partner. Natasha was in heaven — she was dancing with a grown-up who had been abroad. She was seated in a prominent spot, talking to him like a real lady. She held a fan that one of the women had given her and, adopting the pose of a society woman — heaven knows where she had learned it — she chatted with her partner, fanning herself and smiling over the top of the fan.
"Oh my — just look at her!" the countess exclaimed as she crossed the ballroom, pointing at Natasha.
Natasha blushed and laughed.
"Really, Mama! What's there to be surprised about?"

Midway through the third ecossaise, there was a clatter of chairs being pushed back in the sitting room where the count and Marya Dmitrievna had been playing cards with the older, more distinguished guests. They now emerged, stretching after their long sit and putting away their purses and wallets, and filed into the ballroom. Marya Dmitrievna and the count came first, both looking thoroughly pleased. The count, with playful, almost balletic ceremony, offered his bent arm to Marya Dmitrievna. He drew himself up tall, a smile of debonair gallantry lit his face, and as soon as the last figure of the ecossaise ended, he clapped his hands and called up to the musicians in their gallery:
"Semyon! Do you know the Daniel Cooper?"
This was the count's favorite dance from his younger days. (Strictly speaking, the Daniel Cooper was one figure of the anglaise.)
"Look at Papa!" Natasha shouted to the whole room, completely forgetting that she was dancing with a grown-up. She bent her curly head to her knees and made the entire room ring with her laughter.

And indeed everyone watched with smiling pleasure as the jovial old gentleman stood beside his tall, stout partner Marya Dmitrievna, curved his arms, beat time, straightened his shoulders, turned out his toes, tapped lightly with his foot, and — with a smile that kept broadening across his round face — prepared the audience for what was to come. As soon as the provocatively merry strains of Daniel Cooper rang out — something like a cheerful peasant dance — every doorway of the ballroom filled with household servants, men on one side and women on the other, who had come with beaming faces to watch their master enjoy himself.
"Just look at the master! A real eagle!" the old nurse declared loudly from one of the doorways.

The count danced well and knew it. But his partner neither could nor wanted to dance well. Her enormous figure stood upright, her powerful arms hanging at her sides — she had handed her handbag to the countess — and only her stern but handsome face truly participated in the dance. Everything that the count expressed through his entire plump body, Marya Dmitrievna expressed solely through her increasingly beaming face and twitching nose. But while the count charmed the spectators with the surprising agility and unexpected grace of his light-footed maneuvers, Marya Dmitrievna produced no less of an impression through her smallest efforts — a slight roll of the shoulders, a bend of the arm, a stamp of the foot — all of which were marveled at, given her size and usual severity. The dance grew livelier and livelier. The other couples couldn't attract a moment's attention and didn't even try. Everyone was watching the count and Marya Dmitrievna. Natasha kept tugging at sleeves and dresses, urging everyone to "Look at Papa!" — though no one was looking anywhere else. In the pauses, the count waved breathlessly and shouted for the musicians to play faster. Faster, faster, and faster; lighter, more lightly, and ever more lightly — the count whirled around Marya Dmitrievna, now on his toes, now on his heels, until, spinning his partner back to her seat, he executed one final step — kicking his soft foot gently backward, bowing his sweating head, smiling, and sweeping his arm wide — all to a thunder of applause and laughter, led by Natasha. Both partners stood still, breathing hard and mopping their faces with cambric handkerchiefs.
"That's how we used to dance in our day, my dear," said the count. [speaking in French]
"Now that was a Daniel Cooper!" Marya Dmitrievna declared, pushing up her sleeves and puffing heavily.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter XXI
paragraphs: While the sixth anglaise was being danced in the Rostovs' ballroom to a tune the weary musicians kept stumbling over, and while exhausted footmen and cooks were preparing supper, Count Bezukhov suffered his sixth stroke. The doctors declared recovery impossible. After a silent confession, communion was given to the dying man, preparations began for the sacrament of anointing, and the house filled with the particular bustle and anxious anticipation that always accompanies such moments. Outside the gates, a group of undertakers who ducked out of sight whenever a carriage pulled up waited for the expected order for an expensive funeral. The military governor of Moscow, who had been sending aides-de-camp all day to inquire about the count's health, came in person that evening to pay his last respects to the celebrated grandee of Catherine's court.

The magnificent reception room was packed. Everyone rose respectfully when the military governor emerged after spending half an hour alone with the dying man. He acknowledged their bows with a nod, trying to get past as quickly as possible, avoiding the questioning gazes of doctors, clergy, and family. Prince Vasili, who had grown thinner and paler over the past few days, escorted him to the door, murmuring something to him repeatedly in a low voice.

After the military governor left, Prince Vasili sat down alone on a chair in the ballroom, crossed one leg high over the other, leaned his elbow on his knee, and covered his face with his hand. After sitting like this for a while, he stood up and, with a look of alarm in his eyes, hurried with unusually quick steps down the long corridor leading to the back of the house — to the eldest princess's room.

The people in the dimly lit reception room spoke in nervous whispers, and whenever anyone entered or left the dying man's room, they fell silent and watched the door — which creaked faintly when it opened — with eyes full of curiosity or expectation.
"The limits of human life are fixed and cannot be exceeded," an old priest was saying to a lady who had seated herself beside him and was listening to his words with innocent trust.
"I wonder — is it too late for the anointing?" asked the lady, addressing the priest by his clerical title, as if she had no opinion of her own on the matter.
"Ah, madam, it is a great sacrament," the priest replied, passing his hand over the thin gray strands of hair combed back across his bald head.
"Who was that? The military governor himself?" came from the other side of the room. "How young he looks!"
"Yes, and he's over sixty. I hear the count no longer recognizes anyone. They wanted to give him the anointing."
"I knew someone who received that sacrament seven times."
The second princess had just come from the sickroom with red-rimmed eyes and had sat down beside Dr. Lorrain, who was posed elegantly beneath a portrait of Catherine, his elbow resting on a table.
"Beautiful," said the doctor in response to a remark about the weather. "The weather is beautiful, Princess. And besides, in Moscow one feels as though one were in the countryside."
"Yes, indeed," the princess replied with a sigh. "So — may he have something to drink?"
Lorrain considered.
"Has he taken his medicine?"
"Yes."
The doctor glanced at his watch.
"Take a glass of boiled water and add a pinch of cream of tartar," he said, indicating with his delicate fingers what he meant by "a pinch."
"Zere has neffer been a case," a German doctor was saying to an aide-de-camp, "vere a patient surwifes ze sird stroke."
"And what a robust man he was!" the aide-de-camp remarked. "And who's going to inherit all that wealth?" he added in a whisper.
"It von't go begging," the German replied with a smile.
Everyone looked toward the door again as it creaked and the second princess returned with the drink she had prepared following Lorrain's instructions. The German doctor went over to Lorrain.
"Do you think he can last until morning?" the German asked Lorrain in clumsy French. [speaking in French]
Lorrain pursed his lips and wagged a firmly negative finger before his nose.
"Tonight — no later," he said quietly, and moved away with a dignified smile of self-satisfaction at being able to clearly assess and state the patient's condition.
Meanwhile, Prince Vasili had opened the door to the princess's room.

The room was nearly dark; only two small icon-lamps were burning, and the air smelled pleasantly of flowers and incense. It was cluttered with small pieces of furniture — side tables, cabinets, knickknack stands. Behind a screen, the white quilt of a high featherbed was just visible. A small dog began to bark.
"Ah, is that you, cousin?"
She rose and smoothed her hair, which was always arranged so perfectly smooth that it seemed to be made of a single piece glued to her head and lacquered.
"Has something happened?" she asked. "I'm terrified."

"No, nothing has changed. I only came to discuss some business, Catiche," the prince muttered, sinking wearily into the chair she had just vacated. "You've made it warm in here, I must say," he added. "Well — sit down. Let's talk."
*Catherine.
"I thought perhaps something had happened," she said, her expression stony and severe as always. She sat down across from the prince, ready to listen.
"I was trying to nap, my dear cousin, but I can't."
"Well, my dear?" said Prince Vasili, taking her hand and pressing it downward, as was his habit.
It was clear that this "well?" referred to a great deal that both of them understood without saying.

The princess — her body straight and rigid, abnormally long for her short legs — looked directly at Prince Vasili with her prominent gray eyes, showing no emotion. Then she shook her head and glanced at the icons with a sigh. This could have been read as sorrow and devotion, or as exhaustion and a longing for rest. Prince Vasili took it as exhaustion.
"And me?" he said. "Do you think this is any easier for me? I'm as worn out as a post-horse, but I still need to talk to you, Catiche — a very serious talk."

Prince Vasili fell silent. His cheeks began to twitch nervously — first one side, then the other — giving his face an unpleasant expression that would never be seen in a drawing room. His eyes, too, looked strange: one moment craftily insolent, the next darting around with alarm.
The princess, holding her little dog on her lap with thin, bony hands, watched Prince Vasili intently, clearly determined not to break the silence first, even if she had to wait until morning.

"Well, you see, my dear princess and cousin, Catherine Semyonovna," Prince Vasili continued, returning to his theme with an obvious inner struggle, "at a time like this, one must think of everything. One must think of the future — of all of you. I love you all like my own children, as you know."
The princess continued to look at him without moving, her expression unchanged.

"And of course my own family must be considered too," Prince Vasili went on, irritably pushing a small table away without looking at her. "You know, Catiche, that we — you three sisters, Mamontov, and my wife — are the count's only direct heirs. I know how hard it is for you to talk or think about such things. It's no easier for me. But, my dear, I'm nearly sixty and must be prepared for anything. Did you know that I've sent for Pierre? The count" — he gestured toward a portrait — "specifically asked for him."
Prince Vasili looked at the princess questioningly, but couldn't tell whether she was weighing his words or simply staring at him.
"There is one thing I constantly pray God for, cousin," she replied, "and that is that He be merciful to him and allow his noble soul to depart this world in peace..."

"Yes, yes, of course," Prince Vasili interrupted impatiently, rubbing his bald head and angrily pulling the little table back toward him. "But the point is — in short — you yourself know that last winter the count made a will leaving all his property not to us, his direct heirs, but to Pierre."
"He's made plenty of wills!" the princess remarked quietly. "But he can't leave the estate to Pierre. Pierre is illegitimate."

"But my dear," Prince Vasili said suddenly, gripping the table and growing more animated, speaking faster, "what if a letter has been written to the Emperor asking for Pierre's legitimization? Don't you see — given the count's services, such a request would certainly be granted?"
The princess smiled the way people do who believe they understand the subject better than the person speaking to them.

"I can tell you more than that," Prince Vasili continued, seizing her hand. "That letter was written — though it wasn't sent — and the Emperor knew about it. The only question is whether it has been destroyed or not. If it hasn't, then as soon as it's all over" — he sighed to indicate what he meant by "all over" — "and the count's papers are opened, the will and the letter will be delivered to the Emperor, and the petition will undoubtedly be granted. Pierre will inherit everything as the legitimate son."
"And our share?" asked the princess with an ironic smile, as if anything might happen — except that.

"But my poor Catiche, it's as clear as day! He'll become the legal heir to everything, and you won't get a thing. You must know, my dear, whether the will and letter were written, and whether they've been destroyed. And if they've somehow been overlooked, you need to know where they are — and find them. Because..."

"What next?" the princess interrupted, smiling sardonically without changing the expression in her eyes. "I am a woman, and you think we're all stupid. But I know this much: an illegitimate son cannot inherit. A bastard!" she added, as if this French word would conclusively prove her point. [speaking in French]
* A bastard.

"Really, Catiche! Can't you see? You're so clever — how is it you don't understand? If the count has written to the Emperor asking him to recognize Pierre as legitimate, then Pierre won't be Pierre anymore — he'll become Count Bezukhov and will inherit everything under the will. And if the will and letter are not destroyed, then all you'll have is the consolation of having done your duty, and everything that follows from that! That much is certain." [speaking in French]
* And all that follows therefrom.

"I know the will was made, but I also know it's invalid. And you, my dear cousin, seem to think I'm a complete fool," the princess said with the expression women wear when they believe they've said something brilliantly cutting.

"My dear Princess Catherine Semyonovna," Prince Vasili began impatiently, "I didn't come here to argue with you but to talk about your interests as a relative — a good, kind, true relative. And I'm telling you for the tenth time: if the letter to the Emperor and the will in Pierre's favor are among the count's papers, then, my dear girl, you and your sisters are not heirs! If you don't believe me, believe an expert. I've just been speaking with Dmitri Onufrich" — the family lawyer — "and he says the same thing."
At this, something suddenly changed in the princess. Her thin lips went white, though her eyes didn't change, and when she spoke, her voice went through transitions she clearly didn't expect herself.
"That would be just fine!" she said. "I never wanted anything and I don't want anything now."
She pushed the little dog off her lap and smoothed her dress.
"So this is the gratitude — this is the recognition for those who sacrificed everything for him!" she cried. "Wonderful! Splendid! I don't want a thing, Prince."
"Yes, but you're not the only one. There are your sisters..." Prince Vasili replied.
But the princess wasn't listening.
"Yes, I knew it all along but had put it out of my mind. I knew that in this house I could expect nothing but pettiness, deceit, envy, scheming, and ingratitude — the blackest ingratitude..."
"Do you or do you not know where that will is?" Prince Vasili insisted, his cheeks twitching more violently than ever.
"Yes — I was a fool! I kept believing in people, loving them, sacrificing myself. But only the base, the despicable succeed! I know who's been scheming!"
The princess tried to stand, but the prince held her hand. She looked like someone who has suddenly lost all faith in humanity. She shot her companion an angry glare.

"There's still time, my dear. Remember — this was all done hastily, in a moment of anger, during an illness, and was afterward forgotten. Our duty, my dear, is to correct his mistake, to ease his last moments by preventing him from committing this injustice, and not to let him die knowing he's made those unhappy who..."

"Who sacrificed everything for him," the princess finished, ready to stand again but still held fast. "Though he never could appreciate it. No, cousin," she added with a sigh, "I will always remember that in this world, you can expect no reward. In this world there is neither honor nor justice. In this world you have to be cunning and cruel."
"Come now — be reasonable. I know what an excellent heart you have."
"No — I have a wicked heart."

"I know your heart," the prince repeated. "I value your friendship and would like you to think well of me. Don't upset yourself — let's talk sensibly while there's still time — be it a day or only an hour. Tell me everything you know about the will, and above all, where it is. You must know. We'll take it to the count immediately. He's no doubt forgotten about it and will want to destroy it. You understand that my only desire is to faithfully carry out his wishes. That's the sole reason I'm here. I came only to help him — and you."
"Now I see it all! I know who's been scheming — I know!" the princess cried.
"That's not the point, my dear."
"It's that protegee of yours, that sweet Princess Drubetskaya, that Anna Mikhaylovna whom I wouldn't hire as a scullery maid... the vile, despicable woman!"
"Let's not waste time..."

"Oh, don't talk to me! Last winter she weaseled her way in here and told the count such horrible, disgusting things about us — especially about Sophie — I can't even repeat them. It made the count so ill he wouldn't see us for two whole weeks. That's when he wrote this vile document, I'm sure of it. But I thought it was invalid."
"There we are, at last — why didn't you tell me this before?"

"It's in the inlaid portfolio he keeps under his pillow," said the princess, ignoring his question. "Now I know! Yes — if I have a sin, a great sin, it is my hatred of that vile woman!" the princess almost shrieked, utterly transformed. "And what is she doing worming her way in here? But I will give her a piece of my mind. The time will come!"

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter XXII
paragraphs: While these conversations were taking place in the reception room and the princess's room, a carriage carrying Pierre — who had been sent for — and Anna Mikhaylovna — who had felt it necessary to accompany him — was pulling into the courtyard of Count Bezukhov's mansion. As the wheels rolled softly over the straw laid beneath the windows, Anna Mikhaylovna, turning to offer words of comfort to her companion, realized he had fallen asleep in his corner and woke him. Pierre roused himself and followed Anna Mikhaylovna out of the carriage, only now beginning to think about the meeting with his dying father that awaited him. He noticed they had come not to the main entrance but to the back door. As he climbed down from the carriage steps, two men who looked like tradespeople ran from the doorway and hid in the shadows along the wall. Pierre paused and noticed several others of the same sort lurking in the shadows on both sides of the house. But neither Anna Mikhaylovna, nor the footman, nor the coachman — who couldn't have missed seeing them — paid them any attention. "It must be all right," Pierre decided, and followed Anna Mikhaylovna. She hurried up the narrow, dimly lit stone staircase, calling back to Pierre, who was lagging behind, to keep up. Though Pierre couldn't see why he needed to visit the count at all, much less why they had to use the back stairs, Anna Mikhaylovna's air of certainty and urgency convinced him it was all absolutely necessary. Halfway up, they were nearly bowled over by some men carrying pails who came clattering down the stairs in heavy boots. These men pressed against the wall to let Pierre and Anna Mikhaylovna pass without showing the slightest surprise at seeing them.
"Is this the way to the princesses' rooms?" Anna Mikhaylovna asked one of them.
"Yes," a footman replied in a bold, loud voice, as if anything were permissible now. "The door to the left, ma'am."
"Maybe the count didn't actually ask for me," Pierre said when they reached the landing. "I think I should just go to my own room."
Anna Mikhaylovna stopped and waited for him to catch up.
"Oh, my friend!" she said, touching his arm the way she had touched her son's that afternoon. "Believe me, I suffer no less than you do — but be a man!"
"But really — shouldn't I just go?" he asked, looking at her kindly over his spectacles.

"My dear friend! Forget whatever wrongs have been done to you. Remember — he is your father... perhaps in his death agony." She sighed. "I have loved you like a son from the very beginning. Trust me, Pierre. I won't forget your interests."
Pierre didn't understand a word of this, but his growing conviction that everything happening was somehow necessary only deepened, and he meekly followed Anna Mikhaylovna as she opened a door.

This door led to a back anteroom. An old servant of the princesses sat in a corner knitting a stocking. Pierre had never been in this part of the house and hadn't even known these rooms existed. Anna Mikhaylovna, addressing a maid hurrying past with a decanter as "my dear" and "my sweet," asked about the princess's health, then led Pierre along a stone corridor. The first door on the left opened into the princesses' apartments. The maid with the decanter had left the door ajar in her haste — everything in the house was being done in haste just then — and Pierre and Anna Mikhaylovna, passing by, instinctively glanced into the room. Prince Vasili and the eldest princess were sitting close together, deep in conversation. When they saw the two figures pass, Prince Vasili jerked back with obvious irritation, while the princess leaped up and slammed the door shut with all her strength in a gesture of desperation.

This behavior was so unlike the princess's usual composure, and the fear on Prince Vasili's face so at odds with his dignity, that Pierre stopped and looked questioningly at his guide over his spectacles. Anna Mikhaylovna showed no surprise — she merely gave a faint smile and sighed, as if to say this was exactly what she had expected.
"Be a man, my friend. I will look after your interests," she said in response to his look, and walked even faster down the corridor.

Pierre couldn't make sense of any of this, and even less of what "looking after his interests" meant, but he decided that it all had to be this way. From the corridor they passed into a large, dimly lit room adjoining the count's reception room. It was one of those grand but cold apartments Pierre knew only from the front entrance, but even here an empty bathtub now stood on the floor, and water had been spilled on the carpet. They were met by a deacon swinging a censer and a servant who tiptoed past without noticing them. They entered the reception room Pierre knew well, with its two Italian windows looking into the conservatory, its large bust, and the full-length portrait of Catherine the Great. The same people sat there in almost the same positions as before, whispering among themselves. Everyone fell silent and turned to watch as the pale, tear-stained Anna Mikhaylovna entered, followed by the large, heavyset figure of Pierre, who trailed behind her with his head bowed.

Anna Mikhaylovna's face showed she understood that the decisive moment had come. With the decisiveness of a practical Petersburg woman, she entered the room even more boldly than she had that afternoon, keeping Pierre close beside her. She felt that by bringing the person the dying man wished to see, her own presence was guaranteed. Casting a quick glance around the room and spotting the count's confessor, she glided up to him in a sort of gentle bustle — not exactly bowing, but seeming to shrink smaller — and respectfully received blessings from one priest, then another.
"Thank God you've come in time," she said to one of the priests. "We relatives have been in such anxiety. This young man is the count's son," she added more quietly. "What a terrible moment!"
She then approached the doctor.
"Dear doctor," she said, "this young man is the count's son. Is there any hope?"

The doctor glanced upward and silently shrugged. Anna Mikhaylovna mirrored the same gesture — raising her shoulders and eyes, nearly closing them — sighed, and moved away from the doctor to Pierre. In a particularly respectful and tenderly sorrowful voice, she said:
"Trust in His mercy!" And pointing to a small sofa where he should sit and wait, she moved silently toward the door that everyone was watching. It creaked faintly as she slipped behind it.

Pierre, having resolved to obey his guide in everything, moved toward the sofa she had indicated. As soon as Anna Mikhaylovna vanished, he noticed that everyone in the room was watching him with something beyond curiosity and sympathy. They whispered to one another, casting meaningful glances at him — with a kind of awe, almost reverence. He was shown a deference he had never experienced before. A woman he didn't know, who had been talking to the priests, stood up and offered him her seat. An aide-de-camp picked up a glove Pierre had dropped and returned it to him. The doctors fell respectfully silent as he passed and stepped aside to clear his way. At first Pierre wanted to take a different chair so as not to inconvenience the lady, pick up his own glove, and walk around the doctors who weren't even in his path. But then he sensed that all of this would be wrong — that tonight he was someone expected to perform a solemn rite, and that he was therefore obliged to accept their services. He took the glove from the aide-de-camp in silence, sat down in the lady's chair, placed his large hands symmetrically on his knees in the naive pose of an Egyptian statue, and decided that everything was as it should be — that tonight he must not act on his own impulses but simply surrender to the will of those guiding him.

Less than two minutes passed before Prince Vasili entered the room with his head held high, looking majestic. He wore his long coat with three decorations on his chest. He seemed to have grown thinner since the morning; his eyes appeared larger than usual as he scanned the room and spotted Pierre. He went over to him, took his hand — something he had never done before — and pressed it downward, as if testing whether it was firmly attached.
"Courage, courage, my friend! He has asked to see you. That is good!" And he turned to go.
But Pierre felt he should ask: "How is..." He hesitated, unsure whether it was proper to call the dying man "the count," yet ashamed to say "father."
"He had another stroke about half an hour ago. Courage, my friend..."

Pierre's mind was in such turmoil that the word "stroke" suggested a physical blow. He looked at Prince Vasili in confusion, and only later understood that a stroke meant an attack of illness. Prince Vasili murmured something to Lorrain in passing, then went through the door on tiptoe. He couldn't walk on tiptoe well, and his whole body lurched with each step. The eldest princess followed him, and the priests, deacons, and several servants also went through the door. Behind it came the sound of furniture being moved, and at last Anna Mikhaylovna — still wearing the same pale, resolute expression of someone carrying out a duty — hurried out and, lightly touching Pierre's arm, said:
"God's mercy is boundless! The anointing is about to begin. Come."

Pierre walked through the door, stepping on the soft carpet, and noticed that the strange lady, the aide-de-camp, and several servants all followed him in, as if there were no longer any need for permission to enter that room.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter XXIII
paragraphs: Pierre knew this large room well, divided by columns and an arch, its walls draped with Persian carpets. The part behind the columns — with a tall mahogany bed draped in silk curtains on one side and an enormous icon case on the other — was brightly lit with a red glow, like a Russian church during evening vespers. Beneath the gleaming icons stood a long invalid chair, and in it, on snowy-white pillows that had clearly just been changed, Pierre saw the familiar, majestic figure of his father, Count Bezukhov — that gray lion's mane above his broad forehead, those deep, noble wrinkles across his handsome ruddy face. He lay covered to the waist by a bright green quilt, his large, thick hands resting on top of it. A wax candle had been placed between the forefinger and thumb of his right hand, which lay palm down, and an old servant standing behind the chair held it in position. The priests stood nearby, their long hair falling over their magnificent glittering vestments, holding lit candles and slowly, solemnly conducting the service. Behind them stood the two younger princesses, pressing handkerchiefs to their eyes, and in front of them their eldest sister Catiche, her gaze fixed on the icons with a fierce, determined expression, as though declaring that she could not be held responsible for what might happen if she looked away. Anna Mikhaylovna stood by the door beside the unfamiliar lady, her face wearing a meek, sorrowful, all-forgiving expression. Prince Vasili stood near the door by the invalid chair, a wax candle in his left hand, his left arm leaning on the carved back of a velvet chair he had turned around for the purpose, crossing himself with his right hand and raising his eyes heavenward each time he touched his forehead. His face wore a look of serene piety and acceptance of God's will. "If you cannot appreciate these feelings," his expression seemed to say, "so much the worse for you."

Behind him stood the aide-de-camp, the doctors, and the male servants; men and women had separated as in church. Everyone crossed themselves silently, and the only sounds were the reading of the service, the subdued bass chanting, and — in the pauses — sighs and the shuffling of feet. Anna Mikhaylovna, with the self-important air of someone who knows exactly what she is doing, crossed the room to Pierre and handed him a candle. He lit it and, distracted by watching those around him, began crossing himself with the hand that held the candle.

Sophie — the rosy, laughing youngest princess with the mole — watched him from across the room. She smiled, hid her face in her handkerchief, and kept it hidden for a while; then, looking up and seeing Pierre, she started laughing again. She clearly couldn't look at him without laughing but couldn't stop looking either. To remove herself from temptation, she quietly slipped behind one of the columns. In the middle of the service, the priests' voices suddenly ceased, and they whispered among themselves. The old servant holding the count's hand stood up and said something to the ladies. Anna Mikhaylovna stepped forward and, bending over the dying man, beckoned to Lorrain from behind her back. The French doctor stood without a candle, leaning against a column in a respectful pose that conveyed his understanding — despite all differences of faith — of the full significance of the rite being performed, and even his approval of it. He now approached the sick man with the noiseless step of a man in full health. With his delicate white fingers he lifted the free hand from the green quilt, turned sideways, and felt the pulse, considering for a moment. The sick man was given something to drink; there was a stir around him; then everyone returned to their places and the service resumed. During this interruption, Pierre noticed that Prince Vasili left the chair he had been leaning against and — with an air suggesting he knew exactly what he was doing and if others didn't understand, that was their problem — walked past the dying man without stopping, joined the eldest princess, and moved with her toward the far side of the room where the tall silk-curtained bed stood. Both Prince Vasili and the princess left the room through a back door but returned to their places one after the other before the service ended. Pierre paid no more attention to this than to anything else happening around him, having decided once and for all that everything he witnessed that evening was somehow essential.

The chanting of the service ended, and the priest's voice was heard respectfully congratulating the dying man on having received the sacrament. The dying man lay as lifeless and motionless as before. Everyone around him began to stir: footsteps were heard and whispers, among which Anna Mikhaylovna's was the most distinct.
Pierre heard her say:
"He absolutely must be moved to the bed — it's impossible to leave him here..."

The sick man was so surrounded by doctors, princesses, and servants that Pierre could no longer see the reddish-yellow face with its gray mane — which, though he could see other faces too, he had not taken his eyes off for a single moment during the entire service. He could tell by the careful movements of those crowding around the invalid chair that they had lifted the dying man and were carrying him.

"Hold my arm or you'll drop him!" one servant whispered in fright. "Get underneath. Here!" voices called out. The heavy breathing of the bearers and the scuffing of their feet grew more urgent, as though the weight they were carrying was too much for them.

As the bearers — Anna Mikhaylovna among them — passed the young man, he caught a fleeting glimpse between their heads and backs of the dying man's broad, uncovered chest and powerful shoulders, held up by those gripping him under the arms, and of his gray, curly, lion-like head. That head, with its remarkably wide brow and cheekbones, its handsome sensual mouth, and its cold, majestic expression, was not disfigured by the approach of death. It was the same face Pierre remembered from three months earlier, when the count had sent him to Petersburg. But now this head swayed helplessly with the uneven movements of the bearers, and the cold, indifferent gaze was fixed on nothing.

After a few minutes of activity around the high bed, those who had carried the sick man stepped away. Anna Mikhaylovna touched Pierre's hand and said, "Come." Pierre went with her to the bed where the sick man had been laid in a dignified pose befitting the ceremony just completed. He lay with his head propped high on pillows, his hands placed symmetrically on the green silk quilt, palms down. When Pierre approached, the count was staring straight at him — but with an expression whose meaning no mortal could decipher. Either those eyes meant nothing at all, since eyes must look somewhere as long as they can see, or they meant far too much. Pierre hesitated, not knowing what to do, and looked questioningly at his guide. Anna Mikhaylovna made a quick gesture with her eyes toward the sick man's hand, pursing her lips as if blowing it a kiss. Pierre, carefully craning his neck so as not to disturb the quilt, followed her suggestion and pressed his lips to the large, bony, fleshy hand. Neither the hand nor a single muscle of the count's face moved. Pierre looked at Anna Mikhaylovna again. She nodded toward a chair beside the bed. Pierre obediently sat down, his eyes silently asking if he was doing the right thing. Anna Mikhaylovna nodded approvingly. Once again Pierre assumed the stiff, symmetrical pose of an Egyptian statue, clearly distressed that his bulky, clumsy body was taking up so much space and doing his best to appear as small as possible. He looked at the count, who still stared at the spot where Pierre's face had been before he sat down. Anna Mikhaylovna's bearing conveyed her awareness of the deeply moving significance of this moment — father and son, together for the last time. This lasted about two minutes, though to Pierre it felt like an hour. Suddenly the broad muscles of the count's face began to twitch. The twitching grew stronger, his handsome mouth pulled to one side — only now did Pierre realize how close to death his father was — and from that distorted mouth came an indistinct, hoarse sound. Anna Mikhaylovna studied the sick man's eyes intently, trying to guess what he wanted. She pointed first to Pierre, then to the drink, then whispered Prince Vasili's name questioningly, then gestured to the quilt. The sick man's eyes and face showed impatience. He made an effort to look at the servant who stood permanently at the head of the bed.
"He wants to be turned on his other side," the servant whispered, and rose to turn the count's heavy body toward the wall.
Pierre got up to help.

While the count was being turned, one of his arms fell back limply and he made a feeble, futile effort to pull it forward. Whether he noticed Pierre's look of terror at that lifeless arm, or whether some other thought crossed his dying mind — at any rate, he looked at the disobedient arm, at Pierre's horrified face, and back at the arm again, and a faint, pitiful smile appeared on his face — utterly out of keeping with his features — as though mocking his own helplessness. At the sight of that smile, Pierre felt an unexpected tremor in his chest and a tickle in his nose, and tears blurred his vision. The sick man was turned onto his side facing the wall. He sighed.
"He's dozing," said Anna Mikhaylovna, noticing that one of the princesses was coming to take her turn at the bedside watch. "Let's go."
Pierre went out.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter XXIV
paragraphs: There was now no one in the reception room except Prince Vasili and the eldest princess, who were sitting beneath the portrait of Catherine the Great and talking urgently. The moment they saw Pierre and his companion, they fell silent. Pierre thought he saw the princess quickly hide something as she whispered:
"I can't stand the sight of that woman."
"Catiche has had tea set up in the small drawing room," Prince Vasili said to Anna Mikhaylovna. "Go have something, my poor Anna Mikhaylovna, or you won't last."
To Pierre he said nothing — just gave his arm a sympathetic squeeze below the shoulder. Pierre followed Anna Mikhaylovna into the small drawing room.

"There is nothing so restorative after a sleepless night as a cup of this wonderful Russian tea," Lorrain was saying with an air of restrained energy as he stood sipping from a delicate Chinese handleless cup before a table laid with tea things and a cold supper in the small, circular room. Everyone who was in Count Bezukhov's house that night had gathered here to fortify themselves. Pierre remembered this little circular room well, with its mirrors and small tables. During balls at the house, Pierre — who couldn't dance — had loved sitting here watching the ladies pass through in their ball gowns, diamonds and pearls on their bare shoulders, admiring themselves in the brilliantly lit mirrors that multiplied their reflections. Now the same room was dimly lit by just two candles. On one small table, tea things and supper dishes sat in disarray, and in the middle of the night a mixed crowd of people sat there — not celebrating, but whispering somberly, every word and gesture showing that none of them had forgotten what was happening, and was about to happen, in the bedroom. Pierre ate nothing, though he very much wanted to. He glanced questioningly at his guide and saw her tiptoeing again toward the reception room where they had left Prince Vasili and the eldest princess. Pierre concluded this, too, was essential, and after a short pause followed her. Anna Mikhaylovna was standing beside the princess, and they were both speaking in heated whispers.
"Allow me, Princess, to determine what is necessary and what is not," said the younger of the two speakers, clearly in the same agitated state as when she had slammed her door.

"But my dear Princess," Anna Mikhaylovna answered smoothly but firmly, blocking the path to the bedroom and preventing the other from passing, "won't this be too much for poor Uncle at a moment when he needs rest? Worldly conversation — at a time when his soul is already prepared..."

Prince Vasili sat in an armchair in his usual pose, one leg crossed high over the other. His flabby cheeks — which looked as though they hung heavier at the bottom — were twitching violently, but his expression was that of a man unconcerned with what the two women were saying.
"Come now, my dear Anna Mikhaylovna, let Catiche do as she wishes. You know how fond the count is of her."

"I don't even know what's in this document," the younger woman said, addressing Prince Vasili and pointing to the inlaid portfolio she was holding. "All I know is that his real will is in his writing desk, and this is just a paper he's forgotten about..."
She tried to get past Anna Mikhaylovna, but the latter sprang to block her path.

"I know, my dear, kind princess," Anna Mikhaylovna said, gripping the portfolio so firmly it was clear she would not let go easily. "Dear princess, I beg you — I implore you — have some pity on him! I beg you!" [speaking in French]

The princess said nothing. The only sound was the struggle for the portfolio, but it was obvious that if the princess did speak, her words would not be kind to Anna Mikhaylovna. Despite the physical struggle, Anna Mikhaylovna's voice lost none of its honeyed firmness.
"Pierre, my dear, come here. I think he will not be out of place at a family discussion. Isn't that so, Prince?"

"Why don't you say something, cousin?" the princess suddenly shrieked so loudly that those in the drawing room heard and were startled. "Why are you silent while God knows who barges in, making a scene at the very threshold of a dying man's room? Schemer!" she hissed viciously, yanking the portfolio with all her might.
But Anna Mikhaylovna took a step forward to keep her grip, shifting her hold.
Prince Vasili stood up. "Oh!" he said with reproach and surprise. "This is absurd! Let go, both of you!"
The princess let go.
"And you too!"
But Anna Mikhaylovna didn't obey.
"Let go, I say! I'll take responsibility for this. I myself will go ask him — I will! Does that satisfy you?"

"But Prince," Anna Mikhaylovna said, "after such a sacred sacrament, allow him a moment of peace! Pierre, tell them what you think," she said, turning to the young man, who had come close and was staring in astonishment at the princess's furious face — all dignity gone — and at Prince Vasili's twitching cheeks.
"Remember — you will answer for the consequences," Prince Vasili said sternly. "You don't know what you're doing."
"Vile woman!" the princess shrieked, lunging at Anna Mikhaylovna and snatching the portfolio from her hands.
Prince Vasili dropped his head and spread his hands.

At that moment the terrible door — the one Pierre had been watching so long, the one that always opened so quietly — burst open with a crash and banged against the wall. The second princess rushed out, wringing her hands.
"What are you doing?" she cried desperately. "He's dying, and you've left me alone with him!"

Her sister dropped the portfolio. Anna Mikhaylovna, bending quickly, snatched up the contested object and ran into the bedroom. The eldest princess and Prince Vasili, recovering themselves, followed her. A few minutes later the eldest sister emerged, her face pale and hard, biting her lower lip. At the sight of Pierre, her expression showed an irrepressible hatred.
"Yes — now you can be glad!" she said. "This is what you've been waiting for." And bursting into tears, she buried her face in her handkerchief and rushed from the room.

Prince Vasili came out next. He staggered to the sofa where Pierre was sitting and collapsed onto it, covering his face with his hand. Pierre noticed he was pale, and his jaw was trembling and shaking as if from a chill.

"Oh, my friend!" he said, taking Pierre by the elbow. His voice held a sincerity and vulnerability Pierre had never heard in it before. "How much we sin, how much we deceive — and for what? I'm nearly sixty, my friend... I too... Everything ends in death. Death is terrible..." And he burst into tears.
Anna Mikhaylovna came out last. She approached Pierre with slow, quiet steps.
"Pierre!" she said.
Pierre looked at her questioningly. She kissed the young man on the forehead, wetting him with her tears. Then, after a pause, she said:
"He is gone..."
Pierre looked at her over his spectacles.
"Come — I'll go with you. Try to cry. Nothing brings such relief as tears."
She led him into the dark drawing room, and Pierre was grateful that no one could see his face. Anna Mikhaylovna left him, and when she returned he was fast asleep, his head resting on his arm.
The next morning, Anna Mikhaylovna said to Pierre:

"Yes, my dear — this is a great loss for all of us, to say nothing of you. But God will sustain you: you are young, and now, I hope, in command of an immense fortune. The will has not yet been opened. I know you well enough to be sure this won't go to your head, but it does impose responsibilities, and you must be a man."
Pierre said nothing.

"Perhaps later I will tell you, my dear boy, that if I had not been there, God only knows what would have happened! You know Uncle promised me just the day before yesterday not to forget Boris. But there wasn't time. I hope, my dear friend, you will honor your father's wishes?"

Pierre understood none of this and, blushing shyly, looked at Princess Anna Mikhaylovna in silence. After speaking with Pierre, Anna Mikhaylovna returned to the Rostovs' house and went to bed. Waking in the morning, she told the Rostovs and all her acquaintances the details of Count Bezukhov's death. She said the count had died as she herself would wish to die — that his end was not only moving but edifying. As for the final meeting between father and son, it had been so touching she couldn't think of it without tears, and she didn't know who had conducted himself more nobly in those terrible moments — the father, who remembered everyone and everything at the last and spoke such heartfelt words to his son, or Pierre, whom it was pitiful to see, so stricken with grief was he, though he tried hard to hide it so as not to burden his dying father. "It's painful, but it lifts the soul to see men like the old count and his worthy son," she said. About the eldest princess and Prince Vasili, she spoke with disapproval — but in whispers, and as a strict secret.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter XXV
paragraphs: At Bald Hills — the estate of Prince Nikolai Andreevich Bolkonsky — the arrival of young Prince Andrei and his wife was expected any day, but this did not disrupt the regular routine of the old prince's household. General-in-Chief Prince Nikolai Andreevich, nicknamed "the King of Prussia" in society, had lived there continuously since Emperor Paul had banished him to his country estate, together with his daughter Princess Marya and her companion, Mademoiselle Bourienne. Although the new reign had freed him to return to the capitals, he continued living in the country, saying that anyone who wanted to see him could travel the hundred miles from Moscow to Bald Hills, while he himself needed no one and nothing. He liked to say that there are only two sources of human vice — idleness and superstition — and only two virtues: activity and intelligence. He took personal charge of his daughter's education and, to develop these two cardinal virtues, gave her lessons in algebra and geometry until she was twenty, arranging her life so that every moment was occupied. He himself was always busy — writing his memoirs, solving problems in higher mathematics, turning snuffboxes on his lathe, working in the garden, or overseeing the construction that was perpetually underway on his estate. Since regularity is the prime condition for productive activity, the regularity of his household was carried to the highest degree of precision. He always came to meals under exactly the same conditions — not just at the same hour but at the same minute. With everyone around him, from his daughter to his servants, the prince was sharp and invariably demanding, so that without being cruel he inspired the kind of fear and respect that few truly cruel men could have aroused. Although he was retired and held no political influence, every important official appointed to the province considered it his duty to visit the prince, and would wait in the lofty anteroom — just like the architect, the gardener, and Princess Marya — until the prince appeared at the appointed hour. Everyone in that anteroom felt the same mixture of respect and dread when the enormous study door opened to reveal the figure of a rather small old man in a powdered wig, with small withered hands and bushy gray eyebrows that, when he frowned, sometimes hid the gleam of his shrewd, youthfully sparkling eyes.

On the morning of the young couple's expected arrival, Princess Marya entered the anteroom at the appointed hour for the morning greeting, crossing herself with trepidation and saying a silent prayer. Every morning she came like this, and every morning she prayed that the daily encounter might go well.
An old powdered manservant sitting in the anteroom rose quietly and whispered: "Please go in."

Through the door came the steady hum of the lathe. The princess timidly opened the door, which moved noiselessly and smoothly. She paused at the entrance. The prince was working at the lathe; he glanced around and went back to his work.

The enormous study was full of objects clearly in constant use. The large table covered with books and plans, the tall glass-fronted bookcases with keys in the locks, the high standing desk with an open notebook lying on it, and the lathe with tools laid out and shavings scattered around — everything spoke of continuous, varied, and orderly activity. The motion of the small foot in its silver-embroidered Tatar boot and the firm pressure of the lean, sinewy hand showed that the prince still possessed the endurance and vigor of hardy old age. After a few more turns, he took his foot off the pedal, wiped his chisel, dropped it into a leather pouch attached to the lathe, and approached the table to summon his daughter. He never blessed his children — he simply held out his bristly, still-unshaven cheek and, studying her tenderly and attentively, said sternly:
"Feeling well? Good — sit down." He took the notebook of geometry lessons he had written himself and pulled up a chair with his foot.
"For tomorrow!" he said, quickly finding the right page and marking a section with a hard scratch of his nail.
The princess bent over the notebook on the table.
"Wait — here's a letter for you," said the old man suddenly, pulling a letter addressed in a woman's hand from a bag hanging above the table and tossing it to her.
At the sight of the letter, red blotches appeared on the princess's face. She seized it quickly and bent her head over it.
"From Heloise?" asked the prince with a cold smile that showed his still-sound yellowish teeth.
"Yes, it's from Julie," the princess replied with a timid glance and a shy smile.
"I'll let two more letters pass, but the third one I'm reading," the prince said sternly. "I'm sure you write nothing but nonsense. I'll read the third!"
"Read this one if you like, Father," said the princess, blushing even deeper and holding out the letter.
"The third, I said the third!" the prince snapped, pushing the letter away. Leaning his elbows on the table, he pulled the geometry notebook toward him.

"Now then, madam," he began, bending close to his daughter over the book and placing an arm on the back of her chair, so that she found herself enveloped on all sides by the sharp scent of old age and tobacco she had known all her life. "Now, madam — these triangles are equal. Please note that angle ABC..."

The princess stared fearfully at her father's gleaming eyes so close to her own; the red blotches came and went on her face, and it was obvious she understood nothing and was so frightened that her fear would prevent her from understanding anything he said, no matter how clearly he explained it. Whether the fault was the teacher's or the pupil's, the same thing happened every day: the princess's eyes would go dim, she could neither see nor hear, and was conscious only of her stern father's withered face inches from hers, his breath and his smell, thinking only of how to escape to her room and work through the problem in peace. The old man lost his temper every time: he shoved his chair back and forth noisily, made efforts to control himself and not explode, but almost always did explode, scolding her and sometimes flinging the notebook across the room.
The princess gave a wrong answer.
"What a fool!" the prince shouted, pushing the notebook aside and turning sharply away. But he immediately stood up, paced the room, lightly touched his daughter's hair, and sat back down.
He pulled his chair in and went on explaining.

"This won't do, Princess — it simply won't do," he said as Princess Marya picked up the closed notebook with tomorrow's lesson and was about to leave. "Mathematics are essential, madam! I don't want you turning into one of our silly ladies. Get used to it and you'll come to enjoy it," he added, patting her cheek. "It'll drive all the nonsense out of your head."
She turned to go, but he stopped her with a gesture and took an uncut book from the high desk.
"Here — some kind of Key to the Mysteries that your Heloise sent you. A religious book! I don't interfere with anyone's beliefs... I've glanced through it. Take it. Now go. Go."
He patted her shoulder and shut the door behind her himself.

Princess Marya returned to her room with the sad, frightened expression that rarely left her face and made her plain, sickly features even plainer. She sat down at her writing desk — covered with miniature portraits, books, and papers in total disorder. The princess was as untidy as her father was tidy. She set down the geometry book and eagerly broke the seal on her letter. It was from her closest childhood friend — the same Julie Karagina who had been at the Rostovs' name-day party.
Julie wrote in French: [speaking in French]

Dear and precious Friend, How terrible and frightening separation is! Though I tell myself that half my life and half my happiness are bound up in you, and that despite the distance between us our hearts are joined by unbreakable bonds, my heart rebels against fate, and despite the pleasures and diversions around me, I cannot overcome a secret sadness that has lived in my heart since we parted. Why are we not together as we were last summer, in your large study, on the blue sofa — the confidential sofa? Why can I not, as I did three months ago, draw fresh moral strength from your gaze — so gentle, calm, and perceptive — a gaze I loved so much and seem to see before me now as I write?

Having read this far, Princess Marya sighed and glanced at the mirror on her right. It reflected a thin, graceless figure and a plain face. Her eyes, always sad, now looked with particular hopelessness at her reflection. "She's flattering me," the princess thought, turning away and continuing to read. But Julie was not flattering her friend. The princess's eyes — large, deep, and luminous, seeming at times to radiate shafts of warm light — were so beautiful that, despite her plain face, they often gave her a magnetism more powerful than conventional beauty. But the princess never saw the lovely expression her eyes wore when she wasn't thinking about herself. Like everyone, her face took on a forced, unnatural look the moment she glanced in a mirror. She read on:

All Moscow talks of nothing but war. One of my two brothers is already abroad; the other is with the Guards, who are marching toward the frontier. Our dear Emperor has left Petersburg and is thought to be preparing to expose his precious person to the hazards of war. God grant that the Corsican monster who is destroying the peace of Europe may be brought down by the angel the Almighty, in His goodness, has given us as sovereign! Setting aside my brothers, this war has cost me one of the relationships dearest to my heart. I mean young Nikolai Rostov, who was too full of enthusiasm to sit idle and has left the university for the army. I will confess to you, dear Marya, that despite his extreme youth, his departure for the army was a great sorrow to me. This young man, about whom I wrote to you last summer, is so noble and full of that genuine youthfulness so rare among today's world-weary twenty-year-olds — and above all, he is so frank and has such a good heart. He is so pure and poetic that my connection with him, brief as it was, has been one of the sweetest comforts to my poor heart, which has already suffered so much. Someday I will tell you about our parting and everything that was said. It is still too fresh. Ah, dear friend, you are lucky not to know these piercing joys and sorrows. You are fortunate, for the sorrows are usually stronger! I know perfectly well that Count Nikolai is too young to be anything more than a friend to me, but this sweet friendship, this pure and poetic bond, was exactly what my heart needed. But enough of this! The main news that has all Moscow buzzing is the death of old Count Bezukhov and his inheritance. Imagine! The three princesses received very little, Prince Vasili got nothing, and it is Monsieur Pierre who has inherited everything and has been recognized as legitimate — so he is now Count Bezukhov and possessor of the greatest fortune in Russia. They say Prince Vasili played a very contemptible part in the whole affair and returned to Petersburg utterly humiliated.

I confess I understand very little about wills and inheritance, but I do know that since this young man we all used to know as plain Monsieur Pierre has become Count Bezukhov and owner of one of Russia's largest fortunes, it has been very amusing to watch the change in behavior of mothers with eligible daughters, and of the daughters themselves, toward him — though between us, he always struck me as a rather poor specimen. Since everyone has spent the past two years trying to find me a husband — most of whom I don't even know — the Moscow matchmaking chronicles are now speaking of me as the future Countess Bezukhova. But you will understand I have no interest in the position. Speaking of marriages: did you know that the universal auntie Anna Mikhaylovna recently told me, under the seal of the strictest secrecy, about a marriage plan for you? It is none other than Prince Vasili's son Anatole, whom his family wishes to reform by marrying him off to someone wealthy and distinguished — and their choice has fallen on you. I don't know what you will think of this, but I felt it my duty to let you know. He is said to be very handsome and a terrible scoundrel. That is all I have managed to discover about him.

But enough gossip. I am at the end of my second sheet of paper, and Mama is calling me to go dine at the Apraksins'. Read the mystical book I'm sending you — it is an enormous success here. Although there are things in it difficult for our weak human minds to grasp, it is a wonderful book that soothes and elevates the soul. Farewell! My respects to your father and compliments to Mademoiselle Bourienne. I embrace you as I love you.
JULIE
P.S. Do send me news of your brother and his charming little wife.

The princess sat thinking for a while, a pensive smile on her face. Her luminous eyes lit up until her face was completely transformed. Then she suddenly rose and, with her heavy tread, went to the table. She took a sheet of paper, and her hand moved rapidly across it. This was her reply, also in French: [speaking in French]

Dear and precious Friend, Your letter of the 13th gave me great joy. So you still love me, my romantic Julie? The separation you speak of so mournfully does not seem to have had its usual effect on you. You complain of our being apart. What then should I say, who am deprived of everyone dear to me? Ah, if we did not have religion to console us, life would be very sad indeed. Why do you think I would look harshly on your feelings for that young man? In such matters I am severe only with myself. I understand these feelings in others, and though I have never experienced them and therefore cannot approve, I do not condemn them either. But it seems to me that Christian love — love of one's neighbor, love of one's enemy — is nobler, sweeter, and better than the feelings inspired in a romantic young girl by the beautiful eyes of a young man.

The news of Count Bezukhov's death reached us before your letter, and my father was very affected. He says the count was the last representative but one of the great century, and that his own turn is next — but that he will do everything he can to postpone it as long as possible. God preserve us from such a terrible loss!

I cannot agree with what you say about Pierre, whom I knew as a child. He always seemed to me to have an excellent heart, and that is the quality I value most in people. As for his inheritance and Prince Vasili's role in it, it is very sad for both of them. Ah, dear friend, the words of our divine Savior — that it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the Kingdom of Heaven — are terribly true. I pity Prince Vasili, but I am even sorrier for Pierre. So young, and burdened with such wealth — what temptations he will face! If I were asked what I desire most on earth, it would be to be poorer than the poorest beggar. A thousand thanks for the book you sent, which is having such success in Moscow. But since you say that alongside some fine passages it contains things beyond our weak understanding, it seems rather pointless to spend time on what is unintelligible and can therefore bear no fruit. I have never understood the attraction some people feel for confusing their minds with mystical books that only sow doubt and excite the imagination, giving them a tendency toward exaggeration quite contrary to Christian simplicity. Let us instead read the Epistles and Gospels. Let us not try to penetrate their mysteries, for how can we — miserable sinners in this flesh that forms an impenetrable veil between us and the Eternal? Let us study those sublime rules our divine Savior left for our guidance here below. Let us try to live by them, and let us trust that the less we allow our feeble human minds to wander, the better we shall please God, who rejects all knowledge not given by Him — and the less we seek to fathom what He has chosen to conceal, the sooner He will reveal it through His divine Spirit.

My father has not spoken to me about a suitor but has only mentioned that he received a letter and is expecting a visit from Prince Vasili. Regarding this marriage proposal, I will tell you, dear sweet friend, that I see marriage as a divine institution to which we must submit. However painful it may be, if the Almighty lays upon me the duties of wife and mother, I will try to fulfill them as faithfully as I can, without scrutinizing my feelings toward whomever He may give me as a husband.

I have had a letter from my brother announcing his imminent arrival at Bald Hills with his wife. This joy will be short-lived, however, as he must leave again for this terrible war into which we have been dragged, God knows how or why. Not just where you are — at the center of things — but even here, amid rural fieldwork and the natural calm that city people consider characteristic of country life, the rumors of war are heard and felt painfully. My father speaks of nothing but marches and countermarches — things I understand nothing about. And the day before yesterday, on my daily walk through the village, I witnessed a heartbreaking scene... A convoy of conscripts, recruited from our own people, was departing to join the army. You should have seen the state of the mothers, wives, and children of those men! You should have heard their sobs. It seems as though humanity has forgotten the laws of our divine Savior, who preached love and forgiveness — and that people now consider the greatest merit to lie in the skill of killing one another.
Farewell, dear and kind friend. May our divine Savior and His most Holy Mother keep you in their sacred and all-powerful care!
MARYA

"Ah, you're sending off a letter, Princess? I've already sent mine — I wrote to my poor mother," said Mademoiselle Bourienne, the smiling, pretty, fair-haired Frenchwoman, speaking rapidly in her pleasant, melodious voice with its guttural r's. She brought into Princess Marya's earnest, somber, gloomy world an entirely different atmosphere — carefree, lighthearted, and self-satisfied.
"Princess, I must warn you," she added, lowering her voice and clearly savoring her own words, "the prince has been scolding Mikhail Ivanovich. He's in a very bad mood — very gloomy. Be prepared."
"Ah, my dear friend," Princess Marya replied, "I have asked you never to tell me what sort of mood my father is in. I do not allow myself to judge him, and I would not have others do so either."

The princess glanced at her watch and, seeing she was five minutes late for her clavichord practice, went into the sitting room with a look of alarm. Between twelve and two o'clock, according to the daily schedule, the prince rested and the princess played the clavichord.

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter XXVI
paragraphs: The gray-haired valet sat drowsily listening to the old prince's snoring from the large study. From the far side of the house, through closed doors, came the sound of a difficult passage from a Dussek sonata, repeated twenty times over.

Just then a closed carriage and a hooded one drove up to the porch. Prince Andrei got out, helped his small wife alight, and let her enter the house ahead of him. Old Tikhon, wearing a wig, poked his head out the anteroom door, whispered that the prince was sleeping, and hastily closed it again. Tikhon knew that neither the son's arrival nor any other unusual event was to disrupt the appointed order of the day. Prince Andrei evidently knew this too; he checked his watch as if to confirm that his father's habits had not changed since his last visit, and having assured himself they hadn't, he turned to his wife.
"He'll be up in twenty minutes. Let's go see Marya," he said.
The little princess had grown plumper during this time, but her eyes and her short, downy, smiling upper lip lifted just as prettily and merrily as ever when she spoke.

"Why, this is a palace!" she said to her husband, looking around with the expression people wear when complimenting their host at a ball. "Quick — let's go, quick!" She glanced around, smiled at Tikhon, at her husband, and at the footman escorting them.
"Is that Marya practicing? Let's sneak up and surprise her!"
Prince Andrei followed her with a courteous but melancholy expression.
"You've aged, Tikhon," he said in passing to the old man, who kissed his hand.
Before they reached the room where the clavichord was playing, the pretty, fair-haired Frenchwoman, Mademoiselle Bourienne, rushed out, apparently beside herself with joy.
"Oh, what happiness for the princess!" she cried. "At last! I must go tell her!"
"No, no, please don't — you must be Mademoiselle Bourienne," said the little princess, kissing her. "I already know you through my sister-in-law's friendship. She wasn't expecting us?"
They went up to the sitting room door, through which came the sound of the much-repeated passage. Prince Andrei stopped and made a face, as if bracing for something unpleasant.

The little princess entered the room. The passage broke off mid-phrase; there was a cry, then Princess Marya's heavy footsteps and the sound of kisses. When Prince Andrei walked in, the two princesses — who had met only once before, briefly, at his wedding — were in each other's arms, pressing their lips to whichever spot they happened to touch. Mademoiselle Bourienne stood near them, hand pressed to her heart, wearing a blissful smile, equally ready to cry or laugh. Prince Andrei shrugged and frowned, the way music lovers do when they hear a wrong note. The two women released each other, then immediately seized each other's hands, kissed them, pulled away, and kissed each other's faces again — and then, to Prince Andrei's amazement, both began crying and kissed once more. Mademoiselle Bourienne began crying too. Prince Andrei was obviously uncomfortable, but for the two women it seemed perfectly natural that they should cry — apparently it had never occurred to them that this meeting could have gone any other way.

"Oh, my dear!... Oh, Marya!..." they suddenly exclaimed, then laughed. "I dreamed of you last night..." "You weren't expecting us?..." "Oh Marya, you've gotten thinner!..." "And you've gotten plumper!..."
"I recognized the princess right away," Mademoiselle Bourienne put in.
"And I had no idea!" exclaimed Princess Marya. "Oh Andrei — I didn't even see you!"

Prince Andrei and his sister, hand in hand, kissed each other, and he told her she was the same crybaby she'd always been. Princess Marya had turned to her brother, and through her tears her loving, warm, gentle eyes — those large luminous eyes, so beautiful in that moment — rested on Prince Andrei's face.

The little princess chattered without pause, her short, downy upper lip perpetually touching and releasing her rosy lower lip, her face constantly breaking into a smile of sparkling teeth and gleaming eyes. She told them about an accident they'd had on Spassky Hill that could have been dangerous in her condition, then immediately informed them she had left all her clothes in Petersburg and heaven knew what she would wear here, and that Andrei had completely changed, and that Kitty Odyntsova had married an old man, and that there was a real suitor for Marya, a genuine one — but they'd discuss that later. Princess Marya watched her brother in silence, her beautiful eyes full of love and sadness. She was clearly following her own train of thought, independent of her sister-in-law's words. In the middle of a description of the latest Petersburg party, she turned to her brother:
"So you really are going to war, Andrei?" she said with a sigh.
Lise sighed too.
"Yes — tomorrow, even," her brother replied.
"He's abandoning me here, God knows why, when he could have gotten a promotion..."
Princess Marya didn't hear her out. Following her own thoughts, she turned to her sister-in-law with a tender glance at her figure.
"Is it certain?" she asked.
The little princess's face changed. She sighed and said: "Yes, quite certain. Oh, it's so frightening..."
Her lip dropped. She pressed her face against her sister-in-law's and unexpectedly began crying again.
"She needs rest," said Prince Andrei with a frown. "Don't you, Lise? Take her to your room — I'll go see Father. How is he? The same?"
"The same, the same. Though I don't know what your opinion will be," the princess answered cheerfully.

"And the same hours? The walks in the avenues? The lathe?" Prince Andrei asked with a barely perceptible smile, showing that despite all his love and respect for his father, he was well aware of his foibles.
"The same hours, the same lathe, and mathematics too — and my geometry lessons," Princess Marya said gleefully, as if her geometry lessons were among life's greatest pleasures.

When the twenty minutes were up and it was time for the old prince to rise, Tikhon came to summon the young prince to his father. The old man made a departure from his usual routine to honor his son's arrival: he gave orders for Prince Andrei to be admitted to his rooms while he dressed for dinner. The old prince always dressed in the old style — an antique coat and powdered hair. When Prince Andrei entered his father's dressing room — not with the bored, haughty look he wore in drawing rooms, but with the lively expression he showed when talking to Pierre — the old man was sitting in a large leather chair, wrapped in a powdering cloak, submitting his head to Tikhon's care.
"So — the warrior arrives! Come to conquer Bonaparte, have you?" said the old man, shaking his powdered head as much as the pigtail Tikhon was holding to braid would allow.
"You at least had better deal with him properly, or if he keeps going like this, he'll be making subjects of us too! How are you?" And he offered his cheek.

The old man was in good spirits after his pre-dinner nap. (He used to say that a nap after dinner was silver — before dinner, golden.) He cast happy, sideways glances at his son from beneath his thick, bushy eyebrows. Prince Andrei went up and kissed his father on the spot indicated. He made no reply to his father's favorite topic — mocking the modern military and especially Bonaparte.
"Yes, Father — I've come to you and I've brought my wife, who's expecting," said Prince Andrei, following every movement of his father's face with an eager, respectful look. "How is your health?"
"Only fools and rakes get sick, my boy. You know me: I'm busy from dawn to dusk and live clean, so naturally I'm well."
"Thank God," said his son with a smile.
"God has nothing to do with it! Well, go on," the old man continued, returning to his hobby, "tell me how the Germans have taught you to fight Bonaparte with this new science you call 'strategy.'"
Prince Andrei smiled.

"Give me a chance to collect my thoughts, Father," he said, his smile showing that his father's eccentricities didn't prevent his son from loving and honoring him. "I haven't even had time to settle in!"

"Nonsense! Nonsense!" the old man cried, shaking his pigtail to test if it was firmly braided, and grasping his son's hand. "The house for your wife is all ready. Princess Marya will take her over and show her everything — they'll talk each other's ears off. That's the woman's way! I'm glad to have her. Sit down, let's talk. I understand Mikhelson's army, and Tolstoy's too — a simultaneous operation... But what about the southern army? Prussia is neutral — I know that. What about Austria?" he said, rising from his chair and pacing the room, followed by Tikhon who scurried after him handing him articles of clothing. "What about Sweden? How will they cross Pomerania?"

Prince Andrei, seeing his father insisted, began — reluctantly at first, but with growing animation, unconsciously switching from Russian to French as he went — to explain the plan of campaign. He described how an army of ninety thousand was to threaten Prussia and force her out of neutrality; how part of that force was to join Swedish troops at Stralsund; how two hundred and twenty thousand Austrians together with a hundred thousand Russians would operate in Italy and on the Rhine; how fifty thousand Russians and as many English would land at Naples; and how a combined force of five hundred thousand was to attack the French from multiple directions. The old prince showed not the slightest interest during this explanation, and as if not listening, continued dressing while pacing the room. Three times he interrupted unexpectedly. Once he stopped his son by shouting: "The white one, the white one!"
This meant Tikhon was handing him the wrong waistcoat. Another time he broke in to ask:
"And when is she due?" And shaking his head disapprovingly, said: "That's no good! Go on, go on."
The third interruption came as Prince Andrei was finishing. The old man began to sing in his cracked old voice: "Marlborough is off to war — God knows when he'll return." [speaking in French]
* "Marlborough is going to the wars; God knows when he'll return."
His son only smiled.
"I'm not saying I approve of this plan," said the son. "I'm only telling you what it is. Napoleon has surely drawn up his own plan by now — no worse than this one."
"Well, you've told me nothing new," the old man said, and meditatively repeated:
"God knows when he'll return... Go to the dining room." [speaking in French]

chapters.title: Book One (1805) — Chapter XXVII
paragraphs: At the appointed hour the prince, powdered and shaved, entered the dining room where his daughter-in-law, Princess Marya, and Mademoiselle Bourienne were already waiting, together with his architect — who, by one of the old man's peculiar whims, was admitted to the dinner table despite being a person of such modest standing that he could hardly have expected the honor. The prince, who normally observed social distinctions very strictly and rarely allowed even important officials at his table, had unexpectedly chosen Mikhail Ivanovich — who always retreated to a corner to blow his nose on his checked handkerchief — to demonstrate his theory that all men are equal, and had told his daughter more than once that Mikhail Ivanovich was "not one bit worse than you or I." At dinner, the prince usually spoke to the taciturn Mikhail Ivanovich more often than to anyone else.

In the dining room, which like all the rooms in the house was extremely lofty, the household members and footmen — one behind each chair — stood waiting for the prince to appear.
