The head butler, napkin over his arm, was reviewing the table settings, signaling to the footmen, and nervously glancing from the clock to the door through which the prince would enter. Prince Andrei was studying a large gilt frame, new to him, containing the Bolkonsky family tree, which hung across from another such frame with a crudely painted portrait — clearly by the estate's own artist — of a ruling prince in a crown, allegedly descended from Rurik and ancestor of all the Bolkonskys. Prince Andrei looked at the genealogical tree, shook his head, and laughed the way you laugh at a portrait so perfectly capturing its subject that it becomes comical.
"It's just like him, isn't it?" he said to Princess Marya, who had come over to him.
Princess Marya looked at her brother in surprise. She couldn't understand what he found funny. Everything their father did inspired her with reverence and was beyond question.
"Everyone has their Achilles' heel," Prince Andrei continued. "Imagine — with that powerful mind, indulging in something like this!"

Princess Marya couldn't grasp her brother's bold criticism and was about to respond when the expected footsteps were heard from the study. The prince entered quickly and jauntily, as if deliberately contrasting his brisk manner with the stiff formality of the house. At that moment the great clock struck two, and another clock with a higher tone chimed in from the drawing room. The prince stood still; his lively, glittering eyes, beneath their thick bushy brows, sternly scanned everyone present and came to rest on the little princess. She felt what courtiers feel when the tsar enters — that mixture of awe and respect the old man inspired in everyone around him. He stroked her hair and then patted her somewhat awkwardly on the back of the neck.
"I'm glad — glad to see you," he said, looking intently into her eyes. Then he went quickly to his place and sat down. "Sit down, sit down! You too, Mikhail Ivanovich!"
He indicated a place beside him for his daughter-in-law. A footman pulled out her chair.
"Ho ho!" said the old man, casting his eyes over her rounded figure. "You've been in a hurry. That's not good!"
He laughed in his usual dry, cold, unpleasant way — a laugh of the lips, not the eyes.
"You need to walk — walk as much as you can. As much as possible," he said.

The little princess either didn't hear or didn't want to hear his words. She sat silent and seemed flustered. The prince asked about her father, and she began to smile and talk. He asked about mutual acquaintances, and she grew more animated, chattering away, passing along greetings and retelling Moscow gossip.
"Countess Apraksina, poor thing, has lost her husband — she's cried her eyes out," she said, becoming livelier by the minute.
As she grew more animated, the prince watched her with increasing sternness, and then, as if he had studied her enough and formed a clear impression, he turned away and addressed Mikhail Ivanovich.

"Well, Mikhail Ivanovich, our Bonaparte is going to have a rough time of it. Prince Andrei" — he always referred to his son this way — "has been telling me what forces are being assembled against him! While you and I never thought much of him."

Mikhail Ivanovich had no idea when "you and I" had ever said such things about Bonaparte, but understanding that he was being used as a launching pad for the prince's favorite topic, he looked curiously at the young prince, wondering what would come next.
"He's a great tactician!" the prince said to his son, pointing at the architect.

The conversation turned again to the war, to Bonaparte, and to the generals and statesmen of the day. The old prince seemed convinced not only that all the men of the current era were mere children who didn't know the ABCs of war or politics, and that Bonaparte was an insignificant little Frenchman who had succeeded only because there were no longer any Potemkins or Suvorovs to oppose him — but also that there were no real political difficulties in Europe and no real war at all, just a kind of puppet show where today's leaders were playing at doing something important. Prince Andrei cheerfully endured his father's mockery of the new generation and drew him on, listening with evident pleasure.
"The past always looks good," he said. "But didn't Suvorov himself fall into a trap set by Moreau, from which he didn't know how to escape?"

"Who told you that? Who?" the prince shouted. "Suvorov!" He shoved his plate away so hard that Tikhon had to lunge to catch it. "Suvorov! Consider, Prince Andrei — there were two men: Frederick and Suvorov. And Moreau! Moreau would have been a prisoner if Suvorov had had a free hand. But he was hamstrung by those damned war-council bureaucrats. It would have baffled the devil himself! If Suvorov couldn't handle them, what chance does Mikhail Kutuzov have? No, my boy," he continued, "you and your generals won't manage Bonaparte on your own. You'll have to bring in the French so that birds of a feather can fight together. They've sent the German Pahlen to America to fetch the Frenchman Moreau," he said, referring to the invitation extended that year for Moreau to enter Russian service. "Extraordinary! Were the Potemkins, Suvorovs, and Orlovs German? No, my boy — either you've all lost your minds or I've outlived mine. God help you, and we'll see what happens. Bonaparte has become a great commander in their eyes! Hmph!"
"I'm not saying all the plans are good," said Prince Andrei. "I'm only surprised at your view of Bonaparte. Laugh all you want, but Bonaparte is a great general all the same."

"Mikhail Ivanovich!" the old prince called to the architect, who was busy with his roast meat and hoping he had been forgotten. "Didn't I tell you Bonaparte was a great tactician? And look — he says the same thing."
"Certainly, Your Excellency," replied the architect.
The prince laughed his cold laugh again.

"Bonaparte was born lucky. He has splendid soldiers. Besides, he started out fighting Germans. And any fool can beat the Germans. They've never beaten anyone — except each other. He made his reputation fighting them."

The prince then launched into a catalogue of all the blunders that, in his view, Bonaparte had committed in both his military campaigns and his politics. His son offered no rebuttal, but it was clear that no argument, however strong, could make either of them change his opinion. Prince Andrei listened without responding, privately wondering how this old man — living alone in the country for so many years — could know and analyze all the latest European military and political developments with such precision and insight.

"You think I'm an old man who doesn't understand the modern world?" his father concluded. "But it worries me. I don't sleep at night because of it. So tell me — where has this great commander of yours shown his genius?"
"That would take too long to explain," his son answered.
"Well then, go to your Bonaparte! Mademoiselle Bourienne, here's another admirer of your powder-monkey emperor," he exclaimed in excellent French. [speaking in French]
"You know, Prince, I am not a Bonapartist!"
"God knows when he'll return," the prince hummed, out of tune, and with an even more out-of-tune laugh, he left the table. [speaking in French]

The little princess had sat through the entire discussion and the rest of dinner in silence, glancing with a frightened look now at her father-in-law, now at Princess Marya. When they rose from the table, she took her sister-in-law's arm and drew her into another room.
"What a clever man your father is," she said. "Perhaps that's why I'm so afraid of him."
"Oh, but he's so kind!" Princess Marya answered.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter XXVIII
paragraphs: Prince Andrei was to leave the following evening. The old prince, not altering his routine, retired as usual after dinner. The little princess was in her sister-in-law's room. Prince Andrei, wearing a traveling coat without epaulettes, had been packing with his valet in his assigned rooms. After inspecting the carriage himself and watching the trunks loaded in, he ordered the horses harnessed. Only his personal items remained in the room: a small box, a large canteen fitted with silver plate, two Turkish pistols, and a saber — a gift from his father, who had brought it from the siege of Ochakov. All of Prince Andrei's traveling gear was in excellent condition: new, clean, and in cloth cases carefully tied with tape.

When setting out on a journey or changing their way of life, people capable of reflection tend to be in a serious frame of mind. At such moments one reviews the past and plans for the future. Prince Andrei's face looked very thoughtful and tender. With his hands clasped behind him he paced briskly from corner to corner, looking straight ahead and shaking his head pensively. Was he afraid of going to war, or sad about leaving his wife? Perhaps both — but clearly he didn't want to be seen in this mood, because when he heard footsteps in the corridor, he quickly unclasped his hands, stopped at a table as if adjusting a box cover, and assumed his usual calm, impenetrable expression. It was Princess Marya's heavy tread he had heard.

"I hear you've ordered the horses!" she cried, out of breath — she had apparently been running. "And I so wanted one more private talk with you! God knows how long we'll be apart. You're not angry that I came? You've changed so much, Andrusha," she added, as if to explain the question.
She smiled as she spoke his pet name, "Andrusha." It was clearly strange to her that this stern, handsome man could be Andrusha — the skinny, mischievous boy who had been her childhood playmate.
"Where is Lise?" he asked, answering her question only with a smile.

"She was so tired she fell asleep on the sofa in my room. Oh, Andrei! What a treasure you have in your wife," she said, settling onto the sofa across from her brother. "She's like a child — such a sweet, cheerful child. I've grown so fond of her."
Prince Andrei was silent, but the princess noticed an ironic, even contemptuous look flicker across his face.

"One should be indulgent of small weaknesses — who is free of them, Andrei? Don't forget she was raised in society, so her position now is hardly rosy. We should try to understand everyone's situation. To understand all is to forgive all. Think what it must be like for her, poor thing — after the life she's used to — to be separated from her husband and left alone in the country, in her condition! It's very hard." [speaking in French]
* To understand all is to forgive all.
Prince Andrei smiled at his sister the way we smile at people we think we thoroughly understand.
"You live in the country and don't find it terrible," he replied.

"That's different. Why talk about me? I don't want another life and couldn't have one — I've never known anything else. But think, Andrei — for a young society woman to be buried in the country during the best years of her life, completely alone. Papa is always busy, and I — well, you know what poor resources I have for entertaining a woman accustomed to the best society. There's only Mademoiselle Bourienne..."
"I don't like your Mademoiselle Bourienne at all," said Prince Andrei.

"Really? She's very nice and kind, and above all she deserves pity — she has no one, no one at all. To tell the truth, I don't need her, and she even gets in my way. You know I've always been something of a hermit, and even more so now. I like being alone... Father is very fond of her. She and Mikhail Ivanovich are the two people he's always gentle and kind to, because he's been their benefactor. As Sterne says: 'We love people not so much for the good they've done us, as for the good we've done them.' Father took her in when she was left homeless after losing her own father. She's very good-natured, and Father likes her reading. She reads to him in the evenings — beautifully."
"To be perfectly honest, Masha, I imagine Father's temperament sometimes makes things difficult for you?" Prince Andrei asked suddenly.
Princess Marya was first surprised, then horrified by the question.
"For me? Difficult for me?" she said.
"He was always somewhat harsh, and now I should think he's becoming very trying," said Prince Andrei, apparently speaking lightly about their father in order to test his sister.

"You are good in every way, Andrei, but you have a kind of intellectual pride," said the princess, following her own train of thought rather than the conversation, "and that is a great sin. How can one judge Father? Even if one could, what feeling but reverence could a man like him inspire? I am so content and happy with him. I only wish all of you were as happy as I am."
Her brother shook his head skeptically.

"The only thing that's hard for me — I'll tell you honestly, Andrei — is Father's attitude toward religion. I can't understand how a man of his immense intellect can't see what's as clear as day, and can go so far astray. That's the only thing that makes me unhappy. But even here I've noticed a slight improvement lately. His sarcasm has been less sharp, and he received a monk and had a long conversation with him."
"Well, my dear, I'm afraid you and your monk are wasting your powder," Prince Andrei said teasingly but tenderly.
"Oh, my dear! I only pray, and I trust God hears me. Andrei..." she said hesitantly after a moment's silence, "I have a great favor to ask of you."
"What is it, dear?"

"No — first promise you won't refuse! It will be no trouble, and it's nothing unworthy of you — but it would comfort me so much. Promise, Andrusha!" she said, putting her hand in her bag but not yet taking out what she held, as if the object itself were the request and shouldn't be shown before the promise was given.
She looked timidly at her brother.
"Even if it were a great deal of trouble..." Prince Andrei replied, as though guessing what it was.

"Think what you like! I know you're just like Father. Think what you like — but do this for my sake! Please! Father's father — our grandfather — wore it in every one of his wars." She still hadn't taken the object from her bag. "Do you promise?"
"Of course. What is it?"
"Andrei, I want to bless you with this icon, and you must promise me you'll never take it off. Do you promise?"

"If it doesn't weigh a hundred pounds and won't break my neck... To make you happy..." said Prince Andrei. But noticing immediately the pained expression his joke had brought to his sister's face, he caught himself and added: "I'm glad — really, dear, I'm very glad."

"Against your will He will save you, have mercy on you, and bring you to Himself, for in Him alone are truth and peace," she said in a voice trembling with emotion, solemnly holding up before her brother in both hands a small, oval, antique icon of the Savior with a dark face in a gold setting, on a delicately wrought silver chain.
She crossed herself, kissed the icon, and handed it to Andrei.
"Please, Andrei — for my sake!"

Rays of gentle light shone from her large, timid eyes. Those eyes lit up her entire thin, sickly face and made it beautiful. Her brother was about to take the icon, but she stopped him. Andrei understood — he crossed himself and kissed it. His face showed tenderness, for he was genuinely moved, but also a glint of irony.
"Thank you, my dear." She kissed him on the forehead and sat back down on the sofa. They were quiet for a moment.

"As I was saying, Andrei — be kind and generous, the way you always used to be. Don't judge Lise too harshly," she began. "She is so sweet, so good-hearted, and her position right now is very difficult."
"I don't think I've complained about my wife to you, Masha, or blamed her. Why are you saying all this?"
Red patches appeared on Princess Marya's face and she fell silent, as if she felt guilty.
"I haven't said anything to you, but someone else has been talking to you. And that makes me sorry," he went on.

The red patches deepened on her forehead, neck, and cheeks. She tried to speak but couldn't. Her brother had guessed correctly: the little princess had been crying after dinner and had spoken of her fears about the birth, of how terrified she was, and had complained about her fate, her father-in-law, and her husband. After crying, she had fallen asleep. Prince Andrei felt sorry for his sister.

"Know this, Masha: I cannot reproach my wife, have never reproached her, and never will — and I cannot reproach myself with anything toward her either. That will always be so, whatever circumstances I find myself in. But if you want the truth... if you want to know whether I'm happy? No. Is she happy? No. But why this is so, I don't know..."

As he said this, he stood up, went to his sister, and stooping, kissed her forehead. His fine eyes lit up with a thoughtful, kind brightness that was unusual for him, but he was looking not at his sister but over her head, into the darkness of the open doorway.

"Let's go to her — I need to say goodbye. Or you go ahead and wake her — I'll come in a moment. Petrushka!" he called to his valet. "Come here, take these things. Put this on the seat, and this one on the right."

Princess Marya rose and walked to the door, then stopped and said: "Andrei, if you had faith, you would have turned to God and asked Him to give you the love you don't feel — and your prayer would have been answered."
"Maybe so!" said Prince Andrei. "Go on, Masha — I'll come right away."

On his way to his sister's room, along the passage connecting one wing to the other, Prince Andrei ran into Mademoiselle Bourienne, smiling sweetly. It was the third time that day she had met him in a secluded hallway with the same rapturous, artless smile.
"Oh! I thought you were in your room," she said, for some reason blushing and dropping her eyes.

Prince Andrei looked at her sternly. An expression of anger suddenly crossed his face. He said nothing but stared at her forehead and hair without meeting her eyes, with such contempt that the Frenchwoman turned red and walked away without a word. When he reached his sister's room, his wife was already awake, and her cheerful voice — one word tumbling after another — came through the open door. She was speaking in French, as always, and as if after long restraint she was trying to make up for lost time.
"No, but imagine old Countess Zubova — with false curls and her mouth full of false teeth, as if she were trying to cheat old age! Ha ha ha! Marya!" [speaking in French]

Prince Andrei had already heard this same sentence about Countess Zubova, accompanied by this same laugh, from his wife some five times in the presence of others. He entered the room quietly. The little princess, plump and rosy, was sitting in an armchair with her needlework, chattering nonstop, recycling Petersburg anecdotes and even recycled phrases. Prince Andrei came over, stroked her hair, and asked if she felt rested from the journey. She answered and went on chattering.

The coach and six horses stood waiting at the porch. It was an autumn night — so dark the coachman couldn't see the pole. Servants holding lanterns bustled about the entrance. The enormous house blazed with light from its tall windows. The household servants had gathered in the hall to say goodbye to the young prince. All the family were assembled in the reception room: Mikhail Ivanovich, Mademoiselle Bourienne, Princess Marya, and the little princess. Prince Andrei had been summoned to his father's study — the old man wanted to say goodbye privately. Everyone waited for them to emerge.
When Prince Andrei entered the study, the old man sat at the table in his nighttime spectacles and white dressing gown — the outfit in which he received no one but his son — writing. He glanced up.
"Going?" And he went on writing.
"I've come to say goodbye."
"Kiss me here," he said, touching his cheek. "Thank you, thank you!"
"What are you thanking me for?"

"For not dawdling, for not clinging to a woman's apron strings. Duty comes first. Thank you!" And he continued writing, his quill sputtering and squeaking. "If you have anything to say, say it. I can do two things at once," he added.
"About my wife... I'm already embarrassed to be leaving her with you..."
"Why talk nonsense? Say what you mean."
"When her time comes, send to Moscow for a doctor. Have him here..."
The old prince stopped writing and fixed his stern gaze on his son, as if not understanding.

"I know that no one can help if nature doesn't do her work," said Prince Andrei, clearly flustered. "I know that out of a million cases, only one goes wrong. But it's what she wants, and what I want too. She's been hearing things. She had a dream, and she's frightened."
"Hmm... hmm..." the old man muttered, finishing what he was writing. "I'll take care of it."
He signed with a flourish and suddenly turned to his son with a laugh.
"Bad business, eh?"
"What is, Father?"
"The wife!" the old prince said — briefly and pointedly.
"I don't understand," said Prince Andrei.
"Nothing to be done about it, my boy," the old prince said. "They're all the same — you can't unmarry them. Don't worry, I won't tell anyone. But you know it yourself."
He seized his son's hand with his small bony fingers, shook it, stared straight into his son's face with his keen eyes — eyes that seemed to see right through him — and laughed his cold laugh again.

The son sighed — silently acknowledging that his father had understood him. The old man went on folding and sealing his letter, snatching up and tossing aside the wax, the seal, and the paper with his usual speed.
"What can you do? She's pretty! I'll handle everything. Set your mind at ease," he said in clipped phrases as he sealed the letter.
Andrei didn't reply. He was both glad and uneasy that his father had read him so well. The old man stood and handed his son the letter.

"Listen!" he said. "Don't worry about your wife — whatever can be done will be done. Now listen: give this letter to Mikhail Illarionovich." He meant Kutuzov. "I've written asking him to use you properly and not keep you too long as an adjutant — that's a bad position! Tell him I remember him and am fond of him. And write to me about how he receives you. If he's good, serve him. Nikolai Bolkonsky's son doesn't need to serve under anyone who's in disgrace. Now come here."
*Kutuzov.

He spoke so fast he barely finished half his words, but his son was used to understanding him. He led him to the desk, raised the lid, pulled out a drawer, and took out an exercise book filled with his bold, tall, cramped handwriting.

"I'll probably die before you. Remember — these are my memoirs. Hand them to the Emperor after my death. Now here's a bond and a letter: it's a prize for whoever writes a history of Suvorov's wars. Send it to the Academy. And here are some notes for you to read when I'm gone. You'll find them useful."
Andrei didn't tell his father that he would no doubt live a long time yet. He felt he couldn't say it.
"I'll do everything, Father," he said.

"Well then — goodbye!" He held out his hand to be kissed and embraced his son. "Remember this, Prince Andrei: if they kill you, it will hurt me — your old father..." He paused unexpectedly, then suddenly, in a cracked, querulous voice, cried out: "But if I ever hear that you did not conduct yourself as a son of Nikolai Bolkonsky should, I will be ashamed!"
"You didn't need to say that, Father," the son said with a smile.
The old man was silent.

"There's something else I wanted to ask," Prince Andrei continued. "If I'm killed, and if I have a son — don't let him be taken from you, as I mentioned yesterday. Let him grow up with you... Please."
"Not let the wife have him?" said the old man with a laugh.
They stood facing each other in silence. The old man's sharp eyes were fixed on his son's. Something twitched in the lower part of the old prince's face.
"We've said our goodbyes. Go!" he shouted suddenly, in a loud, angry voice, and flung the door open.

"What is it? What happened?" both princesses exclaimed when they caught a glimpse of Prince Andrei at the door and behind him the figure of the old man in his white dressing gown, spectacles and wigless, shouting angrily.
Prince Andrei sighed and gave no answer.
"Well!" he said, turning to his wife.
And that "well" sounded coldly ironic, as if he were saying: "Now put on your performance."
"Andrei — already!" said the little princess, turning pale and looking at her husband with dismay.
He embraced her. She cried out and fell unconscious against his shoulder.
He carefully freed the shoulder she was leaning on, looked into her face, and gently placed her in an armchair.
"Goodbye, Marya," he said softly to his sister, taking her hand and kissing it, and then he walked out of the room with quick steps.

The little princess lay in the armchair while Mademoiselle Bourienne rubbed her temples. Princess Marya, supporting her sister-in-law, still watched the door through which Prince Andrei had gone, her beautiful eyes brimming with tears, and crossed herself in his direction. From the study, like pistol shots, came the repeated sound of the old man angrily blowing his nose. Prince Andrei had barely gone when the study door flew open and the stern figure of the old man in the white dressing gown appeared.
"Gone? Well, that's that!" he said. And glancing angrily at the unconscious little princess, he shook his head reproachfully and slammed the door.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter I
paragraphs: In October 1805, a Russian army was occupying the villages and towns of the Archduchy of Austria, while still more regiments, freshly arrived from Russia, were settling near the fortress of Braunau and burdening the local inhabitants on whom they were billeted. Braunau was the headquarters of the commander in chief, Kutuzov.

On October 11, 1805, one of the infantry regiments that had just reached Braunau had halted half a mile from the town, waiting to be inspected by the commander in chief. Despite the un-Russian look of the surroundings — fruit gardens, stone fences, tiled roofs, and hills in the distance — and despite the fact that the local people gazing curiously at the soldiers were not Russian, the regiment looked exactly like any Russian regiment preparing for inspection anywhere in the heart of Russia.

The previous evening, an order had come that the commander in chief would inspect the regiment during its march. Although the wording was unclear and the question arose of whether the troops should appear in marching order or dress uniform, the battalion commanders consulted and decided to present the regiment in parade order, on the principle that it's always better to bow too low than not low enough. So the soldiers, after a twenty-mile march, were kept up all night mending and cleaning without a moment's sleep, while adjutants and company commanders calculated and recounted. By morning, the regiment — instead of the straggling, disorderly crowd it had been on yesterday's march — presented a well-ordered formation of two thousand men, each knowing his place and his duty, every button and strap in position, everything gleaming with cleanliness. Not just the exterior was in order: had the commander in chief chosen to look beneath the uniforms, he would have found on every man a clean shirt, and in every knapsack the required number of items — "awl, soap, and all," as the soldiers say. There was only one problem no one could do anything about: the boots. More than half the men's boots had holes. This was not the regiment commander's fault — despite repeated requests, the Austrian commissariat had failed to issue replacements, and the regiment had marched some seven hundred miles.

The regimental commander was an elderly, short-tempered, heavyset general with grizzled eyebrows and whiskers, broader from chest to back than across the shoulders. He wore a brand-new uniform still showing its fold creases and thick gold epaulettes that seemed to stand up rather than lie flat on his massive shoulders. He had the air of a man happily performing one of the most solemn duties of his life. He walked back and forth in front of the line, pulling himself up at every step, his back slightly arched. It was clear that the commander adored his regiment, took pride in it, and that his entire mind was consumed by it — yet his swagger suggested that alongside military matters, social life and the fair sex also occupied a significant place in his thoughts.

"Well, Mikhail Mitrich, sir?" he said to one of the battalion commanders, who was pressing forward with a smile. Both men were obviously in high spirits. "We had our hands full last night. Still, I think the regiment isn't bad — wouldn't you say?"
The battalion commander caught the jovial irony and laughed.
"It wouldn't be turned away even on the Tsaritsin parade ground."
"What's that?" asked the commander.
At that moment, two horsemen appeared on the road from town, where lookouts had been posted. They were an aide-de-camp followed by a Cossack.

The aide-de-camp had been sent to confirm the previous day's ambiguously worded order: the commander in chief wished to see the regiment exactly as it had been on the march — in greatcoats and packs, with no special preparation whatsoever.

A member of the Austrian War Council had visited Kutuzov the day before with proposals and demands for him to link up with the armies of Archduke Ferdinand and Mack. Kutuzov, who didn't consider this junction advisable, intended — among other arguments to support his view — to show the Austrian general the sorry state in which the troops had arrived from Russia. For this purpose he planned to meet the regiment on its march: the worse its condition, the more pleased the commander in chief would be. Although the aide-de-camp didn't know these details, he delivered the firm order that the men must be in greatcoats and marching gear, and that the commander in chief would be displeased otherwise. Hearing this, the regimental commander hung his head, silently shrugged, and spread his arms in a gesture of frustration.
"A fine mess we've made of things!" he muttered.

"There — didn't I tell you, Mikhail Mitrich? If the order said 'on the march,' it meant greatcoats!" he said reproachfully to the battalion commander. "Oh, my God!" he added, stepping forward decisively. "Company commanders!" he bellowed in a voice trained for command. "Sergeants major! How soon will he be here?" he asked the aide-de-camp, shifting to a tone of respectful deference clearly directed at the personage in question.
"In an hour, I'd say."
"Will we have time to change?"
"I don't know, General..."

The regimental commander went up to the line himself and ordered the men to change into greatcoats. The company commanders dashed off to their companies; the sergeants major started bustling about — the greatcoats weren't in the best shape — and the perfectly ordered, silent squares instantly began to sway and stretch and buzz with voices. Soldiers ran in every direction, slinging knapsacks over their shoulders, pulling straps over their heads, unbuckling overcoats and wrestling their arms through the sleeves.

Within half an hour, everything was back in order, but the squares had turned from black to gray. The regimental commander walked to the front of the formation with his jerky steps and surveyed it from a distance.
"What is this? This!" he shouted and stopped dead. "Commander of the third company!"
"Commander of the third company to the general! General wants the commander! Third company commander!" The words rippled down the line, and an adjutant ran off to find the missing officer.

When the garbled message — transformed into "The general to the third company!" — finally reached its target, the missing officer appeared from behind his company. Though a middle-aged man not given to running, he came trotting awkwardly toward the general, stumbling on his toes. The captain's face showed the anxiety of a schoolboy asked to recite a lesson he hasn't learned. Red spots appeared on his nose — the redness evidently attributable to drinking — and his mouth twitched nervously. The general looked him up and down as he arrived panting, his pace slowing as he drew near.

"You'll have them in petticoats next! What is this?" the regimental commander shouted, thrusting his chin forward and pointing at a soldier in the third company's ranks wearing a greatcoat of bluish cloth that stood out from all the others. "What have you been playing at? The commander in chief is coming and you abandon your post? Eh? I'll teach you to put your men in fancy dress for a parade! Eh...?"
The company commander, eyes fixed on his superior, pressed two fingers ever more rigidly to his cap, as if all his hopes of salvation lay in that pressure.
"Well? Why don't you answer? Who's the one dressed up like a Hungarian?" the commander demanded with a scathing sneer.
"Your Excellency..."
"Well? 'Your Excellency' what? 'Your Excellency!' Nobody knows anything!"
"Your Excellency, it's the officer Dolokhov, who has been reduced to the ranks," the captain said softly.
"Has he been demoted to field marshal or to private soldier? If he's a soldier, he wears regulation uniform like everyone else."
"Your Excellency, you gave him permission yourself, during the march."

"Permission? Permission? That's just like you young fellows," said the regimental commander, cooling down slightly. "Permission, indeed... You say one word and they..." He paused, his irritation flaring again. "I beg you to dress your men properly."

The commander turned to glance at the adjutant, then continued his jerky march down the line. He was clearly pleased with his own show of authority and, looking for further cause for outrage, walked on. After snapping at one officer for an unpolished badge and another for crooked alignment, he reached the third company.
"Ho-o-ow are you standing? Where is your leg? Your leg!" the commander shouted in a voice of pained exasperation, though there were still five men between him and Dolokhov in his bluish-gray coat.
Dolokhov slowly straightened his bent knee, staring straight at the general's face with his clear, insolent eyes.
"Why a blue coat? Off with it... Sergeant major! Change his coat... the ras—" He didn't finish.
"General, I am obliged to follow orders, but I am not obliged to endure—" Dolokhov broke in quickly.
"No talking in the ranks! No talking!"
"—insults," Dolokhov concluded, his voice loud, clear, and ringing.
The general's eyes and the soldier's met. The general fell silent, angrily yanking down his tight scarf.
"I request you to be so good as to change your coat," he said as he turned away.

chapters.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter II
paragraphs: "He's coming!" shouted the lookout at that moment.

The regimental commander, his face flushing, ran to his horse, seized the stirrup with trembling hands, threw his body across the saddle, righted himself, drew his saber, and — with a look of happy determination, his mouth slightly twisted — prepared to shout. The regiment quivered like a bird preening its feathers and went still.
"Att-en-TION!" the regimental commander thundered, in a soul-shaking voice that expressed joy for himself, sternness for the regiment, and welcome for the approaching chief.

Down the broad country road, lined with trees on both sides, came a high, light-blue Viennese carriage, creaking faintly on its springs, drawn by six horses at a brisk trot. Behind it galloped the staff and a Croat escort. Beside Kutuzov sat an Austrian general in a white uniform that looked strange among the Russian black. The carriage stopped in front of the regiment. Kutuzov and the Austrian general were speaking in low voices, and Kutuzov smiled faintly as he stepped heavily down from the carriage, as if those two thousand men holding their breath to watch him — and the regimental commander — simply didn't exist.

The command rang out, and again the regiment quivered as, with a jingling sound, it presented arms. Then in the dead silence, the feeble voice of the commander in chief was heard. The regiment roared: "Health to your Excel... lel... lency!" and silence fell again. At first Kutuzov stood still while the regiment moved past; then he and the general in white, accompanied by the staff, walked between the ranks.

From the way the regimental commander saluted the commander in chief and devoured him with his eyes, standing at obsequious attention, from the way he walked behind the generals through the ranks — leaning forward, barely restraining his jerky movements — and from the way he sprang forward at every word or gesture from the commander in chief, it was clear that he performed his subordinate duties with even more zeal than his commanding ones. Thanks to the strictness and diligence of its commander, the regiment was in excellent shape compared to others that had reached Braunau at the same time. There were only 217 sick and stragglers. Everything was in order except the boots.

Kutuzov walked through the ranks, sometimes stopping to say a friendly word to officers he had known from the Turkish war, sometimes to the soldiers. Looking at their boots, he shook his head sadly several times, pointing them out to the Austrian general with an expression that seemed to say he wasn't blaming anyone but couldn't help noticing the state of things. The regimental commander rushed forward each time, afraid of missing a single word about his regiment. Behind Kutuzov, at a distance that allowed every softly spoken word to be heard, followed about twenty men from his staff. These gentlemen talked among themselves and sometimes laughed. Closest to the commander in chief walked a handsome adjutant — this was Prince Bolkonsky. Beside him was his comrade Nesvitsky, a tall, extremely stout staff officer with a kind, smiling, handsome face and moist eyes. Nesvitsky could barely contain his laughter, provoked by a dark-complexioned hussar officer walking beside him. This hussar, keeping a perfectly straight face without the slightest change of expression, watched the regimental commander's back and mimicked his every movement. Each time the commander lurched forward, the hussar lurched forward in precisely the same way. Nesvitsky laughed and elbowed the others to look at the comedian.

Kutuzov walked slowly and languidly past thousands of eyes bulging from their sockets to watch their chief. When he reached the third company, he suddenly stopped. His staff, caught off guard, involuntarily pressed closer.
"Ah, Timokhin!" he said, recognizing the red-nosed captain who had been scolded over the blue greatcoat.

You would have thought it impossible for a man to stretch himself taller than Timokhin had during the regimental commander's scolding, but now, with the commander in chief addressing him, he drew himself up to such an extent that it seemed he couldn't have held the pose a moment longer. Kutuzov clearly understood and wished him well — he quickly turned away, a barely perceptible smile flickering across his scarred, puffy face.
"Another Ismail comrade," he said. "A brave officer! Are you happy with him?" he asked the regimental commander.
The latter — unaware he was being reflected like a mirror by the hussar officer behind him — started, stepped forward, and answered: "Highly satisfied, Your Excellency!"
"We all have our weaknesses," Kutuzov said with a smile as he walked on. "He used to have a fondness for Bacchus."

The regimental commander, afraid of being blamed for this, said nothing. The hussar, meanwhile, noticed the red-nosed captain's face and his sucked-in belly, and mimicked his expression and posture with such precision that Nesvitsky couldn't help laughing. Kutuzov turned around. The officer clearly had complete control of his face and, in the instant it took Kutuzov to turn, managed to pull a grimace and then snap into the most serious, respectful, and innocent expression imaginable.
The third company was the last, and Kutuzov paused, apparently trying to recall something. Prince Andrei stepped forward from the staff and said in French: [speaking in French]
"You asked me to remind you about the officer Dolokhov, reduced to the ranks in this regiment."
"Where is Dolokhov?" Kutuzov asked.

Dolokhov, who had already changed into a soldier's gray greatcoat, didn't wait to be called. The well-built figure of the fair-haired soldier, with his clear blue eyes, stepped forward from the ranks, approached the commander in chief, and presented arms.
"Do you have a complaint to make?" Kutuzov asked with a slight frown.
"This is Dolokhov," said Prince Andrei.
"Ah!" said Kutuzov. "I hope this has been a lesson for you. Do your duty. The Emperor is merciful, and I won't forget you if you earn it."

The clear blue eyes met the commander in chief's gaze with the same boldness they had shown the regimental commander — as if their expression could rip apart the veil of protocol that separates a commander in chief from a common soldier.

"I ask one thing of Your Excellency," Dolokhov said in his firm, clear, deliberate voice. "I ask for an opportunity to make amends for my offense and prove my devotion to His Majesty the Emperor and to Russia!"

Kutuzov turned away. The same fleeting eye-smile he had shown Captain Timokhin crossed his face. He turned with a slight grimace, as if to say that everything Dolokhov had told him — and everything he could tell him — had long been known, that he was weary of it, and that it was not at all what he wanted. He walked back to his carriage.
The regiment broke into companies and headed for their assigned quarters near Braunau, where they hoped to receive boots and clothing and to rest after their grueling march.

"You won't hold it against me, Prokhor Ignatych?" said the regimental commander, riding up to Captain Timokhin as the third company headed for its quarters. The commander's face, now that the inspection was safely over, was beaming with irrepressible delight. "It's the Emperor's service... can't be helped... sometimes one gets a bit carried away on parade... I'm the first to apologize — you know me! And he was very pleased!" He held out his hand to the captain.
"Don't mention it, General — as if I'd dare!" replied the captain, his nose growing redder as he smiled, showing where two front teeth were missing — knocked out by a rifle butt at Ismail.
"And do tell Mr. Dolokhov I haven't forgotten him — he can rest easy. And tell me, please — I've been meaning to ask — how is he behaving? In general..."
"As far as the service goes, he's very correct, Your Excellency. But his character..." Timokhin said.
"What about his character?" the commander asked.
"It varies from day to day," the captain answered. "One day he's sensible, well-mannered, and kind. The next he's a wild animal. In Poland, if you can believe it, he nearly killed a Jew."
"Well, well," the commander remarked. "Still, one must feel for a young man in trouble. He has important connections, you know... So just..."
"I understand, Your Excellency," said Timokhin, his smile showing he had caught his commander's drift.
"Well, of course, of course!"
The regimental commander found Dolokhov in the ranks and, reining in his horse, said to him:
"After the next action — epaulettes."
Dolokhov looked up but said nothing. The mocking smile on his lips didn't change.

"Well, that's settled then," the commander continued. "A round of vodka for the men — on me!" he added loud enough for the soldiers to hear. "Thank you all! God be praised!" And he rode on past the company to catch up with the next.
"He really is a decent fellow — you can serve under him," Timokhin said to the subaltern beside him.
"In a word — a real King of Hearts," the subaltern said with a laugh. (The regimental commander's nickname was King of Hearts.)
The officers' cheerful mood after the inspection was contagious. The company marched on gaily. Soldiers' voices could be heard on every side.
"They said Kutuzov is blind in one eye?"
"He is! Completely blind!"
"No, friend — he's sharper-eyed than you. Boots and leg wrappings... he noticed everything..."
"When he looked at my feet, friend... well, I thought to myself..."
"And that other one with him, the Austrian — he looked like someone had smeared him with chalk. White as flour! I bet they polish him up like they polish the guns."
"Hey, Fedeshon! Did he say when the fighting starts? You were standing right near him. They all said Bonaparte himself is at Braunau."

"Bonaparte himself! Listen to this idiot — the things he doesn't know! The Prussians are in revolt now. The Austrians are putting them down, see. Once they're dealt with, the war against Bonaparte starts. And he says Bonaparte's in Braunau! You really are a fool. You ought to listen more carefully!"
"Damn quartermasters! Look — the fifth company is already turning into the village. They'll have their porridge cooked before we even reach our quarters."
"Give me a biscuit, you devil!"
"And did you give me any tobacco yesterday? That's just it, friend! Ah well, never mind — here you go."
"They ought to call a halt here, or it'll be another four miles without food."
"Wasn't it nice when those Germans gave us rides! You just sit there and they carry you along."
"And here, friend, the people are really poor. Back there they were all Poles — under the Russian crown — but here they're all proper Germans."
"Singers to the front!" came the captain's order.

About twenty men ran to the head of the column from various ranks. The lead singer, a drummer, turned to face the others and, with a flourish of his arm, launched into a long, drawn-out soldiers' song beginning with the words "Morning dawned, the sun was rising" and ending with "On then, brothers, on to glory, led by Father Kamensky." This song had been written during the Turkish campaign and was now being sung in Austria — the only change being that "Father Kamensky" had been replaced with "Father Kutuzov."

Having jerked out the last words in the military fashion and swept his arms as if hurling something to the ground, the drummer — a lean, handsome soldier of about forty — looked sternly at the singers and narrowed his eyes. Satisfied that all eyes were on him, he raised both arms as if carefully lifting some invisible but precious object above his head, held it there for a few seconds, then suddenly flung it down and began:
"Oh, my bower, oh my bower...!"

"Oh, my bower new...!" twenty voices joined in. The castanet player, despite the weight of his gear, rushed out front and walked backward before the company, jerking his shoulders and brandishing his castanets as if threatening someone. The soldiers, swinging their arms and keeping time instinctively, marched with long, easy strides. Behind the company came the sound of wheels, the creak of springs, and the clatter of hooves. Kutuzov and his staff were heading back to town. The commander in chief signaled for the men to continue marching at ease, and he and everyone in his retinue showed visible pleasure at the singing, the dancing soldier, and the cheerful, smartly marching troops. In the second file from the right flank — the side the carriage passed — a blue-eyed soldier drew attention without trying. It was Dolokhov, marching with particular grace and confidence in time with the song, looking at the passing dignitaries as if he pitied anyone who wasn't marching with the company at that moment. The hussar cornet from Kutuzov's staff who had been mimicking the regimental commander dropped back from the carriage and rode up to Dolokhov.

Hussar cornet Zherkov had once belonged to Dolokhov's wild circle back in Petersburg. Having encountered Dolokhov abroad as a common soldier, Zherkov hadn't seen fit to acknowledge him. But now that Kutuzov had personally spoken to the demoted officer, he addressed him with the warmth of an old friend.
"My dear fellow, how are you?" he called through the singing, keeping his horse in step with the company.
"How am I?" Dolokhov answered coldly. "As you can see."
The lively song gave a special edge to Zherkov's easy, carefree tone and to the deliberate coldness of Dolokhov's reply.
"How do you get along with the officers?" Zherkov asked.
"Fine. They're good men. And how did you worm your way onto the staff?"
"I was assigned. I'm on duty."
Both fell silent.

"She let the hawk fly upward from her wide right sleeve," the song continued, stirring an involuntary sense of courage and high spirits. Their conversation would probably have gone differently without that song.
"Is it true the Austrians have been beaten?" Dolokhov asked.
"The devil only knows. They say so."
"Good," Dolokhov answered — brief, clear, and sharp, as the song seemed to demand.
"Come by some evening — we'll have a game of faro!" said Zherkov.
"What, do you have too much money?"
"Do come."
"I can't. I've sworn off. I won't drink and I won't gamble until I'm reinstated."
"Well, that'll only last until the first battle."
"We'll see."
They were silent again.
"Stop by if you need anything. One can be useful on the staff, at least..."
Dolokhov smiled. "Don't bother. If I need something, I won't ask — I'll take it."
"Well, I was only..."
"And I was only..."
"Goodbye."
"Stay well..."
"It's a long, long way — to my native land..."

Zherkov touched his spurs to his horse; it pranced excitedly, unsure which foot to lead with, then settled into a gallop. He passed the company and caught up with the carriage, still keeping time to the song.
